en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Text on the Accomplishment of Methods 1.
The Section on Perception, etc.
I pay proper homage to the Buddha,
who grants the fulfillment of wishes,
and to the Dhamma, which bestows welfare like a jewel; [this is] the introduction to the beginning of the book, *Siddhamattha*.
Having respectfully bowed to the Saṅgha, the accomplishment of this work is now declared.
The power of Moggallāna in grammar and the Piṭakas—how utterly he has transcended all poetic artifice! Oh, how truly marvelous!
For it was said by the ancient masters of the Sinhalese tradition:
"Whatever power resides in Pāṇini, and in Candra, Kātyāyana, and the others—
that very power I consider to be embodied here, taking the form of Moggallāyana."
The *Sutta* and the *Vutti* were composed by that very same person, and the *Pañcikā* was also made by him alone;
therefore, its treatise is considered well-composed and most beautiful.
Within it, the *Sutta* should be understood as being of two kinds, according to the distinction between the action (*kamma*) and the meaning (*attha*).
Having clearly explained the first [section] by means of the word "tesu" and so forth, and the second in its threefold manner— making it very lucid, easy to understand,
and concise— listen with concentrated minds as I expound it with a pervasive flow.
1. The forty-three consonants (*vaṇṇa*).
The forty-three phonemes (*akkhara*) beginning with *a* and ending with the *niggahīta* (the nasal stop) are called consonants. They are as follows:
Dha, na, pa, pha, ba, bha, ma; ya, ra, la, va, sa, ha, ḷa, aṃ. By this [rule], what is the purpose of the statement “*e o naṃ vaṇṇe*”?
The expression “forty-three” (*titālīsa*) indicates that in some instances there is an elision of syllables (*vaṇṇalopa*); by this, forms such as “*paṭisaṅkhā yoniso*” are established.

Those whose beginning is delimited by the letter *a* are called “*a-ādayo*” (those beginning with *a*). “Forty-three” (*titālīsa*) means three and forty; or, by this irregular formation (*nipātana*), there is an elision of the fourth part (*catabhāgalopa*). They are called “syllables” (*vaṇṇā*) because meaning (*attha*) is expressed (*vaṇṇīyati*) by them.

Here it is asked: "Why, unlike the Ācariya-Kaccāyana and others, was the designation *akkhara* (syllable) not applied to forty-one phonemes, but instead the designation *vaṇṇa* (letter/phoneme) applied to forty-three? It is said in reply:
"That is the Māgadhī root-language, by which men are poets, by which the Brahmins speak their sacred texts, and by which even the Fully Enlightened Ones spoke."
According to the Magadha tradition, here [the term *vacana*] is better understood as follows:
even in cases such as *seyyo*, *oṭṭho*, and *sotthi*, there is a string of forty-three syllables that pervades everything without exception, which possesses the quality of being straight and upright.

However, it is not the case that a term for a whole is applied to its parts—as in "trees are a forest"—nor is a term for a part applied to the whole—as in "the ocean was seen by me. To demonstrate this, the designation of *vaṇṇa* (phoneme) is made for each individual unit.
“Attentive listening is the attainment of the Buddha’s teaching,” and because it has been said, “For when there is a corruption of syllables—
such as through laxity or harshness— the meaning becomes difficult to discern. Therefore, a wise person,
properly attending upon the teacher with the five qualities beginning with exertion, should master the phonemes.

In this regard, the sequence of the vowels beginning with *a* is dependent upon the order of the places of articulation (*ṭhāna*) and so forth. For it is through the places, instruments (*karaṇa*), and efforts (*payatana*) that phonemes (*vaṇṇa*) are produced. Therein, there are six places of articulation:

by way of the throat (*kaṇṭha*), palate (*tālu*), head (*muddha*), teeth (*danta*), lips (*oṭṭha*), and nose (*nāsikā*). Among these, the throat is the place for the vowel *a*, the *ka*-group, and the *ha* consonant;

the palate for the *i*-vowel, the *ca*-group, and the *ya* consonant; the head for the *ṭa*-group, *ra*, and *ḷa*; the teeth for the *ta*-group, *la*, and *sa*; the lips for the *u*-vowel and the *pa*-group; and both the throat and the palate for the *e*-vowel. *O*... [and so on].
The throat is the place of articulation for the letter *va*; the teeth are the place of articulation for the letter *va*; the nose is the place of articulation for the *niggahīta* (anusvāra);
and for *ṅa*, *ñña*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *māna*, the place of articulation is their own respective places as well as the nose.
And in this regard: The letter *ha*, when joined with the fifth [consonants] and with those ending in *ṭṭha*, [is nasalized].
It should be understood as "from the heart" (*oraso*);

that which is born from the throat is not joined with it. For example: *avaṅho* (as in *avaṅa hoti*, *tañhi*, *taṇhā*, *pubbanho*, *amhe*, *guyhaṃ*, *gārayhā*, *ārulho*, *bahvakkharaṃ*). The grammatical operation (*karaṇaṃ*)—
The middle of the tongue is the source of the palate-born [sounds],
the tip of the tongue is the source of the head-born [sounds],
and the edge of the tongue is the source of the tooth-born [sounds].

That [articulation] involves the formation of the *kaṭhāna* (the point of articulation). *Payatana* is the effort for the utterance of phonemes; what is that? It is the distinction of the modes of formation such as "closed" (*saṃvuta*) and so forth:

the state of being closed for the letter *a*; the state of being open for the remaining vowels and for the letters *s* and *h*; the state of being touched (*phuṭṭha*) for the consonant groups (*vaggā*); and the state of being slightly touched (*īsaṃphuṭṭha*) for *y*, *r*, *l*, and *v*.

Thus, among the phonemes (akkhara) distinguished by their place of articulation, mode of formation, effort, audition, and time, the vowels are the supports (nissaya), while the others are supported (nissita). In this regard:
The first two [of each group] are said to be the supports, the vowels; the consonants (byañjana) are supported from them.
Within each class (vaga), the first two are the supports, the vowels; thereafter follow the place of articulation and the degree of lightness.

The term “*ādayo*” (beginning with *ā*) recurs as far as “the nasal stop (*bindu*) and the *niggahīta*. Furthermore, that [term] is connected with the locative form “*atthavasā vibhattivipariṇāmo*” (by reason of the sense, there is a change of case-ending).
The term “*vaṇṇā*” (phonemes) recurs. 2.

**The Ten Vowels:** Those ten phonemes beginning with *ā* and ending with *o*, as specified at the start, are called vowels (*sara*). They are: *a, ā; i, ī; u, ū; e, ai; o, au*. They are called *sara* because they proceed (*saranti*) with a predominant [vocalic] nature, or because they cause [the following consonants] to flow forth (*sārenti*) toward a consonant (*byañjana*).
The phrase “the ten vowels” recurs [as the subject].
3. Two by two of like quality:
In these ten beginning with *a* and so forth, there are two by two that are called “of like quality” (*savaṇṇā*), respectively. For example: *a* and *ā*, *i* and *ī*, and so on.
*u-ū*, *e-e*, *o-o*. These are similar (*samāna*) and identical (*sadisa*) vowels (*vaṇṇa*), being identical by virtue of their place of articulation (*ṭhānato*).
The phrase "two by two" carries over to the two [categories] that will be mentioned hereafter. 4.
The preceding [vowel] is short (*rassa*).
Among those same ten vowels, whichever pairs are of identical color, each preceding one is designated as short (*rassa*). For example: *a, i, u, e, o*.

Among these, in order to show that "only those preceding a consonant cluster are seen, while the last two are [long]," they are included here because of their correctness (*sādhutā*), just as in the examples *seyyo*, *oṭṭho*, and *sotthi*.
Due to their association with the duration of the short vowel, they possess the quality of ending in *-t* (as in *tabbanta*).
Or short. What is called the duration of a short vowel is a time measured by the snap of a finger or the blink of an eye;

by that measure, a short vowel has one mora (*matta*), a long vowel has two morae, and a consonant has half a mora. In Vedic meter (*chanda*), the teachers accept even one and a half morae as a short vowel. 5.
The subsequent [vowel] is long.

Among the ten vowels beginning with *ā*, those that are of the same color (*savaṇṇa*) occur in pairs; whichever one is subsequent in each pair is designated as "long" (*dīgha*). These are: *ā, ī, ū, e, o*. They are called "long" either because they possess a long duration of time or because they consist of two morae (*mātrā*).
6. Consonants (*byañjana*):
Among the [vowels] beginning with *ā*, the thirty-three consonants starting with *k* and ending with *niggahīta* (the anusvāra) are known as consonants. For example: *ka, kha, ga, gha*.
Ṅa, ca cha ja jha ña, ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa, ta tha da dha na, pa pha ba bha ma, ya ra lava sa ha ḷa aṃ.

These are called *byañjanā* because meaning (*attha*) is manifested (*byañjiyati*) by them. In the case of *ka*-letters and so forth, the letter *a* is for the purpose of pronunciation. The term "beginning with *ka*" (*kādayo*) recurs [in the subsequent rules].
7. The Five Groups of Five:
Among the vowels and so forth, the groups beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma* are called the "five groups of five" (*pañcapañcakā vaggā*). For example: *ka kha ga gha ṅa*;
*ca cha ja jha ña*; *ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa*; *ta tha da dha na*; *pa pha ba bha ma*. Thus, there are five [groups].
The measure of these is five; thus, they are "five-fives" (*pañcapañcaka*). Those beginning with *y* are called "classes" (*vagga*).
Furthermore, by virtue of their initial consonants, they receive the designations "ka-class," "ca-class," and so forth, just like the triads of wholesome states (*kusalattika*) and the like.
8. The nasal dot (*bindu*) is the *niggahīta*.
Among the vowels beginning with *a*, that sound consisting of a mere dot (*bindu*) is designated as *niggahīta*. That which is grasped and uttered in dependence upon a short vowel is *niggahīta*;

or alternatively, it is so called because the vocal organs (*karaṇa*) are restrained (*niggahetvā*). Having restrained the vocal organs, that which is spoken by the mouth without opening it is called *niggahīta*; thus it is said that the dot follows the vowels.
The designation *bahvakkhara* (many-syllable) is for the purpose of a literal designation (*anvatthasaññā*); however, *jha*, *lā*, and so forth, are conventional designations (*ruḷhīsaññā*).

Vowels (*sara*) and their corresponding consonants (*savaṇṇa*), short vowels (*rassa*), long vowels (*dīgha*), consonants (*byañjana*), the classes of consonants (*vagga*), and the *niggahīta*—this is the sequence of the rules for designations.
(The Rules for Sandhi. Conjunction (*sandhi*) is said as follows:
*loka aggapuggalo*, *paññā indriyaṃ*, *tīṇi imāni*, *no hi etaṃ*, *bhikkhunī ovādo*, *mātu upaṭṭhānaṃ*.

"Let the venerable one come together," "the sense-sphere is overcome," "I have wealth," "all [of them]," "there would be three qualities," "non-existent ones are not seen here"—in these cases, by the designation "vowel" (*sara*), there is elision of the vowel (*saro lopo sare*). 26.
*Saro lopo sare*.

A vowel (*sara*) is subject to elision (*lopanīya*). "Vowel" (*sara*) is a designation for that which undergoes the grammatical operation (*kāriya*), and "elision" (*lopa*) is a designation for the operation itself.

Elision means non-appearance or non-utterance. "Vowel" (*sara*) is stated in the singular number to denote the class (*jāti*). "In a vowel" (*sare*) is a locative case (*sattamī*) expressing immediate proximity (*opasilesika*).

Consequently, a grammatical operation does not take place when there is an intervention by a consonant (*vaṇṇa*) or time (*kāla*), as in *tva + asi* [becoming *tvamasi*] and *katamā cānanda aniccasaññā*. This applies to all instances of euphonic combination (*sandhi*).
The term "vidhi" (rule) is understood [to apply here]. 14.

In the case of the seventh case (locative), the preceding [element] functions according to the principle of the *thera-aṭṭhinī* (the Elder’s Bone); this is because of the grammatical maxim (*paribhāsa*) that a weak rule cannot serve as the basis for a strong one. This is stated in the description of the seventh case.
*Pubbasseva vidhi*: this is the elision of the preceding vowel (*pubbasaralopa*). Examples include:

*lokaggapuggalo*, *paññindriyaṃ*, *tīṇimāni*, *no hetaṃ*, *bhikkhunovādo*, *mātupaṭṭhānaṃ*, *sametāyasmā*, *abhibhāyatanaṃ*, *dhanaṃmatthi*, *sabbeva*, *tayassu dhammā*, and *asante+ttha na dissanti*.
Because the grammatical operation (*kāriya*) is prescribed for the preceding [vowel], it is indicated by the locative case (*sattamī*).
Since "otherness" (paratā) is understood [from the context], the word "other" (parā) also applies to the words of others.

Now, for whom: "perception" (saññā), "like a shadow" (chāyā iva), "also" (iti api), "you are not an ascetic" (assamaṇī asi), "the eye-faculty" (cakkhundriyaṃ), "you are ungrateful" (akataññū asi), "like in the sky" (ākāse iva), "those two also" (te api), "I salute" (vande ahaṃ), "I, he" (so ahaṃ), "these four" (cattāro ime), "an outcaste" (vasalo iti), "Moggallāna."

In *asi bījako*, what indeed is the discussion? When the elision of the preceding vowel (*pubba-sara-lopa*) has already occurred at the beginning, [the rule] “*saro lopo sare*” (a vowel is elided before a vowel) applies.
27. *Paraṃ kvaci*: A vowel following another vowel is sometimes subject to elision. As in: *yassa dāni*, *saññāti*, *chāyāva*, *itipi*, *assamaṇīsi*.
The faculty of the eye; you are ungrateful; like space; those too; I bow to them; I am he; these four; under the power of greed;
you are Moggallāna, the sower; what talk indeed; early in the morning. "Where?"—what? the faculty of wisdom; the five faculties; supreme among beings; nineteen;
for whom these [exist]; the teaching of the Sugata; the taint of views; the flood of views; the sense-base of the eye.

How can that be obtained here? The rule "conjunctions arise from the elision of vowels" (*vivakkhāto sandhayo bhavanti*) is understood; thus, the desired grammatical operation is also accomplished here.
The term *kvaci* ("sometimes") is a governing heading (*adhikāra*) for all conjunctions; therefore, there is no over-extension of the rule. (The section on Elision Conjunctions).
The phrase "or a following vowel" (*saro paro vā*) also continues to apply.
In the phrase *tassa idaṃ vāte īritaṃ*, the *vā* does not undergo elision; rather, the *ū* of *ūru* becomes *u*, as in *ati iva aññehi*.

Regarding *vi udakaṃ*, here there is elision of the preceding vowel (*pubba-saralope*). 29. *Yuvaṇṇānaṃ meo luttā*: When vowels are elided, *e* and *o* optionally replace the following *i*-vowels and *u*-vowels respectively. The rule of correspondence applies to similar sounds.

24. Because the word *vaṇṇa* follows [the word] *savaṇṇa*, by that [rule], even those [vowels] with a common phonetic quality (*savaṇṇa*) are included, as well as its own form; thus, for *ī* and *ū* as well, there is *e* and *o*.

This [term *vaṇṇa*] has been introduced here for the purpose of including long vowels as well, in every instance where a short vowel is used to designate a class (*jāti*). Of this [word *vaṇṇa*], [the forms] *vāteritaṃ* and *nopeti* are examples.
*vāmoru*, *atevaññehi*, *vodakaṃ*. These two final examples are for the purpose of negating the rule that "when *avaṇṇa* is elided, *e* and *o* [arise] only [in those cases].

[Examples: *vātveva*, *tassidaṃ*. How is it that [we get] *paccorasmiṃ*? By means of a division of the grammatical rules (*yogavibhāga*). Having analyzed *pati urasmiṃ*, the *ya*-substitute occurs by the rule "after *ya* before a vowel" (*yavā sare*);
then, by the rule "the *ca* [substitute] for *tavagga*, *varaṇa*, etc. (*tavaggavaraṇādi*), and by the rule "after *vagga* or *lasa*... (*vaggalasehi*)... [the form is established].
The term "te" [refers to] the preceding form, and by the rule "yuvaṇṇānam e o" (with the separation of the *yoga*), there is also "ussa. Why [is it said] "because of elision"? For example:

"dasa ime dhammā," "yathā idam," and "kusalassa upasampadā. Because the word "kvaci" follows as a restriction against over-extension (*atippasaṅga*), the application of the alternative rule is not fixed;
therefore, there is an alternative in cases such as "upeto" and "avecca. [Examples include: "tārakitā" and "yassindriyāni."
In such cases as *mahiddhiko*, *sabbītiyo*, *tenupasaṅkami*, and *lokuttaro*, there is no [application of] the rule (*vidhi*).

[Examples include: *paṭisanthāravutti assa*, *sabbavitti anubhūyate*, *vi añjanaṃ*, *vi ākato*, *dāsī ahaṃ*, *ahuvā pure*, *anu addhamāsaṃ*, *anu eti*, *su āgataṃ*, *su ākāro*, *du ākāro*, *cakkhu āpāthaṃ*, *bahu*.
There is an exception (*ābādha*); [the rule] "pātu akāsi" applies, but not in the case of *bhū-āpanalānilaṃ*. Here, the terms "yuvaṇṇānaṃ" and "ve" are understood [from the previous rules].
30. *Yavā sare*:
When a vowel (*sara*) follows, the semivowels *y* and *v* optionally replace the *i*-vowels and *u*-vowels respectively. As in: *paṭisanthāravutyassa*.
Everything is experienced as a syllable (*byañjana*). Regarding the explanation of syllables:

in the rule "long and short [vowels] in syllables," I shall say "long" for *dīgha*, *ahāpure*, *anvaddhamāsaṃ*, *anveti*, *svāgataṃ*, *svākāro*, *dvākāro*, *cakkhvāpāthaṃ*, *bahvābādho*, *pātvākāsi*, and *na tveva*;
and *bhvāpanalānilaṃ*. Also, *vātveva* and *viākato*; and *sāgataṃ*.
This Dhamma has been realized by me; I am your son; those five [fetters] of his have been abandoned;
those which were his, those today; as much as his body was, so much is his height; what is the point? then indeed his; I indeed today;
he, I; he today; he is just that; from whatever source; he, I—thus here, after a vowel (*yava-sare*), the particle *ve* is also understood.
30. When a vowel follows, each *e* and *o* optionally becomes *ya* and *va* respectively. Regarding the rule "long and short vowels before a consonant," [examples are]:
*adhigato kho myāyaṃ dhammo*, *putto tyāhaṃ*, *tyāssa pahīnā pañca*, *tyāhaṃ*, *yyassa*, *tyajja*.
As far as his body extends, so far extends his fathom; what is the point? Now then, regarding this:
"I am today," "I am indeed," "I myself," "just I," "on account of which," "I am indeed. "Just wind," "this is it," "that I am. In some cases indeed:
"Wealth exists," "sons exist," "they have not come," "they are not here"—these four.
“Go,” “eḷakaṃ,” “go,” “assaṃ,” and “go ajinaṃ”—here, the term “in the case of *sara*” (vowel) is understood.
32. *Gossāvaṅa*:

When followed by a vowel (*sara*), the substitution of *ava* occurs for *go*. And since that [substitution] would otherwise apply to the whole word by the rule “*ṭānubandhānekavaṇṇā sabbassā*,” the phrase “*antassā*” (of the final part) is understood.
18. *Ṅa-anubandha*:
That which has the letter *ṅa* as its *anubandha* (suffix), even if it consists of multiple phonemes, becomes [the substitute] for the vowel *o* alone.

Because of the statement, “A *saṃketa* (conventional marker) is a non-constituent *anubandha*,” there is no actual employment of the letter *ṅa*. For *anubandhas* perish immediately after being pronounced; the *anubandha* exists only for a purpose (*payojana*).
Conventional usage: *gaveḷakaṃ*, *gavāssaṃ*, *gavājinaṃ*.
Thus, in this context—36.
*vī* and *tissa* become *ve* optionally.
When the word *eva* follows, *it* optionally becomes *vo*.

And that—17. Regarding what is marked by the genitive case: whatever grammatical operation applies to that which is indicated by the genitive, it should be understood as applying to that which ends in the syllable *ta*. Thus, there is the substitution of *i* in place of the original element. In the place of the substitute...

*Ādissati* means "is substituted"; thus it is *ādesa*. Only [the substitution] of *i* occurs. Elsewhere, there is the substitution of *y*, such as in the rule “*tavaggavaraṇānaṃ ye cavaggabayañā*,” where *t* becomes *c*, and in the rule “*vaggalasehi te*,” where *y* becomes *c*; these alone [are the exceptions].

Why [does he say] *eva*? He says *icca* (thus). (This is the *Ādesasandhi*). The sandhis for *ti aṅgulaṃ*, *ti aṅgikaṃ*, *bhū ādayo*, and *migī bhantā udikkhati* are now stated. The phrase “*mayadā sare*” is understood to follow.
45. *Vanataragā* and *cāgamā*:

these are also augmentations (*āgama*) that occur before a vowel in certain instances. Even though the application of augments is not fixed—meaning that sometimes the vowel itself becomes the augment—the words *vana*, *tara*, and *ga* serve as indicators [of when this occurs].
Otherwise, the prescription of the augment *y* for words beginning with *pada* and so forth would be purposeless.

If, in this context, the augment *a* were to apply only to those [words] that undergo an indefinite augment (*aniyatāgamīna*), then since the form "nipajja" is already established by the augment *ya* alone, the intention is that the augment *y* for the consonant in the rule "padādīnaṃ kvaci" would be purposeless. [Examples: *tivaṅgulaṃ*, *tivaṅgikaṃ*, *bhūvādayo*.
The doe looks around apprehensively; it is said [of her] that she possesses skill and rectitude. From here it does not go away, having gathered [its strength].

"Because of this," "therefore," "from this day forward. Continuous, without abode, without fuel, effortless, unsurpassed, devoid of essence, difficult to transcend, difficult to approach, difficult to surmount, he appeared; might he come again; repeated; once more indeed.

He returns again; alas for the morning meal! [This is] the fourfold army, the fourfold protection, the attainment of the four bases of psychic power, for the purpose of crossing the four floods, for the sake of the master; this is a mere livelihood, this is simply the earth-element.
Like the king of stars among the constellations, like lightning in a mountain cave, like a mustard seed on the tip of an awl, like a bull—[one should dwell] only with the virtuous.
Separately indeed, quickly indeed. It will come swiftly, it will come heavily; thus they say here. By what is it accomplished for you here?
Like a noble steed with a whip, one should honor him in the sky. For each and every one, by which some here [are led].
It shines indeed, it exists indeed; as this is, as this very thing is; not this, not here. These six, these nine phenomena; for awakening alone.

The earth itself is the element; in those very things, by those very things, that very thing, distinct, it manifested, it expressed, it delimited, it exhausted, it overwhelmed, it sought, it concluded, it was the fixed application.
Exalted, arising, proclaimed, arisen, uttered, it rises, just once, something indeed, by something indeed, in something indeed, somewhere indeed.

For those liberated through right knowledge, it is rightly given; rightly indeed, as much as needed, as much as desired, as much as there is, just that much, again and again, for whatever purpose, at whatever interval, at that very interval, liberation through its own constituent parts—for this purpose, for one's own purpose, for that purpose, one should be devoted to one's own welfare;
in every other respect, for those liberated through mental knowledge.

“*Bahudeva ratti*. Indeed, because the governing rule (*adhikāra*) has a fixed optionality (*vavatthitavibhāsattā*), even in the case of the phoneme (*byañjana*), one may ordain (*vuṭṭhāpeyya*) nuns; it does not take long—just that.

Regarding the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), the six factors (*aṅga*), the sixty-six, the six shoulders (*aṃsa*), and the six bases (*āyatana*), here the terms “*vā sare*” and “*āgamo*” are understood to carry over (*vattate*).

49. *Cha* + *lo*: The letter *ḷ* optionally becomes an augment (*āgama*) for the following vowel. The word *cha* is in the singular because it is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*). Examples: *chaḷabhiññā*, *chaḷaṅgaṃ*, *chaḷasīti*, *chaḷaṃsā*, *chaḷāyatanaṃ*. When the option is not applied: *chaabhiññā*. (This concludes the section on Augment Sandhi. *Lopa* means non-appearance (*adassana*). It refers to the original element (*ṭhāni*) which, having been elided, is no longer seen.
(Note: The final line appears to be a mnemonic verse summarizing the technical definitions.)
Substitution (*ādesa*) is that which takes the place [of something else]. Augment (*āgama*) is the arising of what was previously non-existent.

**Vowel Sandhi (*Sarasandhi*):** The prohibition of vowel sandhi in cases such as *kaññā iva*, *kaññāva*, and so forth, is stated because a negation presupposes a prior possibility. When the elision (*lopa*) of preceding vowels would otherwise occur, the terms "vowel" (*saro*) and "indeed" (*ve*) are understood to carry over from the previous rules.
28. Two [words] or more do not stand in a sequence of prior and posterior, nor are even two ever elided. Examples: *kaññā iva*, *kaññeva*, *kaññāva*;

The forms beginning with *tadam* are established. According to the principle that "whatever is not governed by a specific rule (*lakkhaṇa*) is due to irregularity (*nipātana*"), they are formed by means of a different rule.
Omissions, elisions, and transpositions not specifically prescribed here are to be understood everywhere by this very rule.

This should also be regarded as being like the *pisodara* and other [irregular] formations of others. Examples: *phusitaṃ* = a drop of water; *phusita-mudaraṃ* becomes *pisodaraṃ*. When *issa* takes the vowel *a*, it becomes *iminā* = *tadaminā*.
*Sakiṃ-āgāmī* becomes *sakadāgāmī*. When *dha* becomes *da*, *ekaṃ idha ahaṃ* becomes *ekamidāhaṃ*. In *vidha*, there is the substitution of *vi*.
When *ava* is substituted for *saṃvi* and *hāra* is substituted for *dhā*, and when *va* is substituted for the sound *ri* and *la* for *ha*, *vārivāhaka* becomes *valāhaka*.
When *jī* is the substitute for *jīvana*, *mūta* is the substitute for *mūta* [of *jīvana*], thus *jīvanassa mūto* becomes *jīmūto*.

When *su* is the substitute for *chava* and *sāna* is the substitute for *sayana*, *chavassa sayanaṃ* becomes *susānaṃ*. When *udu* is the substitute for *uddha* and *khala* is the substitute for *kha*, then by the rule "after a vowel, [the following consonant] is doubled,"...
When *dvi* and so forth are applied, *khaṃ* becomes *udu*, thus forming *udukkhala*. When *pi* is substituted for *pisita* and *sā* for *as*, *pisitāsa* becomes *pisāca*.

When *mayū* is substituted for the word *mahī* and *ra* for *ravati*, *mayūra* is formed, meaning "one who cries out on the earth. In this way, other applications should also be understood from usage. And here—
The addition of a phoneme, the substitution of a phoneme, two others: the modification and the elision of a phoneme;
and the connection of a verbal root with a pre-eminent meaning.
Now, etymological derivation (*nirutta*) is said to be fivefold:

(1) *okāgama* (the addition of a prefix), as in "one appointed at the gate" (*dvāre niyutto*) = *dovāriko*; (2) *vipallāsa* (metathesis), as in "a lion" (*sīho*) from the word *hiṃsa*; (3) *vikāra* (modification), as in "one's own" (*nijako*) = *niyako*;

(4) *vaṇṇalopa* (elision of a phoneme), as in "girdle" (*mekhalā*) from "a garland of urine" (*mehanassa khassa mālā*), where the letters *ha*, *na*, and *ma* are elided; (5) [suffix addition], as in "peacock" (*mayūro*).
"Atthe" means "because of the application of excellence.
"Yathariva tathariva" consists merely of particles. In the phrase "Jaraggavā vicintesuṃ, varaṃ hākaṃ bhusāmive," the word *iva* has the sense of the particle *eva*. This is a *niggahīta-sandhi*.
It is a *paṭisedha-sandhi* (prohibition sandhi) among the *sandhissara* (vowel-conjunction) types.
Furthermore, there is the euphonic combination of consonants with their corresponding objects (vowels); likewise, the combination of the *niggahīta* [anusvāra].
Indeed, these combinations are fivefold.
Thus ends the first chapter, the Chapter on Sandhi, in the Payogasiddhi.
2. The Chapter on Names (Nāmakaṇḍa).
Now, names (nāma) are being explained. It is called "name" (nāma) because it bends toward its object and because it names the object by itself.

The term *dabba* (substantive) is twofold: according to gender (*liṅga*) and whether it is literal or conventional; and threefold: according to masculine, feminine, and neuter gender—as in *rukkho* (tree), *latā* (creeper), and *vanaṃ* (forest).

It is fourfold: according to commonality (*sāmañña*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and arbitrary name (*yadicchānāma*)—as in *rukkho* (tree), *nīlo* (blue), *pācako* (cook), and *sirivaḍḍho* (Sirivaḍḍha).
It is eightfold: according to the distinctions of the inherent nature (*pakati*) of the vowels *avaṇṇa*, *vaṇṇu*, *vaṇṇo*, *kāra*, and the nasal *niggahīta*.
Here, the word *kiṃ* ends in the *niggahīta* (anusvāra). That from which a suffix (*paccaya*) is first applied is called the base (*pakati*), namely: a word (*sadda*) and a root (*dhātu*).
Regarding those [bases] with gender, first, the masculine word *sugata*, ending in the vowel *a*, is joined with the seven case-endings (*vibhatti*). When *sugata* stands [as the base]: 1.

**Dve dve + kānekesu nāmasmā si yo aṃ yo nā hi sa naṃ smā hi sa naṃ smiṃ su** [The following suffixes are applied: *si*, *yo*, *aṃ*, *yo*, *nā*, *hi*, *sa*, *naṃ*, *smā*, *hi*, *sa*, *naṃ*, *smiṃ*, *su*.
Of these, there are two pairs each, occurring respectively from nouns that function in both singular and plural senses.

Since these constitute seven dyads, and because it is stated that "the base word (*pāṭipadika*), the primary suffix (*kitaka*), the secondary suffix (*taddhita*), and the compound (*samāsa*)—provided they possess meaning, are declinable, and are not suffixes—are called 'nouns' (*nāma*)," that noun is termed a "base word" (*pāṭipadika*).
Some [teachers] maintain that a noun possesses a pentad consisting of its own meaning, substance, gender, number, and object (*kamma*) and so forth.
They say it is "pāṭipadika. Therefore, this is said:
"Others have explained that the meanings of words consist of the base (sakattha), the gender (liṅga), and the case-meaning (saddattha);
whereas number, the object [of the action] (kamma), and so forth, are considered to be expressed by the case-endings (vibhatti)."

Some have stated that the meanings of words consist of the individual referent (*saka-attha*), gender (*liṅga*), number (*saṅkhyā*), the five beginning with the object (*kamma-ādi*), and case endings (*vibhatti*). However, others maintain that case endings are merely indicators (*jotaka*).

Following that, since there would be an indefinite application of the rule that "the singular is used when one thing is to be expressed, and the plural when many are to be expressed," the governing heading "from a noun" (*nāmasmā*) is established.

37. Regarding "in the sense of the nominative" (*paṭhamatthe*): when there is merely the denotation of a noun (*nāmassa abhidheyyamattē*), the first case-ending occurs according to the speaker's intention. Thus, from the first case, there are the singular and plural endings.

*Si* and *yo* are the first case endings. Since the letter *s* in *si* is a phonetic adjunct (*anubandha*), it is not employed [as a separate sound]. Its purpose is the conventional designation (*saṅketa*) "what is this? (*kiṃ amhi sū*).

Likewise, [the rule applies] to the vowel *a* and the consonant *k*. Here, "tathā" (likewise) indicates an extension (*atidesa*). An extension is the application of properties belonging to one thing to another thing. When a singular form is to be expressed, the nominative singular case ending (*si*) occurs.

The word "ataḥ" (from *a*) is understood [as governing the context]. Since *ataḥ* is a qualifier of a noun (*nāma*), by the paribhāṣā rule "a rule [applies] to that which ends in a qualifier," the operation applies from a noun ending in the vowel *a*.

109. After a masculine noun ending in *a*, *si* becomes *o*. When the preceding vowel is elided, [the form] is *sugato tiṭṭhati*. When plurality is to be expressed, the plural number (*bahuvacana*) is used. This should be applied in the same way for the subsequent cases as well. 41. After [a stem ending in] *a*, the case endings *ya* and *na* become *ṭā* and *ṭe* respectively.

After a noun ending in short *a*, the first and second case endings become *ṭā* and *ṭe* respectively. Because of the *ṭ*-consonant suffix, the rule "when a suffix has *ṭ* as its suffix, it replaces the whole [stem] even if it consists of multiple syllables" applies, resulting in a total replacement. Thus: *sugatā tiṭṭhanti*.
The phrase "the first case in the sense of mere presence" continues to apply.
38. In the vocative.
The first case ending occurs after a word used in the sense of mere address; thus, in the singular, *si* is [the suffix].
112. *Go syālapane*:
In address, *si* is designated as *ga*.
“Elision” (lopa) applies.
117. After a noun:
elision occurs of *ga* and *sī*. O Sugata, remain for long! (*Bho sugata ciraṃ tiṭṭha.*)
The term "ge" is used [in this rule]. 59.

The long vowel of *ayu* or the long vowels of *ai*, *au*, and *ic* become long when followed by "ge," provided that "ge" is a long vowel according to the three genders; for example: *bho sugata sugatā ciraṃ tiṭṭha*.
*Sakkate sugatā*—some maintain that this is a long-distance address, but since it is seen to be used even for addressing someone nearby, that [interpretation] should not be accepted.
In the plural, *yossa* becomes *ṭā*: *sugatā ciraṃ tiṭṭhatha*. 2.
The second case is used for the object (*kamma*).
The second case ending occurs for that which is the object of an action. "Aṃ" and "yo" are the second case endings.

Here, the status of being the second, third, and so forth, is stated in the rules on case endings (*vibhattisutta*) by taking the first case ending and the others as reference points, because they are designated in relation to those respective cases. The singular form of the second case is *aṃ*; the vowel *a* is not applied [in this specific rule].
Example: *sugataṃ passa* (see the Well-Gone One). The plural form of the second case is *yo*; for this, *ṭe* is substituted: *sugate passa* (see the Well-Gone Ones).
19. The Third Case in the Agent and the Instrument:

The third case ending occurs for the agent (*kattṛ*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*) among the grammatical factors (*kāraka*). *Nā* is the third case ending. *Nā* is the singular form of the third case. The phrase "nā assā" (of that which is *nā*) is understood [from the previous rule].
108. After a noun ending in short *a*, there is always a substitution of *en* for the following nominative case ending. Example: *sugatena kataṃ* (done by the Sugata).
98. [The suffix] *ssu* is substituted for the dative case ending after *su* and *hi*.
For that which ends in *a*, *su* becomes *sve*. [Examples: *sugatehi*. The word "also" (*ve*) continues [from the previous rule]. 95.
In the case of *smā*, *hi*, and *smin*, [the suffixes] *mhā* and *abhimhi* [are substituted].

In place of *nām*, *asmā*, *paresam*, *smā*, *hismim*, *naṃ*, *mhā*, and *abhimhi*, the forms *hi*, *ssa*, *bhi*, *ādese*, *sugatebhi*, *karaṇe*, *sugatena*, *loko*, *puññaṃ*, *karoti*, *sugatehi*, and *sugatehi* occur respectively. 24. The Dative Case (*Catutthī*) in the Sense of Recipient (*Sampadāna*).
In that grammatical factor of the recipient, the fourth case (*catutthī*) may occur. *Sa* and *naṃ* are the fourth case endings. *Sa* is the singular form of the fourth case.

Although the form *sugatassa* is established by the long reading *ssa naṃ* in the *Vibhattisutta*, the expression *ssassa* is employed here for the sake of brevity, because in the rule-sūtras prescribing operations such as *jhalā sassa no*, the term *ssassa* involves a greater burden of syllables.
— 51. *Suña sassa*.

The word *nām* (name) does not become the genitive (*parassa*) [of the following word], nor does it become the locative (*suñāgamo*). And while the term "genitive" (*chaṭṭhiyā*) is being applied—[Pāṇini 1.1.72 states:

"A letter with a *ñ* or *k* as its indicatory mark (*anubandha*), whether initial or final, is a designation for that which has been specified as a genitive. Here, the initial portion is the rule: letters having *ñ* or *k* as their *anubandhas*, whether at the beginning or the end, serve as technical designations. The vowel *u* is for the sake of pronunciation; the letter *ñ* is a conventional marker (*saṃketa*) within this sutta. [Example: He gives a gift to the Sugata (*sugatassa dānaṃ deti*).
1.58. Regarding the heading "Bahulam" (mostly):
those skilled in grammar consider the *Bahulādhikāra* (the section on "mostly") to be like a wish-fulfilling tree (*kappaduma*). And that [section] states:
"In some cases there is the occurrence or non-occurrence [of a rule], in some cases another [rule applies], or in some cases [it applies] here and there."
"By the word 'mostly' (bahula), the entire rule [is understood] according to the tradition"—
thus they consider the fourfold "mostly. Or rather,
it is simply "from this" (ato vā).

44. *Sassā*: For a dative ending beginning with *s*, following a word ending in long *ā*, there is optionally, in most cases, the substitution of *āyo* for the dative suffix *sā*. [Examples: *sugatāya*. Since this suffix *āya* is generally seen only in the sense of the dative of purpose (*tādatthe*), it will not be illustrated further hereafter. The plural form of the dative is *naṃ*;
the term "long" (*dīgho*) continues to apply.
89. Before words beginning with *su* and *naṃhi*, the long vowel occurs; [this applies] before *sugata* and so forth. 29.
From the fifth [case], except for *avadhi*.
The fifth case ending occurs after [a word] expressing the sense of separation (avadhikāraka). *Smā* + *hi* constitute the fifth case. *Smā* is the singular number of the fifth case;
the terms *ato*, *ṭāṭe*, and *ve* also continue in application.
43. *Smā* + *smiṃnaṃ*.

After a noun ending in short *a*, the case endings *smā* and *smiṃ* become optionally *ṭā* and *ṭe* respectively. Thus: *sugatā* (from the sugata), *apehi sugatamhā* or *sugatasmā* (depart from the sugata). For the fifth case plural, it is *sugatebhi* or *sugatehi*.

39. The Sixth Case in Relation to Connection: Connection is distinct from the [direct] kārakas; in that regard, the sixth case ending occurs. *Sa* and *naṃ* are the sixth case; *sa* is the singular of the sixth case, as in *sugatassa vihāro* (the dwelling of the sugata); *naṃ* is the plural of the sixth case, as in *sugatānaṃ*.

14. The seventh case ending occurs in the sense of the locus (ādhāra) as the grammatical factor (kāraka). The suffix *smin* is called the seventh case (*sattamī*). *Smiṃ* is the singular form of the seventh case: in the locative singular, [the forms] are *sugatamhi*, *sugate*, or *sugatasmiṃ*. The plural form of the seventh case is *su*; by the rule “*su hisva sse*,” it becomes *e*, resulting in *sugatesu*.

[The nominative forms are] *sugato*, *sugatā*. [The vocative forms are] *bho sugata*, *bho sugatā*, *bhavanto sugatā*. [The accusative forms are] *sugataṃ*, *sagate*. [The instrumental singular is] *sugatena*.
Sugatebhi, sugatehi. In the instrumental case: sugatena, sugatebhi, sugatehi. Sugatassa, sugatāya, sugatānaṃ.
Sugatā, sugatamhā, sugatasmā, sugatebhi, sugatehi. Sugatassa, sugatānaṃ.
Sugate, sugatamhi, sugatasmiṃ, sugatesu.

The Well-Gone One, the Well-Gone One. It bows to the Well-Gone One. Done by the Well-Gone One. Conquered by the Well-Gone One. May I give to the Well-Gone One. Gone away from the Well-Gone One. Heard from the Well-Gone One. Delights in the Well-Gone One.
Thus—gods, asuras, humans, serpents, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, humans, piśācas, and pretas;
Mātaṅgas, elephants, horses, boars, lions, tigers, leopards,
tortoises, hyenas, deer, horses, and jackals; those whose abodes are light and darkness,
and who possess blue and generosity through yoga.
Those who desire the Dhamma come from the towns and villages of Vāyāma;
the Saṅgha is free from strife, harsh speech, resentment, the influxes, anger, and greed,
as well as aggression, rigidity, intoxication, conceit, negligence, and calumny.
Punnāgas, pūgas, panasa trees, asanas, campakas, ambas,
hintālas, tālas, vakulas, ajjunas, and kiṃsukas;
mandāras, kundas, pucimandas, and karañja trees—
The meanings are: peacock, bird, egg-born, crane, and swan.

It is the word *sugata* itself [that provides the meaning], because every word does not have its meaning restricted solely to its literal phonetic sense; rather, they express a meaning by way of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth. Therefore, it is said:
"By means of conjunction, disjunction, association, and opposition;"
Meanings [are determined] by context, grammatical gender, proximity to other words,
semantic capacity, specific location, time, proficiency, suitability,
metaphorical usage, variations in intonation, and connection with qualifiers.
And meanings are distinguished through the word’s function as a factor (*tadaṅga*), its being the primary element (*padhāna*), and so forth; they are not derived from the sound alone.

Here, first, by way of association (*saṃyoga*): in the phrase “let a mare-cow with a colt be given,” *kisoro* means a young horse; through association with that, it is understood to be specifically a mare.
By way of dissociation: from the prohibition expressed as “let the non-mares be brought,” it is understood that only mares are meant. By way of association:

in the case of “Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa,” because of the association of both, Rāma is understood to be Dāsarathi (Rāma of the Lineage of Daśaratha) alone, not one designated by another name such as Jāmadagnya; and Lakṣmaṇa too is Somitti (Lakṣmaṇa of the Lineage of Sumitrā) alone, not just anyone who possesses auspicious marks.

By way of opposition: in the case of “Rāma and Arjuna,” because Bhaggava (Balarāma) and Sahassabāhu (Arjuna Kārtavīrya) are mutually opposed, they alone are understood, not Dāsarathi and Sabyasāci (Arjuna Pāṇḍava).

In terms of meaning (*atthato*): when one says, "Bring salt; I am entering the battlefield," the entry onto the battlefield occurs by means of a specific vehicle; thus, in this sense, it refers to a "lord of horses" (*turaṅgapati*), but not to a specific kind of salt. In terms of context (*pakaraṇato*):

when the procedure for a meal is being prepared and one says, "Bring salt," even though there is no other word present, the understanding refers to salt because it is observed to be included among the collection of requisites for a meal; such is the nature of the occasion.

By way of characteristic (*liṅga*): “First, bring Devadatta, who has propitiated his teacher”—here, by the characteristic of having propitiated a teacher, his great learning (*bāhusacca*) is understood, but not just any quality of a deity. By way of proximity (*sannidhāna*):
it is understood that “Ajjuna is one who has performed valor,” not that Ajjuna is one who has not performed valor. By way of capacity (*sāmatthiya*):
“The maiden is without a belly”—from this, it is understood that in the absence of a belly, there is no such thing as a maiden; rather, it refers to the waist-region of that slender-limbed girl.

By way of illustration (*ocitrato*): regarding the phrase “this one is like Rāma,” since Rāma is more commonly known in connection with Daśaratha, it is understood as Daśaratha alone, and not Bhagīratha-Rāma.
By way of place (*desato*): the word “*poṭṭhapā*” is a term of praise in some regions, but a term of abuse in others. By way of time (*kālato*):
the word “*pace*” refers in certain parts of the Deccan to the cooking of rice-gruel in the forenoon, but to the cooking of boiled rice in the evening.

By way of division (*byattito*): "half of the village" (*gāmassa addhaṃ*) refers to an equal portion, due to its neuter gender; whereas "half of the village" (*gāmassa addho*) with a masculine gender refers to an unequal portion.

By way of suitability (*anurūpato*): "The king protects the herd of cattle well" (*narapati sādhu rakkhati gomaṇḍalaṃ*). Since protecting the circle of the earth is suitable for a king, he is intent (*pati*) upon the protection of the circle of the earth alone, and not upon the guarding of a herd of cattle.

By way of metaphorical designation (*upacārato*): Metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) is the attribution of a certain nature to that which does not possess that nature. And this [designation] consists of: its purpose (*tadaṭṭho*), its quality (*taddhammo*), and its association (*taṃsahacariyo*).
"Near that" (*taṃsamīpa*) is fourfold; therein, in order, [the examples are]: "The beds rise up," "The fire-boy," "Insert the stick," and "A tiger in the Ganges.
The word *kākut*—that is, the word *kāku*—is used for a woman, and it is seen in the sense of transformation, grief, fear, and distress; it refers to transformations of the body.
Even though someone has not actually done something, when asked by another, "Did you do that?", he may say with an angry knitting of the brows, "I did it.
Here, the act of knitting the brows indicates his admission of non-doing. As for the relationship:

in the expression, "One should behave properly toward one's mother; one should be obedient toward one's father," although the words "mother" and "father" are not explicitly qualified as possessive (e.g., *samātari*, *sapitari*), it is understood that "she is his mother and he is his father."

By way of indication (*upalakkhaṇato*): in the expression “curd that must be guarded against crows,” the word “crows” indicates the common characteristic of all things that cause harm; thus, it excludes everything else as well, such as dogs. By way of conventional usage (*vacanato*):
the word “wife” (*dārā*) is plural when referring to a spouse, but elsewhere it is used with an indefinite sense.

By way of being a constituent part (*tadaṅgattā*): when it is said, “prepared food,” because of its being an accessory to that, the preparation of the seating, the bowl, the sauce, and so forth—which are its implements—is also understood.
By way of its primary significance: through the king’s departure expressed as “the lord of the earth departs,” the departure of those who depend upon him is also understood.
And it has been said:
“In the suttas of interpretable and definitive meaning, that which is to be known is merely the literal sense of the words.”
There is no need for further explanation here; the sutta is of explicit meaning (*nītattha*).
Thus ends the method of forms and the connection with the verb for other masculine nouns ending in *a* as well.

We shall now state the distinction that exists in the word *sugata*. Hereafter follows the sixth case (*chaṭṭhī*), which is identical to the fourth (*catutthī*), and the plural of the fifth (*pañcamī*).
And because they are completed by the third plural ending, they are not shown here.
The [terms] *gumbam*, *si*, *ato*, and *sissā* are understood to recur.
110. *kvace vā*.

After a noun ending in short *a*, the suffix *si* optionally becomes *e* in some instances. Thus: *gumbe*, *gumbo*, *gumbā*; *bho gumba*, *gumbā*, *bhavanto gumbā*, and so forth, which are similar to the [forms of] the Sugata.
Likewise, when it ought to be said *phussitagge*, one says *phussitaggo*; when it ought to be said *vattabbe*, one says *vattabbo*, and so forth.
Because the suffix *si* plus the letter *k* is obligatory, in certain alternative cases, the form beginning with *ekāra* (*e*) is commenced: thus, in the case of *sisso* plus *kāra*.

Thus it becomes: because the substitution of *am* for the vowel *e* in the neuter domain by the rule "aṃ napuṃsake" overrides [the previous rule], yet due to the application of the term "generally" (*bahulaṃ*), it sometimes occurs even in the neuter, as in *sukhe dukkhe*.
The words "of *y*" (*yossa*) and "*ṭe*" are also carried over [from the preceding rules].

135. After *ekacca* and other words ending in *-a*, the suffix *ṭe* occurs for the [nominative] plural. *Ekacco*, *ekacce*. *Bho ekacca*, *ekaccā*, *ekacce*. *Ekaccaṃ*, *ekacce*. Thus it is for these first-group words.
*Kodho*, *kodhā*. *Bho kodha*, *kodhā*, *kodhā*. *Kodhaṃ*, *kodhe*.
The forms *nassa* and *sā* are also used [in this sense].
107. Regarding *kodhādīhi*:

*nassa* or *sā* occurs after words such as *koha*. *Kodhasā* means "by anger. *Atthasā* means "by the purpose. The word *attha* is also seen in the neuter gender, as in: *“ye uttamatthāni tayi labhimhā”* (“the supreme goals which we obtained from you”).
And "smino ṭī" is stated [as a rule].
175. From the *div-ādi* group:

after nouns belonging to the *div-ādi* class, "ṭi" always replaces "smin. As in *divi*, likewise *bhuvi*. Here, in the case of "ṭi," there is always the insertion of the letter *v* and the shortening of the vowel. Here, the word *bhū* is equivalent to the word *vadhū*.
The term "ve" (or) is understood [to apply here].

144. After stems beginning with *man*, the suffixes *smiṃ*, *saṃ*, *nā*, *smānaṃ*, *si*, *so*, *o*, *sā*, and *sā* optionally become *si*, *so*, *o*, *sā*, and *sā* respectively, according to their order. Thus: *mano*, *manā*; *bho mana*, *bho manā*.
Manā. Mano, manaṃ, mane. Manasā, manena; manehi, manebhi. Manaso, manassa; manānaṃ.
Manasā, manā, manamhā, manasmā; manehi, manebhi. Manasi, manamhi, manasmiṃ; manesu.
Thus also for vaco, payo, and tejo.
*Tapa*, *ceta*, *tama*, *yasa*; *aya*,
*vaya*, *sira*, *sara*, *uro*—
these are the words beginning with *ma*.

In the *Rūpasiddhi*, the words *aha* and *raha* are listed among [the particles] beginning with *man*. Because *aha* is derived from the root *āp* (to obtain), and because *raha* is a particle (*nipāta*), and because *rahasi* is a particle that is a substitute for a case-ending (*vibhattianta-paṭirūpaka-nipāta*), they are not included here.
The word *gacchantam* follows, as do the words *si* and *ve*. We shall not repeat them further below, because they are understood through their recurrence in the *Vutti* itself.
148. *Ntassaṃ* (The suffix *-ntassaṃ*).

The *aṃ* substitute optionally occurs for the *ntapaccaya*. According to the principle that "among what is heard and what is inferred, the connection with what is heard is stronger," because [the rule] says "of *nta*" (*ntassa*), the *aṃ* applies only to *nta*, not to the inferred word ending in it.

This is likewise in all subsequent instances where the substitution of *nta* and *ntu* is prescribed. By the rule "gasinaṃ," there is elision (*silopa*) of the final consonant. Thus: *gacchaṃ*, *gacchanto*.
215. In the first *yo* [case], for the forms ending in *nt* and *ntu*, the substitution of *nto* occurs optionally.

And because of the rule of "frequently" (*bahulādhikārā*), this applies only to the masculine: *gacchanto*, *gacchantā*. 218. In the locative case (*ge*), for the forms ending in *ṭa*, *ṭā*, and *aṃ*...
For the endings *nt* and *ntūnaṃ* when followed by case-suffixes, the substitutions *ṭa*, *ṭā*, and *aṃ* occur invariably or frequently. *Bho gaccha*, *gacchā*, *gacchaṃ*;
*gacchanto*, *gacchantā*. 92. *Ntassa ca ṭa vaṃse*:
Before the suffixes *vaṃ* and *se*, the suffix *nta* optionally becomes *ṭa*, as does *ntu*. This is a restricted option (*vavatthitavibhāsā*). *Gacchaṃ*, *gacchantaṃ*; *gacchante*.

217. For the case endings *to*, *tā*, *ti*, *tā*, *sa*, *smā*, *smiṃ*, *nā*, *su*, *sa*, *smā*, *smiṃ*, *nā*, *su*, and for those ending in *nta* and *ntu*, the forms *to*, *tā*, *ti*, and *tā* optionally occur respectively. *Gacchatā*, *gacchantena*; *gacchantehi*, *gacchantebhi*. *Gacchato*, *gacchassa*, *gacchantassa*. 216.
*Taṃ* [and *naṃ*] in the locative (*mhi*).

In the case of the suffixes *-anta* and *-antūna*, when followed by case endings, *taṃ* optionally occurs. Gacchataṃ, gacchantānaṃ (genitive plural). Gacchatā, gacchantā, gacchantamhā, gacchantasmā (instrumental/ablative singular). Gacchati, gacchante, gacchantamhi, gacchantasmiṃ, gacchantesu (locative singular and plural). In the same way:
mahaṃ (I), caraṃ (walking), tiṭṭhaṃ (standing), dadaṃ (giving), bhuñjaṃ (eating), suṇaṃ (hearing), pacaṃ (cooking);
jayaṃ (conquering), jīraṃ (aging), vacaṃ (speaking), pīyaṃ (drinking), saraṃ (remembering), kubbaṃ (doing), japaṃ (reciting), vajaṃ (avoiding).
Icchādayo.
Bhavanta si, 149. Bhūto.
This is the Niyama-sutta. In the nominative singular (*simhi*), *aṃ* is always substituted for the final vowel of the word *bhūdhātu* due to a subsequent re-statement (*punabbidhāna*).

Thus: *bhavaṃ*. 146. For the word *bhava*, there is optionally the substitution of *bhontā* before *ga*, *ya*, *no*, and *ase*. There is also the substitution of *nto*. Thus: *bhonto*, *bhontā*, *bhavanto*.
*Bhavantā*. Furthermore: *bho*, *bhō*, *bhonta*, *bhontā*, *bhava*, *bhavā*, *bhavaṃ*; *bhonto*, *bhontā*, *bhavanto*, *bhavantā*.

In the alternative where *bhonta* is substituted, the substitutions *ṭa*, *ṭā*, and *aṃ* do not occur due to the rule of diversity (*bahulādhikārā*). [Examples: *bhavaṃ*, *bhavantaṃ*; *bhonte*, *bhavante*. [Instrumental:
*bhotā*, *bhontena*, *bhavatā*, *bhavantena*; *bhavantehi*, *bhavantebhi*. [Genitive: *bhoto*, *bhontassa*, *bhavato*.
*Bhavassa*, *bhavantassa*, *bhavato*, *bhavantānaṃ*. *Bhavatā* and so forth are the same as [the forms] for one who is going (*gacchantasamaṃ*).

*Bho* is a particle used for addressing; it is seen even in the plural, as in: “From where, indeed, do you three people come, O sirs? Similarly, *bhante*. It is established by means of the word *bhadde* [from the stem] *bhadda*; *bhaddante* is formed by doubling the letter *d*.

*Saṃ*, *santo*, *santā*. *Bho*, *sa*, *sā*, *saṃ*, *santo*, *santā*. *Saṃ* [in the phrase] *santaṃ*—when the *lopa* (elision) of *na* occurs according to the rule "elision after a conjunct," as in *yaṃ yañhi rāja bhajati, santaṃ vā yadi vā asaṃ*—[we have] *sante*, *satā*, *santena*.

145. *Sato* becomes *saba* before the word *santa* when followed by the letter *bha*: *sabbhi*, *santehi*. Because it is a permanent (*nicca*) [substitution], the form *santebhi* does not occur. *Sato*, *sassa*, *santassa*, etc., follow the same pattern as the forms for *gacchanta*.

150. For the words *mahant* (great) and *arahant* (worthy), the suffix *ṭā* optionally replaces *si*. For *mahant*, *ṭā* optionally replaces the final *nt*. Thus: *mahā*, *mahaṃ*, *mahanto*; *mahanto*, *mahantā*. *Arahā*, *arahaṃ*, *arahanto*, *arahantā*, and so forth, follow the same pattern as *gacchant* (going). [The suffix] *si* [is applied] after *asmā*.
154. After *rāja* and other [words], and after *yuva* and other [words] beginning with *yuva*, the suffix *ā* is substituted for the final vowel of another word.
156. *Yona + māno*.

After *rāja* and so forth, and after *yuvan* and so forth, either *ām* or *ā* is substituted [for the nominative plural ending]. From *asmad*, [the forms] are *asma* and *asmā*. [The forms] are *bho*, *asma*, *asmā*, *asmāno*, and *asmā*. 155.
Optionally, *ānaṅ* is substituted for *rāja* and so forth, and for *yuvan* and so forth, before the ending *am*. [The forms] are *asmānaṃ* or *asman*, and *asmāno* or *asme*.

80. After *kamma* and other [words], the suffix *eno* optionally replaces *nā*. [Examples: *asmena*, *asmanā*; *asmehi*, *asmebhi*. *Assassa*, *asmānaṃ*. *Asmā*, *asmamhā*, *asmasmā*, and so forth. 79. After *kamma* and other [words]...
The suffix *smin* optionally becomes *ni* after *kamma*. [The forms are: *asmani*, *asme*, *asmamhi*, *asmamhi*, *asmesu*.

*Kamma*, *camma*, *vesma*, *bhasma*, *brahma*, *atta*, *ātuma*, *ghamma*, and *muddha*—these are the words beginning with *kamma*. *Muddha*, *gaṇḍivadhanva*, *aṇima*, *laghimā*, and so forth, are equal to *asma*.
*Rāja*, *brahma*, *sakha*, *atta*, *ātuma*, *gaṇḍivadhanva*, *asma*, *aṇima*, *laghimā*, and so forth, are the words beginning with *rāja*.
By the rule *dhammo vā ññatthe*, because [the word] is listed among *rājā* and others in the *gaṇa*-sutta, it may become *daḷadhammo* or *daḷadhammā*.
*Yuva*, *sā*, *suva*, *maghava*, *puma*, *vattaha*—these are the *yuvādi* group. *Rājā*, *rājāno*, *rājā*.
*Bho rāja*, *rājā*, *rājāno*, *rājā*. *Rājānaṃ*, *rājaṃ*, *rājāno*, *rāje*.

123. Regarding the reading "Rājassi nāmhi ‘Sabbadattena rājinā’," this [section] has begun here. Alternatively, it is "rājassi" followed by "nāmhi. [The form] "rājinā" [is used]. 222. In the cases of the nominative and accusative plural, [the form is] "raññā."
In the case of *rāja* when followed by the suffix *-s*, it always becomes *raññā*. This is because the term *sabba* possesses multiple phonetic forms (*anekavaṇṇattā*).

Thus: *raññā*. 124. In the case of *su*, *naṃ*, and *hisu*, the vowel *ū* optionally replaces the final vowel of *rāja*. [The rule] "of that which ends in the sixth case" applies to the final syllable. Thus: *rājūhi* or *rājehi*; *rājūbhi* or *rājebhi*.
223. For the word *rāja*, when it is inflected (*savibhatti*), these substitutions occur:
*rañño*, *raññassa*, *rājino*, and *rājassa*. [The forms] *rañño*, *raññassa*, *rājino*, and *rājūnaṃ* [are thus derived].
221. *Rājassa* becomes *raññaṃ*.

In the case of the genitive singular ending *naṃ*, it becomes either *rañño* or *raññaṃ*. [Examples: *rañño*, *raññaṃ*. In the case of the instrumental plural endings *rājūhi*, *rājehi*, *rājūbhi*, and *rājebhi*:
[Examples: *raññā*, *rājūhi*, *rājehi*, *rājūbhi*, *rājebhi*. 224.

In the case of the locative singular ending *smiṃ*, it becomes *raññe* or *rājini*. In the case of the locative singular ending *smiṃ*, *raññe* and *rājini* always occur for the word *rāja* when followed by a case ending. [Examples: *raññe*, *rājini*; *rājūsu*, *rājesu*.
225. Regarding the rule "or in a compound" (*samāse vā*), that which was stated by the *gaṇa*-sutta—that there is no *nā*, *asmā*, or *smiṃ*—is optional. Thus:
*kāsiraññā*, *kāsirājinā*, *kāsirājena*; *kāsirājūbhi*, *kāsirājebhi*, *kāsirājūhi*, *kāsirājehi*; *kāsirañño*, *kāsiraññassa*.

Of the king of Kāsi, [belonging] to the king of Kāsi. From the king of Kāsi, from the king of Kāsi. Of the kings of Kāsi, of the kings of Kāsi. In the king of Kāsi, in the king of Kāsi, in the king of Kāsi, in the king of Kāsi; in the kings of Kāsi, in the kings of Kāsi.
Path, path-way, path. O path, O path, O path-way, O path. Of the path, the path; [in] the paths, [in] the paths.
192. After *puṃsa*, *kamma*, *thāma*, and *addhāna*, [the suffixes] *sa* and *smā* optionally occur;

after *puṃs* and the others, *sa* and *smā* optionally occur when *nām* follows—thus, by the rule [stating] "after *addhā*, [the suffix] *eno* is substituted for *nām*" (Pāṇini 7.1.75), we have *addhena* or *addhānā*; [in the plural] *addhehi* and *addhebhi*. And regarding the vowel *u*: 1.9.
*Iyuvaṇṇā jhalā nāmassante* ("The semi-vowels *y* and *v* are substitutes for the vowels *i* and *u* at the end of a noun-base").
The name *pāṭipadika* refers to the first day of the lunar fortnight; at the end of that [name], the vowels *i* and *u* are designated as *jhal*, according to their respective order.

*I* and *u* are *iyu*; *iyu* and those vowels (*vaṇṇā*) are *iyuvaṇṇā*. Because it is stated, "In a dvanda compound, that which is heard at the end relates back to each member individually," the word *vaṇṇa* (vowel) is related back to each [term] individually, and thus it is expressed as "*ivaṇṇuvaṇṇā*."
81. After a *jhala* [consonant], the suffix *sassa* becomes *no*;
after a *jhal* [consonant], the suffix *sassa* optionally becomes *no*. [Examples: *addhuno*, *addhussa*, *addhassa*; *addhānaṃ*. 82. After a *nā* [vowel], the suffix *smā* [becomes *ssā*].

The forms *jhalato* do not exist for this [word]; rather, they are: *addhunā*, *addhumhā*, *addhusmā*, *addhā*, *addhamhā*, *addhasmā*. Regarding the phrase "from *kamma* and so forth," the suffix *smin* becomes *ni*:
thus, *addhani*, *addhe*, *addhamhi*, *addhasmiṃ*, *addhesu*. If the word *addha* expresses time or duration (*kāla-ddhāna*), it does not express a part (*bhāga*).
*Attā*, *attāno*, and so on, up to the second case, are like *rājā*; because they belong to the group beginning with *kamma*, these forms are *attena*, *attanā*.

195. In the case of *suhi*, there is no substitution of *na* for *atta*. According to the grammatical maxim (*paribhāsa*) "those ending or beginning with *ñ* as an adjunct," the letter *k* serves to indicate the final constituent; thus: *attanehi*, *attanebhi*, *attebhi*.
194. *No-ttātumā*.
*Atta* and *ātuma* are used for one’s own self (*attano*) or for oneself (*attassa*, *attānaṃ*).
196. *Smā*, *assa*, *nā*, *brahmā*, and *ca*:

*Brahmā* is always used for another’s self (*parassa*), with *smā*, *assa*, *nā*, etc. [The forms are: *attanā*; in the locative singular (*smimhi*), there are *ni*, *attani*, *atte*, *attamhi*, *attasmiṃ*; and in the plural, *attanesu* and *attesu*. *Ātumā* is the same as *attā*.

*Brahmā*, *brahmāno*, *brahmā*; or as in the sutta “*brahmassu vā*,” by means of the grammatical split (*yogavibhāga*) “*brahmassū*,” [the form] *brahmassu* is established. Through the elision of the *u* following *brahmassa*, *brahmunā* is also accomplished. This [usage] is seen in the *Brahmasamyutta*. 60. *Gha*: *brahmādi* etc.

This is an *ākati*-class (a class based on form). *Ākati* means “kind” (*jāti*); thus, it is a class defined by its form. From the technical designation *gha*, [the suffixes are applied] after *brahma*, *kattu*, *isi*, *sakha*, and so forth.
And there is also *gasse*. O Brahmā, *brahme*; Brahmās, *brahmāno*; of Brahmās, *brahmānaṃ*; to Brahmā, *brahmaṃ*; to Brahmās, *brahmāno*; O Brahmā, *brahme*.
In the locative singular, *nāmhi* becomes *Brahmassu*; [in the plural] *niccaṃ*. By Brahmā, *brahmunā*; by Brahmās, *brahmehi*, *brahmebhi*.
190. Regarding *brahma*: it becomes *brahmam* or *brahmussa*. [By the rule] “*jhalā sassa no*,” the *s* becomes *no*. Thus: *brahmuno*, *brahmussa*, *brahmassa*; *brahmūnam*, *brahmānam*.
[By the rule] “*smāssa nā brahmā ce*,” the *smā* becomes *nā*; with the vowel *u*, it is *brahmunā*. [By the rule] “*ambvādīhi*”...
As for *smino*: because this belongs to the class of forms ending in *-i*, the forms of *brahma* beginning with the nominative (*kamma*) are also stated here. [The forms are:
*brahmani*, *brahme*, *brahmamhi*, *brahmasmiṃ*; *brahmesu*.
*Sakha* follows the same pattern as *rāja* and others.
2,157. *Āyo* and *sakhā* [become] *yona* when followed by *māyo*;
or they become *no* and *āno*. [Examples: *sakhāyo*, *sakhāno*. 159. *No* and *nā* [are substituted] before *se* and *su*.
The [suffix] *sakhassa* occurs constantly after words ending in *-no*, *-nā*, and *-sesu*.
161. After words ending in *-yo*, *-svaṃ*, *-hi*, or *-su*, as well as after *cāraṅa*, the form *sakhassa* or *āraṅa* occurs before the case endings *smā* and *naṃ*.

171. After *āraṅ* and *āravādesa*, *ṭo* is substituted for the case endings of other [cases]. In the nominative singular (*sakhāro*), it becomes *sakhā*. But in the vocative (*ge*), by the rule "gha + brahmādite," *e* is substituted;
thus, *sakhe*, *sakha*, *sakhā*. The plural is like the nominative. In the genitive (*amhi*), by the rule "vā + mhā + naṅ," *ānaṅ* is substituted; thus, *sakhānaṃ*, *sakhāraṃ*.
*sakhaṃ*, *sakhāyo*, *sakhāno*, *sakhino*. 172. *Ṭo* or *ṭe* [are substituted] after [a stem ending in] *āra* or its substitutes;
for the [case endings] beginning with *yu*, *ṭo* or *ṭe* are substituted respectively. Elsewhere, *ṭo* is used after *āraṅ* [stems]. [Examples: *sakharā*.
*Sakha* [is the base form]. The inclusion of the long vowel (*ā*) is for the sake of brevity. [The forms are: *sakhinā*, *sakhārehi*, *sakhehi*.
According to the rule "jhala replaces *sa* except when followed by *no*," *sa* is replaced by *no* after a *jhal*-consonant; thus: *sakhino*, *sakhissa*, *sakhārānaṃ*. 160. *Smā + naṃsu vā*.
From *sakhassa* or *sakhānam* [the form] *sakhīnam* arises. From *sakhīnam*, *sakhānam*. 171.

After a word ending in *ā* that has undergone the substitution of *ā* (for *a*), *nā* and *smānam* always become *ṭā*. Thus: *sakhārā*; by virtue of the rule of frequent occurrence (*bahulādhikāra*), also from *sakhārasmā*. "After *nā*, *smā*, and *assā*"—thus it is *nā*: *sakhinā*, *sakhismā*, *sakha*, *sakhamhā*, *sakhasmā*.
158. From *sakhā* [comes] *sakha*;

from *sakhā* [comes] *sakha*, which is permanent [in the vocative]. In the case of *sakhāresu* and *sakhesu*, the usage of *sakhi* and *sakhī* is seen only in the feminine; therefore, by the rule "from *nada* etc., *ṅī*," the suffix *ṅī* is applied, or else there is shortening because it is a form of address (*ālapanattā*).
By the rule "from *yuvan* etc., *ā*," [we have] *yuvā*.

181. After [the group of words] beginning with *yu*, the forms *na* or *ne* optionally replace the suffixes *ya* or *na*. Although the form *yonaṃ māno* is established by the rule "na after the second case," the inclusion of the term "ne" is out of respect for the textual tradition; thus, the mention of *na* is included for the sake of brevity according to the sequence. 179. In the case of *no*, *nā*, and *nesu*:
[the following applies].
Let there not be *mā* for *yuvan* and the others in the nominative (*nām*) cases. *Yuvā*, *yuvā*; *bho yuva*, *yuvā*, *yuvāno*, *yuvā*. *Yuvānaṃ*, *yuvaṃ*, *yuvāno*, *yuvāne*, *yuve*.
*Yuvānā*. 178. *Su-hi-sv-anaṅ*: In the locative (*su*), instrumental (*hi*), and vocative (*sva*) cases, *anaṅ* is substituted for *yuvan* and the others. *Yuvānehi*, *yuvānebhi*.
193. *Yuvan* becomes *yuvā*, *sassi*, or *sassa*.
The forms *yuvino*, *yuvassa*, and *yuvānaṃ* [are also used]. 180. *Smā* and *smiṃ* become *naṃ*;
*nā* and *ne* [become *naṃ*].

The forms *yuvā* and so forth in this [section] are not constant; they follow the sequence as follows: *yuvā*, *yuvānehi*, *yuvānebhi*; *yuvāne*, *yuvānesu*. The words *maghavan* and *puman* are identical to the word *yuvan*.
This is the distinction: 187. After the word *puman*, the suffix *aṃ* optionally replaces *ga*. Thus: *pumaṃ*, *puma*, *pumā*; *pumāno*, *pumā*. *Pumānaṃ*, *pumaṃ*, *pumāno*, *pumāne*, *pume*.

185. *Nāmhi pumassā hoti nāmhi pumānā.* Regarding the rule "among the [terms] ending in *lakkhaṇika* and *paṭipadotta*, only that which ends in *paṭipadotta* is taken, not the *lakkhaṇika*," according to this principle,
only the case-ending (*vibhatti*) of *paṭipadotta* is taken, and not that of *nāsmāssa*, because the latter has already undergone the *lakkhaṇika* treatment.

And *paṭipada* is an imitative sound (*anukaraṇa-sadda*) derived from the non-case form "nāmhī," meaning that which has become the path (*paṭipada*). It is not used in its technical sense (*lakkhaṇika*).

Regarding the rule "In the case of *pum*, *kamma*, *thāma*, and *addhāna*, [the suffix] *sa* may optionally become *smā*," when *utta* is applied, [we have] *pumunā* (for the masculine) and *pumena*. [The forms are:
*pumuno*, *pumussa*, *pumassa*; *pumunā*, *pumā*.
184. *Pumā* becomes *puṃso* or *ne*. [The forms] *pumāne*, *pume*, *pumamhi*, and *pumasmiṃ* [are used]. 186.
And after *sumhā*.

Regarding the masculine gender, that which was stated as being constant for *pum* and so forth may optionally occur; thus, there is either the augment *ānaṅ* or the vowel *ā*. [Examples: *pumāne*, *pumāsū*, *pumesu*. *Vattahā*, *vattahāno*, *vattahā*—and so forth—is the same as the word *yuvan*.
189. *Vattahā sa-naṃ naṃ no-nānaṃ*:
For *vattahā*, the forms *sa*, *naṃ*, *naṃ*, *no*, and *nānaṃ* occur constantly according to their respective order. [Examples: *vattahāno*, *vattahānānaṃ*.

That which ends in the vowel *a*: [the suffix] *si* (nominative singular), *yos* (genitive plural), and *su* (locative plural) undergo *ghona* (nasalization). 64. [Sūtra 1.3.29]. *ekavacana-y-os-su-ghonaṃ*.

*Gho* and *o* are *gho*; that which is not *gho* is *agho*. In the expression "aghonaṃ," when the prohibition of *gho* (*agho*) is not applied, there is optionally a shortening of *gho* before suffixes such as *ssam* and so on;

however, before the singular number and the feminine suffixes *yo*, there is invariably a shortening of *gho*. Thus, the prohibition of *gho* is for the purpose of precluding the application of contradictory meanings.

The inclusion of the letter *o* is for the sake of subsequent rules. [This applies] to nouns ending in *gho* or *o*, excluding those ending in *gho* or *o*, in the singular number and the feminine suffixes *yo*.
"It becomes short when the [suffix] *tiliṅga* (the feminine suffix) arrives"—this refers to the rule:

"In the case of the locative singular (*simhi*), there is no shortening for a non-neuter [stem]" (*sismiṃ nānapuṃsakassa*). Thus, in the case of the feminine suffix (*simhi*), there is no shortening. For example: *sā*. "Like Parjanya, the manifestation of the grammatical rule..."

“It rains on the water too, it rains on the land too”—from this rule, the *ā* [is applied] after *yuva* and *aditta*. In the case of *yussa*, by the rule “*yonaṃ no vā ne*,” there is *no* for *yussa*.

By the rule “*no nānesvā*,” there is *ā*, thus *sāno*. In the alternative where *no* does not occur, because the governing rule “*yona+māno*” is a fixed option (*vavatthitavibhāsā*), *māno* occurs invariably;
therefore, in the alternative where *no* and *ne* do not occur, there is *sā*. Thus, the contingency of the form *seti* does not arise.
It becomes *sāno*. Likewise in the case of the absence of the feminine marker (*nettābhāva*).
188. *Sāssaṃ + se cā + naṅ*:

The substitution of *āna* for the word *sā* occurs invariably before the endings *aṃ*, *se*, and *ge*. [Thus: *bho sāna*, *sānā*, *sāno*; *sānaṃ*, *sāne*, *sāno*; *sānā*, *sānehi*, *sānebhi*; *sānassa*, *sānaṃ*; *sānā*, *sānehi*, *sānebhi*; *sāne*, *sānesu*.

Suvā, yuvāva. The specific rule for the short vowel is: "In the case of two words ending in a single vowel, there is the substitution of the nasalized vowel (a-ghona). However, in the case of *ge*—130. *Ge vā*:
In the presence of *ge*, the short vowel optionally occurs for the three genders of the word *agho-na*. Thus: *bho suva*, *suvā*.
Ending in the vowel ā.
[The rule] "muni" is for elision (*silopa*).
When *jha* is substituted—93. In the masculine, *jhi* becomes *yu*.

For a word ending in *jh*, *ṭā* or *ṭe* occurs in the masculine when followed by *issa* or *yu*. [Objection: Why is *jh* mentioned? [Reply: So that it does not apply to a whole group (*samudāya*) ending in *ī*.
[Objection: Why is *ī* mentioned? [Reply: So that it applies to the vowel *ī* as well.

Because of the general designation "from *at*" (*ato*), although *ṭā* and *ṭe* would have been obtained from the *a* of the technical term (*lakkhaṇika-akāra*), they do not occur due to the force of the non-prescription (*avidhāna-sāmatthiya*). And this force [of the non-prescription] exists because otherwise [the rule] would be untenable.
114. By the rule "there is elision of *jhal*," there is elision of *yo*; thus, when *yo* is elided—88.
When *yo* is elided before *ni*, there is lengthening.

In the case of *yonaṃ* (the genitive plural ending *-yānam*) and *lopenisu* (the locative plural ending *-esu*), the long vowel (*dīgha*) occurs. Regarding *muni* and *munayo*: why does the elision of *ya* (*yolopa*) not occur here?
