being on all sides (*samantato-bhāva*), delimitation (*pariccheda*), avoidance (*vajjana*), embracing (*āliṅgana*), dwelling (*nivasana*), honoring (*pūjā*), eating (*bhojana*), knowing (*avajānana*), and declaring faults (*dosakkhāna*).

Regarding its characteristics and so forth: In the sense of being on all sides: *parivuto* (surrounded). In the sense of delimitation: *pariññeyyaṃ* (to be fully understood). In the sense of avoidance: *pariharati* (he avoids).

In the sense of embracing: *parissajati* (he embraces). In the sense of clothing: *yo vatthaṃ paridahessati* (whoever shall put on a garment). In the sense of honoring: *paricariyā* (service). In the sense of feeding:

*bhikkhuṃ parivisati* (he serves a monk). In the sense of despising: *paribhavati* (he treats with contempt). In the sense of speaking ill: *paribhāsati* (he reviles). In the sense of shining forth, as in the case of characteristics and so forth:
*rukkhaṃ pari vijjotate vijju* (lightning flashes around the tree), and so on.

*Upeti* [is used] in the senses of approaching (*upagamana*), nearness (*samīpa*), attainment (*uppatti*), similarity (*sādissa*), excellence (*adhika*), cultivation (*paribhāva*), destruction (*nāsana*), declaration of faults (*dosakkhāna*), perception (*saññā*), prior karma (*pubbakamma*), worship (*pūjā*), the manner of being grasped (*gayhākāra*), and intensity (*bhusattha*), etc. In the sense of approaching:
"He should sit down near one who is already seated" (*nisinnaṃ vā upanisīdeyya*). In the sense of nearness: "near the city" (*upanagaraṃ*). In the sense of attainment:

"he is reborn in the heavenly world" (*saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati*); or alternatively, *upapatti* = *yutti* (logical connection), as in "he views it according to its logical connection" (*upapattito ikkhati*).
*Upekkhā* (equanimity); *upamānaṃ* (a comparison) when it is equal; *upamā* (a simile); *upakhāriyaṃ* (a khārī measure) when it is greater; *upasampanno* (ordained) in the sense of being above;

*upavāso* (fasting) in the sense of abstaining from food; *upavadati* (he reviles) in the sense of proclaiming faults; *upadhā* (deception) in the sense of perception; *upasaggo* (calamity); *upakkamo* (effort) in the sense of prior action; *upakāro* (assistance);

*buddhupaṭṭhāko* (an attendant of the Buddha) and *mātupaṭṭhānaṃ* (attendance on one's mother) in the sense of veneration; *soceyyapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ* (the manifestation of purity) in the sense of being taken hold of.
*Bhu* signifies "in the world" (*sattha*); *upādāna*, "distress" (*upāyāsa*), and "support" (*upanissaya*).

*Ā* is used in the senses of facing toward (*abhimukha-bhāva*), upward action (*uddha-kamma*), limit (*mariyādā*), pervasion (*abhividhi*), attainment (*patti*), desire (*icchā*), embracing (*parissajana*), beginning of an action (*ādi-kamma*), grasping (*gahaṇa*), dwelling (*nivāsana*), proximity (*samīpa*), and calling (*āvhāna*), etc.
In the sense of facing toward: *āgacchanti* (they come). In the sense of upward action: *ārohati* (he ascends).
In the sense of a boundary: *āpabbataṃ khettaṃ* (a field extending as far as the mountains); in the sense of pervasion:

*ākumāraṃ yaso Kaccāyanassa* (the fame of Kaccāyana extends even to children); in the sense of attainment: *āpattiṃ āpanno* (fallen into an offense); in the sense of desire: *ākaṅkhā* (longing); in the sense of embracing: *āliṅganaṃ*;

in the sense of the commencement of an action: *ārambho*; in the sense of taking up: *ādīyati* or *āliṅgati*; [in the sense of smearing: *ālimpati*]; in the sense of dwelling: *āvasatho*, *āvāso*; in the sense of proximity: *āsannaṃ*; in the sense of addressing: *āmanteti*.
Pa, para, pa, sa, anu, ava, o, ni, du, rabhi, byā, dhi, su; ati, ni,
ppati, pari, apa, yo, upa, ā— these twenty [prefixes] have been explained according to the sequence of the rules for prefixes (upasagga).
And here—Prefixes, particles, and suffixes: these three are each expressive of many meanings; so say the etymologists.
118. There is the elision of all case-endings (*vibhatti*) for those that are "numberless" (*asaṃkhya*), meaning for all others where no number such as singular and so forth exists.
Although there is a distinction among those numberless endings, the application of *syādi* [suffixes] occurs: "mā... [etc.]
In phrases such as *no ajja vikantiṃsu*, the status of being a word (*pada*) is established because they end in case endings (*vibhatti*).

Furthermore, the formation of *vo* and *no* and so forth occurs both through their derivation and because they are seen to express meanings such as the nominative (*paṭhamā*) and others. Examples include *pahāra* (striking), *parābhava* (defeat), *apahāra* (removal), *saṃhāra* (withdrawal), *avahāra* (taking away), and *ohāra* (utterance).
They are called prefixes (*upasagga*) because they attach themselves to verbs (*pāda*) and convey meaning.
Particles (nipāta) fall at the beginning, middle, and end of words;
such is the prepositional word (opasaggika-pada).
A non-substantive (asattavācika) particle (nepātika) serves meanings such as conjunction, option, negation, and completion.

*Ca* is used in the senses of conjunction (*samuccaya*), subsequent mention (*anvācaya*), mutual connection (*itaretarayoga*), collection (*samāhāra*), restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), and so forth. *Vā* is used in the senses of option (*vikappa*), comparison (*upamāna*), conjunction (*samuccaya*), fixed alternative (*vavatthitavibhāsa*), and so forth.
*Na*, *no*, *mā*, *a*, *alaṃ*, and *halaṃ*—these are used in the sense of negation (*paṭisedha*).

According to the principle that "two negations convey the original meaning," in the phrase "but those forms are not conditions, nor are they" (*na tesaṃ pana rūpānaṃ paccayā na ca honti*), [the two negatives imply] "they certainly are" (*na ca na honti = honteva*).
It conveys its natural meaning (*pakati-attha*). The particle *alaṃ* is used in the senses of mastery (*pariyatti*) and ornament (*bhūsana*).
The sense of fulfillment (*pūraṇattha*) is twofold: fulfillment of the self (*attapūraṇa*) and fulfillment of the word (*padapūraṇa*).
In this regard, [the particles] *atha*, *khalu*, *vata*, *atho*, *assu*, *yagghe*, *hi*, *carahi*, *naṃ*, *taṃ*, *ca*, *tu*, *vā*, *vo*, *pana*, *have*, *kīva*, *ha*, *tato*, and *yathā* [are used].
Indeed, *sudaṃ*, *kho*, *ve*, *haṃ*, *enaṃ*, (*evaṃ*, *rū*), *seyyathidaṃ*, and so forth, serve to complete the phrasing.
Among these, *atha* is used for questions, immediate succession, topical headings, and so on. *Khalu* is used for negation, restriction, and well-known facts.
*Vata* is used for emphasis, lamentation, compassion, and intention. *Atho* is used for subsequent reference. *Hi* is used for cause and restriction.

*Ca* is used for emphasis (*visesa*), as a reason (*hetu*), and in the sense of exclusion (*nivattanā*) and so forth. *Pana* is also used for emphasis. *Have* and *ve* are used in the sense of certainty (*ekaṃsa*).

*Haṃ* is used for dejection (*visāda*) and astonishment (*vimha*). [It is also used] in the sense of sorrow (*visāda*) and possibility (*sambhava*). *Seyyathidaṃ* is used in the sense of "what is that? (*taṃ katamaṃ*). The fulfillment of meaning (*atthapūraṇa*) is twofold:
that which is joined with a case ending and that which is not joined with a case ending. *Atthi*, *sakkā*, and *labbhā*—these [are such].

This is the first [section]. *Āvuso*, *ambo*, *bho*, *haṃbho*, *are*, *hare*, *re*, and *je*—these are used for addressing. *Divā*, *bhiyyo*, *namo*, and *rū*—these are used in the first and second cases.
*Sayaṃ*, *sāmaṃ*, *saṃ*, *sammā*, and *kinti*—these are used in the sense of the third case (*sayaṃ* = by oneself).

Words ending in the suffixes *so*, *to*, and *dhā*, as well as *suttaso*, *padaso*, *aniccato*, *dukkhato*, *ekadhā*, *dvidhā*, and so forth [are used in the same way]. Words ending in the suffixes *tave* and *tuṃ* are used only in the fourth case.
*Kātave* means "to be done," *dātave* means "to be given"; *kātuṃ* means "to do" and *kāretuṃ* means "to cause to do"; (*dātuṃ*, *rū*) *dāpetuṃ* means "to cause to give," and so forth.

*So* ending in the suffix *-to* occurs in the sense of the ablative case, as in *dīghaso* ("from afar"), *oraso* ("from one's own [son]"), *rājato* ("from the king"), or *corato* ("from the thief"), and so forth.

*To* also occurs in the sense of the locative case, as well as those ending in suffixes such as *-tra* and *-ttha*, as in *ekato* ("on one side"), *purato* ("in front"), *pacchato* ("behind"), *passato* ("at the side"), *piṭṭhito* ("from behind"), *pādato* ("from the foot"), *sīsato* ("from the head"), *aggato* ("from the top"), *mūlato* ("from the root"), *yatra*, *yattha*.
*yahiṃ*, *tatra*, *tattha*, *tahiṃ*, etc. *samantā*, *sāmantā*, *parito*, *abhito*, *samantato*, *ekajjhaṃ*, *ekamantaṃ*, *heṭṭhā*, *upari*,
*uddhaṃ*, *adho*, *tiriyaṃ*, *sammukhā*, *paramukhā*, *āvi*, *raho*, *tiro*, *uccaṃ*, *nīcaṃ*, *anto*,
*antarā*, *antaraṃ*, *ajjhattaṃ*, *bahiddhā*, *bāhirā*, *bāhiraṃ*, *bahi*, *oraṃ*, *pāraṃ*, *ārā*, *ārakā*.
*Pacchā*, *pure*, *huraṃ*, and *pecca*— these [express] the seventh [tense]. *Sampati*, *āyati*, *ajja*, *aparajjha*, *suve sve*, *uttarasuve* (rū), *hiyyo*,
*pare* (*parasuve*, rū), *sajju*, *sāyaṃ*, *pāto*, *kālaṃ*, *kallaṃ*, *divā*, *rattaṃ*, *niccaṃ*,
*satataṃ*, *abhiṇhaṃ*, *abhikkhaṇaṃ*, *muhuṃ*, *muhuttaṃ*, *bhūtapubbaṃ*, *purā*, *yadā*, *tadā* (*kadā*, rū).
*Iccādayo* (and so forth) belong to the locative case of time (*kālasattami*). Thus end those [particles] joined with case endings. Among those not joined with case endings:
*appeva*, *appevanāma*, and *nu* are used in the sense of doubt (*saṃsaya*). *Addhā*, *aññadatthu*, *taggha*, *jātu*, *kāmaṃ*, and *sasakkaṃ* are used in the sense of certainty (*ekaṃsa*).
*Evaṃ* and *iti* are used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). *Kacci*, *nu*, *nanu*, and *kathaṃ*...
*Kiṃ* and *rū*: these are used in the sense of questioning. *Evaṃ*, *iti*, and *itthaṃ*: these are used in the sense of illustration (*nidassana*).
*Iti* is also used in the senses of cause (*hetu*) and the conclusion of a statement (*vākyaparisamatti*). *Yāva*, *tāva*, *yāvatā*, *tāvatā*, *kittāvatā*, *ettāvatā*, and *kīva*:

these are used in the sense of limitation (*paricchedana*). *Evaṃ*, *sāhu*, *lahu*, *opāyikaṃ*, *paṭirūpaṃ*, *āma*, and *sādhu*: these are used in the sense of acceptance (*sampaṭicchana*). *Tathā* and *yathā* [are used] as *yatheva*.

In the same way, *evaṃ*, *evameva*, *evampi*, *yathāpi*, *seyyathāpi*, *seyyathāpināma*, *viya*, *iva*, *yathariva*, *tathariva*, *yathānāma*, *tathānāma*, *yathāhi*, *tathāhi*, *yathāca*, and *tathāca*—these have the sense of resemblance (*paṭibhāga*).
Furthermore, *yathā* is used in the senses of fitness (*yoggatā*), wish (*icchā*), non-transgression of the word-meaning (*padatthānativatti*), and demonstration (*nidassana*).
*Evaṃ* is used in the senses of instruction (*upadesa*), question (*pañha*), and so forth.

*Ca*: in the sense of inclusion (*anuggaha*). *Dhi*: in the sense of reproach (*garaha*). *Aho*: in the senses of reproach, praise (*pasaṃsana*), and aspiration (*patthana*). *Nāma*: in the senses of reproach, praise, perception (*saññā*), and inquiry (*pañha*).
*Sādhu*: in the senses of praise and entreaty (*yācana*). *Iṅgha* and *handa*: in the sense of incitement (*codana*).

*Sādhu*, *suṭṭhu*, and *evam etam*: in the sense of rejoicing (*anumodana*). *Kira*: in the senses of hearsay (*anussavana*) and untrustworthiness (*asaddheyya*). *Nunā*: in the senses of inference (*anumāna*), recollection (*anussaraṇa*), and reflection (*parivitakka*).
*Kasmā* is used in the sense of asking for a reason. *Yasmā* and *tasmā* likewise; *tathā hi* and *tena* are used in the sense of cutting off the reason [i.e., providing a conclusion].

*Saha*, *saddhiṃ*, and *amā* (also *samaṃ* and *rū*) are used in the sense of simultaneous action. *Vinā* and *rite* are used in the sense of separation. *Nānā* is used in the sense of manifold, diverse, or many kinds.

*Puthu* is used in the sense of separate, distinct, or not aggregated. *Duṭṭhu* and *ku* are used in the sense of loathsomeness (*jigucchā*). *Puna* is used in the sense of again or a second time. *Appa* is used in the sense of not first.

How [are they used]? *Dhā* is used in the sense of "he says" (*kiñcaiti*) and in the division of numbers (*saṃkhyāvibhāge*). *Īsakaṃ* is used in the sense of slightness (*appamāne*) and smallness (*appamatte*). *Saṇikaṃ* is used in the sense of slowness (*mandatthe*).
*Khippaṃ*, *araṃ*, *lahuṃ*, *āsu*, *tuṇhaṃ*, and *aciraṃ* are used in the sense of speed (*sīghatthe*). *Ciraṃ* and *cirassaṃ* are used in the sense of a long time (*dīghakāle*).

*Ce* means "if" (*yadi*) and is used in the sense of doubt (*saṃkāvaṭṭhāne*). *Dhuraṃ* is used in the sense of firmness (*thira*) and determination (*avadhāraṇe*). *Dhuvaṃ* is also used in the sense of firmness and determination.
*rū*. *Hā* expresses sorrow (*visāda*). *Tuṇhī* means silence (*abhāsana*). *Sacchi* means directly perceived (*paccakkha*). *Musā* means false, wrong, untrue (*micchā-alika-asacce*).
*Suvatthi* is used in blessings (*āsiṭṭha*), and so forth. Verbal roots ending in the suffixes *-tuna*, *-ktvāna*, and *-ktvā* occur in the sense of longing (*ussukkanatthe*).
For example: *passituna*, *passiya*, *passitvāna*, *passitvā*; *disvā*, *disvāna*, *dassetvā*; *dātuna*, *datvāna*, *datvā*, *upādāya*, *dāpetvā*, *viññāya*, *viceyya*.
"Having removed," "having approached," "having struck down," "having reached," "having undertaken," "having come"—and so forth.
A distinction is made according to case endings; likewise for nouns with gender, and for "you" (*tumha*) and others in their respective genders.
However, there is no such distinction for particles such as *neva*, *atthi*, and so on.
Thus, this particle-word (nipātapada) should be understood as being free from nouns, verbs, and prefixes.
It is a non-derivational word (nepātika).
Furthermore, there are masculine genders, feminine genders, and neuter genders.
That which has a gender marker (tiliṅga) and that which lacks a gender marker (aliṅga)—the nominal [base] is established as fivefold.
Thus ends the second section, the Section on Nouns, within the *Payogasiddhi*.
3. The Section on Grammatical Relations (*Kārakakaṇḍa*).
Now, the different meanings of the case-endings (*vibhatti*) are stated.

In this context, they are called *vibhatti* because they divide even a single meaning according to factors such as the object (*kamma*) and so forth, and according to number such as singularity (*ekatta*) and so forth; these are the endings beginning with *-si*.

They are, moreover, sevenfold by way of the divisions beginning with the nominative (*paṭhama*). Among them, for example, the nominative case is [defined] as "the nominative occurs in the sense of mere identity" (*paṭhamā atthamatte*).
[The suffix] *hoti*. When the vowel *o* of *sissa* is elided and replaced by *a*, [the resulting forms] are "man" (*naro*), "woman" (*itthī*), and "neuter" (*napuṃsakaṃ*).
The meaning of a noun consists of its own referent, substance, gender, number, and the fivefold set beginning with object (*kamma*);
this is called the general meaning of that [noun].
Thus, the meaning of a name (nāma-attha) is fivefold:
birth (jāti), action (kriyā), quality (guṇa), substance (davba), and likewise the name itself (nāma).
The meaning of a word (sadda-attha) and the word itself (sa-sadda) are each divided fivefold in this context.
How is it that the word for "genus" (*jāti*) is also a word for "quality" (*guṇa*), and so forth?
Among distinct things, there arise cognitions and words that are non-distinct—such as "strength" in the case of a "strong man" (*sabala*) and others.
This is the genus (*jāti*) which resides in them, like a garland (*mālā*) strung upon a thread (*sutta*).

Those who know that [grammar] maintain that the meaning of a word (*padattha*) consists of the agent and other factors of action (*kattukammaṭṭha*), which are established by the collection of kārakas and are not themselves substantial entities (*adabbabhūta*).
Therefore, that which is distinct from the substance (*dabba*) and serves as the cause for the cognition of it is the *nimitta* (the signifier).
That which has the nature of perishing, though devoid of qualities, is called a "quality" (guṇa).

Here, the meaning is as follows: by the word "and" (*ca*), both that which has the nature of perishing, such as "the cloth is white," and that which has the nature of not perishing, such as "space is vast," are called "qualities" when they are separate from the self (*atta*) and lack [intrinsic] qualities.
Whatever is distinguished in any way, that is called a "substance" (*dabba*).
Therefore, even genus (*jāti*) and so forth are such [generalities], yet their substantiality (*dabbatta*) is postulated.

Herein, when "genus of cow" or "genus of horse" is stated, the genus is the substance. When "blue quality" is stated, the quality is the substance. And because the action of cooking is distinguished from actions such as going, the action itself is the substance.
In some cases, that which possesses a name and a substance is spoken of as the designatum (*saññī*).
"Name" (nāma) refers to that which is consciousness (citta), while "perception" (saññā) is the word for its designation.

Even though name possesses substantiality (dabbatta), it is recognized by the term "consciousness" and so forth alone, and not by terms such as "pot" or "cloth" despite their possessing substantiality;

therefore, "name" is stated as the designatum (saññī). Because it expresses that [designation], consciousness and the rest are determined to be the "word for the designation" (saññāsadda)—this is the intended meaning.
This fivefold meaning is twofold: the literal meaning (*saddattha*) and the meaning understood through implication (*sāmatthiyā gamyamānattha*).

For instance, in the statement “The fat man does not eat by day,” the negation of eating during the day is the literal meaning, whereas eating at night is understood through implication. Therefore, it is said:
“The operation of a word in the comprehension of meaning may be threefold.”
Regarding the phrase "The primary [meaning] is the nature of the characteristics and the marks":
here, however, the primary meaning applies when the object is immediately present; the characteristic meaning applies when the object is concealed;
and the other meaning of the sentence functions only with respect to the object itself.

The word "bed" (*mañca*) is primary when used in its direct sense; it is indicative when used in a transferred sense, as in "the beds are shouting"; and it is suggestive when used in the sense of an entire sentence, such as a verse.
According to the distinction of function, the word itself is considered threefold:
denotative, indicative, and suggestive. Its meaning is likewise held to be threefold.
The word *vaca* is indicative (*lakkhaṇika*), and thus the term *byañjana* (phoneme) is well-expressed;
according to the stated sequence, it becomes fivefold through the divisions of *jāti* (genus) and so forth.
38. In the sense of addressing—
The first case ending occurs after words used for addressing (āmantaṇā) and so forth, when there is merely the sense of the object. "O man," "O woman," "O neuter.
Addressing is the act of making someone face one by means of a word;
it applies to an existing entity. In the case of what is to be enjoined, there is no such thing as "let him be a king."

Action (*kriyā*) is the cause; however, the factor (*kāraka*) that performs the action is sixfold, distinguished as object (*karman*), agent (*kartṛ*), instrument (*karaṇa*), recipient (*sampradāna*), limit (*apādāna*), and locus (*adhikaraṇa*). This is as follows: 2.2.

The second case ending is used for the object (*karman*). That which is performed—that is, that which is connected with the action of the agent—is the object (*karman*); in that factor of the object, the second case ending is employed.
It exists. It is threefold, by way of the divisions of production (*nibbatti*), transformation (*vikati*), and attainment (*patti*).
Among these, in the case of productive action (*nibbattikamma*): a mother gives birth to a son; food produces pleasure; Datta makes a mat.

In the case of transformative action (*vikati*): he turns wood into charcoal; he fashions gold into a bracelet; he reaps rice. In the case of attaining action (*patti*): Datta enters the house; he sees the sun.
One hears the Dhamma and attends upon the wise.
And it is said:
"Kamma is considered to be threefold, distinguished by way of its arising, its transformation, and its attainment."
"An abode that is accessible for the performance of tasks, like a house with a pleasant hearth.

In the sense of "he makes a vast, beautiful mat," there is indeed the status of object (*kamma*) for that which is endowed with qualities; this is because it is connected to the action in the phrases "he makes it vast" and "he makes it beautiful.
However, in the expression "rice is being cooked" (*odano paccati*), the status of object is not understood from the word *odana* [alone].
Furthermore, [the object is expressed] by way of verbal expression (ākhyātata). As in the case of desired action (*icchitakamma*):

"He milks milk from the cow," "He asks for a cow from the owner of cows," "He shuts the cows in the pen," "He asks the boy the way," "He begs a cow from the owner of cows," and "He gathers fruits from the tree."
The meaning of "rukkha" (tree) is as follows: he teaches the Dhamma to his pupil. Here, forms such as *payo* (milk) and *gāvaṃ* (cow) are desired;
whereas *gāvuṃ*, *gomantaṃ*, and so on, are undesired. Likewise, even in the case of what is undesired, one crushes a thorn or swallows poison.
And even in that which is neither desired nor undesired, one approaches the foot of a tree while going to the village.

In the case of *adhi-ṭhā* and *adhi-sāna* used with a location (*ādhāra*), as in: "he will lie upon the earth" (*pathaviṃ adhisessati*), "he stands over the village" (*gāmaṃ adhiṭṭhāti*), and "he dwells in the tree" (*rukkhaṃ ajjhāvasati*).

Here, "upon the earth" (*pathaviṃ*) means "on the earth" (*pathaviyaṃ*). Similarly, it applies to *abhi* preceded by *ni*, as in "it enters into the Dhamma" (*dhammaṃ abhinivisate*) or "in the Dhamma.
Likewise for *upa* and *anu* preceded by *vasati*: "he dwells near the village" (*gāmaṃ upavasati*) and "he dwells along the village" (*gāmaṃ anuvasati*).
He dwells in a monastery (*vihāra*), he inhabits a village (*gāma*), he resides in a house (*agāra*);

here "village" (*gāma*) means "in the village. Likewise, in the case of drinking and wandering: "he drinks from a river," "he wanders through a village"; the meaning is "in the river. "If he will not speak to me"—the meaning is "with me.
The accusative case is also used for the object of a verb of opposition; as in: "May the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) occur to you, Cunda."
The meaning is: "May the factors of enlightenment speak to him. The meaning of "an analogy occurs to me" (*upamā maṃ patibhāti*) is "an analogy presents itself to me" (*upamā maṃ upaṭṭhāti*).

In the phrase "it does not occur to him" (*tassa na paṭibhāti*), the genitive case is used according to the rule for the governing noun (*dhātunāyutte*). 3. [The accusative is used] with words expressing time or distance when there is continuous connection (*kāladdhānam accantasamyoge*).
The second case ending occurs after words expressing time or distance when they denote absolute connection with a substance, a quality, or an action. Regarding time:

*sattāhaṃ gavapānaṃ* (drinking of cows for seven days), *māsaṃ maṃsodanaṃ* (rice and meat for a month), *saradaṃ ramaṇīyā nadī* (the river is beautiful throughout autumn), *sabbakālaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ nandanaṃ* (the Nandana grove is beautiful at all times), *tayo māse abhidhammaṃ deseti* (he teaches the Abhidhamma for three months).
Regarding distance: *yojanaṃ vanarāji* (a row of trees for a league), *yojanaṃ dīgho pabbato* (a mountain long for a league), *kosaṃ sajjhāyati* (he recites for a kos).
In such instances as "Having dressed [in the morning] at the time of the early morning" (*pubbanhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā*) and "At one time the Blessed One...

on this night the four Great Kings," the accusative case is used for words expressing time in connection with an uninterrupted duration (*accantasaṃyoga*); alternatively, it may be a reversal of the case-ending (*vibhattivipallāsa*) due to the rule of frequent application (*bahulaṃvidhāna*).

In phrases such as "The recitation was learned in a month" (*māsena anuvāko dhīto*) and "The recitation was learned in a fortnight" (*kosenānuvāko dhīto*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇatthe*).
4. Regarding the application [of case endings] for verbs meaning "going," "knowing," "eating," "sound," "intransitive," and "roasting" etc.:

when these verbs—those meaning going, knowing, eating, sound, intransitives, and those such as *bhajati* (to break)—are used in the causative sense (*payojje*), the second case ending occurs for the agent (*kattari*). Examples:
*datto gamayati māṇavakaṃ gāmaṃ*, "Datta causes the boy to go to the village," or *yāpayati*, "he causes to subsist"; *guru bodhayati*, "the teacher causes [the pupil] to know."
He causes the young brahmin to know the Dhamma, or he causes him to experience it. The mother feeds her son rice-gruel, or she causes him to eat it.

The teacher causes the pupil to recite the Veda, or he causes him to read it. When used with a meaning other than "causing to act," the second case is used for the object. The man causes Datta to eat, or he causes him to taste.
The man causes another to fry, causes another to pound, or causes another to spread out [a mat].
5. The second case ending optionally occurs for the agent (*kattari*) when *harati* and similar verbs are employed. For example: *poso hāreti bhāraṃ dattaṃ*, or *datteneti*.
*rājā dassayate janaṃ*, or *janeneti*. *dattaṃ abhivādayate guruṃ*, or *datteneti*. *ajjhohāreti*.
"Barley meal was given," or "by Datta. "Datta causes [the meal] to be made," or "by Datta. In these examples, the instrumental case is used for the agent throughout. 6. Not for *khāda* and so forth:

For the causative forms of verbs such as *khāda* (to eat), the accusative case is not used for the agent. This [rule] is intended to prohibit [the application of the rule] in certain instances of verbs meaning "motion" (*gatyattha*) and others.

He causes [something] to be eaten by means of a tooth; he causes [something] to be taken up by means of a tooth; he causes [someone] to be summoned by means of a tooth; he causes [something] to be made to sound by means of a tooth;
he causes [someone] to be led by means of a tooth; he causes [someone] to cry out by means of a tooth. 7. Those joined with *jh* and so forth.

The second case ending occurs when [a word] is joined with *dhi* and other such particles. In the example *dhi ratthu maṃ putikāyaṃ*, the meaning is: "Shame on me, who am in between Rājagaha and Nālandā—that is, in the middle, which is the space between Rājagaha and Nālandā.
In *samādhāna-mantarena mucalinda-mabhito saraṃ*, this second case ending is used in the sense of the sixth case (the genitive).
8. With respect to the meanings of "characteristic" (lakkhaṇa) and so forth, the second case ending occurs after a word joined with the prefix *abhi*.

In the example "The moon shines upon the tree" (*rukkham abhivijjotate cando*), the tree is the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) and the moon is that which is characterized (*lakkhitabba*); therein, by means of the prefix *abhi*, the fact that the tree functions as the characteristic is made manifest.
"A tree is called 'joined with' (abhinā yutto). "Devadatta was kind toward his mother" (*sādhu devadatto mātaram-abhi*); the meaning is that he attained kindness toward his mother.
"The moon shines upon every tree" (*rukkham rukkham-abhi*); the meaning is "tree after tree. 9.
*pati* and *pari* [are used] in the sense of division (*bhāga*).
The second case ending occurs after a word joined with *patiparī* in the sense of "characteristics" (*lakkhaṇa*), etc., and in the sense of "a share" (*bhāga*). Examples:
*rukkhaṃ pati vijjotate* (it shines toward the tree), *sādhu devadatto mātaraṃ pati* (Devadatta is kind toward his mother), *rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ pati tiṭṭhati* (he stands facing each tree).
The phrase *yaṃ ettha maṃ pati siyā* (whatever there may be here for me) has the sense of "that which is my share," meaning "let that be given. The same applies to *rukkhaṃ parī*, etc.

10. *Anunā* is the second [case ending] in the sense of a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), etc. It flashes forth following the tree (*rukkhamanu vijjotate*); it rained following the act of truth (*saccakiriyaṃ manu vassi*). It is both a cause and a characteristic: "Devadatta was good toward his mother" (*sādhu devadatto mātaramanu*); "it flashes forth from tree to tree" (*rukkhaṃ rukkhamanu vijjotate*); "whatever there may be here following me" (*yad ettha mamamanu siyā*). 11. *Saha* has the sense of the hand (*hattha*).

The second case ending occurs after a word joined with *anu* when it signifies accompaniment (*sahattha*). For example, *pabbataṃ anu tiṭṭhati* means "he stands together with the mountain" (*pabbatena saha*);

this is the sense. 12. Regarding inferiority (*hīna*): the second case ending occurs after a word joined with *anu* when it signifies inferiority. For example, *anusāriputtaṃ paññavanto bhikkhū* means "the wise monks are inferior to Sāriputta in wisdom" (*sāriputtato paññāya hīnā*); this is the sense.

13. When the prefix *upa* is used in the sense of inferiority (*hīnattha*), the second case ending is employed after a word joined with it: *upasāriputtaṃ paññavanto* ("those possessing wisdom are inferior to Sāriputta"). 16.
The third case ending is used for the agent and the instrument (*kattukaraṇesu*).
The third case ending occurs for the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the agent (*kāraka*). The Dhamma was taught by the Victor; Māra was conquered by the Buddha; the man was bitten by a snake.
Where even the cause of a cause is spoken of as a cause, there too the third case is used:
the village was burned by thieves; the meal was prepared with grass; the monasteries were caused to be built by the faithful.

The agent who, being self-dependent, brings about an action—whether dissociated or associated with it—is called the "doer" (*kattā*). Furthermore, that instrument (*karaṇa*) is twofold, by way of being internal or external:
for example, one performs work with the hand, sees a form with the eye, or cognizes a mental object with the mind; or, as in "he reaps the field with a sickle," or "he burns the hut with fire."
Just as the instrument (karaṇa) is twofold—external and internal—as in "he cuts rice with a sickle" and "he beholds the moon with his eye";
likewise, in "naturally handsome" and "Gotama by clan," the third case ending is used for the instrument because of the occurrence of the root *bhū* (to become). Thus it is.

Renowned by the name Sāriputta, a Buddha born of the Khattiya caste, seven years of age at birth, a reed-worker by craft, twenty-nine years of age—thus he runs on even ground, he runs on uneven ground; he buys grain with two *doṇas* for the price of one.
17. With his own hand.
The third case may be used with the word *saha* when it means "together with. Like the sixth case, the third case occurs only when [the companion] is not the primary factor. Examples:

*puttena sahāgato* (came together with a son), *puttena saddhiṃ āgato* (came along with a son); *vitakkena saha vattati* (it exists together with thought); *puttena saha thūlo* (fat together with a son); *nisīdi bhagavā saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena* (the Blessed One sat down together with the community of monks);
*sahassena samaṃ mitā* (measured as equal to a thousand); *sabbehi me piyehi manāpehi nānābhāvo* (separation from all those who are dear and pleasing to me).

18. Regarding the third case ending used for the sense of "acting upon" (lakkhaṇe lakkhaṇe vattamānato tatiyā): She complained to her neighbors because of her split head and the blood flowing from it;
she would have another new bowl exchanged for one that was less than five years old; he saw the wandering ascetic with his triple staff.
Blind in one eye, crooked in one hand, lame in one foot, hunchbacked in the back.
Thus, by means of that deficient limb, the deformity of the person possessing the deficiency is characterized. 19.
In the sense of cause (hetumhi).

The third case (instrumental) is used for the cause (*hetu*) of an action characterized by dwelling (*vāsa*), etc. He dwells because of food; he dwells because of knowledge; one does not become an outcast by birth, but one becomes an outcast by action; one is wealthy through giving; a family [is distinguished] by conduct; by that [conduct], the hand is a giver of desires. 20.
The fifth case (*pañcamī*) is optionally used for the cause (*hetu*) ending in *-ṇa*. Bound on account of a hundred, or by means of a hundred.

21. When a quality (*guṇa*) has become subordinate (*paraṅgabhūta*) to a cause (*hetu*), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) optionally occurs. For example: *jaḷattā baddho* (bound because of dullness), or *jaḷattena* (by means of dullness); *paññāya mutto* (liberated by wisdom); *hutvā abhāvato aniccā* (impermanent because of the non-existence of having been);

*saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodho* (with the cessation of formations, there is the cessation of consciousness). Because of the rule of frequent application (*bahulavidhāna*), it also occurs in the sense of the seventh case (*sattamī*).

At that time, during that season, while engaged in a discussion on the Dhamma, Dhataraṭṭha from the east, Virūḷhaka from the south, and Kapilavatthu from the north approached the Blessed One, saying, "He shall be your teacher in my stead.
He ate for a month; in a single day he entered Bārāṇasī; in nine months he had a monastery built; [he spent] one kahāpaṇa.

"Deficient" (*ūno*), "deprived of wealth" (*dhanena vikalō*), "a quarrel with a sword" (*asinā kalaho*), "skilled in conduct" (*ācārena nipuṇō*), "mixed with sugar" (*guḷena missakaṃ*), "affable in speech" (*vācāya sakhilō*), "purpose served by a gem" (*maṇinā atthō*), "purpose served by wealth" (*dhanena atthō*), "he goes for a *yojana*" (*yojanena gacchati*)—in such cases, the third case ending is used either for the cause (*hetumhi*) or the instrument (*karaṇe*).

In the expression "he approves himself by himself" (*attanāva attānaṃ sammannati*), the third case ending is used for the agent (*kattari*) because of the frequent application of the rule regarding the reflexive pronoun (*paccatte bahulaṃvidhānā*). Likewise, [one says] "he sows in the field with sesame seeds" (*tilehi khette vapatīti*).
In the sense of the object (*kammatthe*), and in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyatthe*) as in "we are liberated from that Great Ascetic.
24. The Dative Case (*catutthī*) is used for the recipient (*sampadāne*):
that which is regarded as a recipient, whether insentient or sentient, is the recipient; and that [recipient] is expressed by the suffix *-dā*.
This [dative case] is indeed connected with the expression of the recipient (dhātu). In that context, the fourth case occurs.

And that [recipient] is threefold, according to non-prevention, urging, and consent, as in: "he gives a flower to the Buddha," "he gives water to the Bodhi tree," "he gives wealth to a beggar," and "he gives a gift to the monks."

The recipient (sampadāna) is said to be threefold by way of non-rejection, attainment, and permission: the tree, the beggar, and the monk. When there is an intention to express the locus (ādhāra), the locative case is also used, as in:
"Give to the Saṅgha, Gotamī"; "When given to the Saṅgha, I myself will be honored"; and "The woman who, having offered a garland made of straw to the Cetiya..."
25. *Tādatthye* (For the sake of that).

The dative case may be used in the sense of *tādatthya*. *Tādatthya* means the state of being for the sake of that (*tad-attha-bhāva*). In that state of being for the sake of that, the dative case may be used only when it is intended to be expressed.

"The state of being for the sake of that" is a genitive case used in the sense of a relationship between cause and effect (*nimitta-nimittī-sambandha*); therefore, this [rule] is an exception to the genitive.

In the relationship between a cause (*nimitta*) and its effect (*nimittin*), the dative case is used for the cause itself—as in "the sacrificial post" (*yūpa*)—but not for the effect itself, such as the wood.

Examples include: "wood for the sacrificial post" (*yūpāya dāru*); "he goes for the sake of cooking" (*pākāya vajati*); "I renounce my life for the sake of the Buddha's service" (*buddhassatthāya jīvitaṃ pariccajāmi*);

"neither for sport nor for intoxication, but for the fulfillment of what is deficient"; and "it leads to welfare, benefit, and happiness; it conduces to compassion for the world and to living in comfort."

Thus, this [use of the genitive] is stated here for the purpose of illustrating that it is the sixth case (genitive), since it has been established as the fourth case (*catutthī*) in the passage to be explained below:
"To whom is it pleasing?", "May the schism in the Saṅgha not be pleasing even to you, Venerable Sirs," "It is acceptable to the Saṅgha," and "The food does not suffice for him.
Here, the sixth case occurs when there is a desire to express a relationship; and thus, there would be no contradiction.
Because of their identical form, and because in such cases the connection [of the case ending] is accepted by grammarians (*saddikā*). For thus it is stated in the *Bhāgavutti*:

"The case endings of the subordinate word (*upapada*) are exceptions (*pavāda*) to the genitive. whereas in "Whose [Dhamma], or yours? (*kassa vā tuyhaṃ*), rather than saying "yours," one says "whose."
Or, "you approve of the Dhamma": this shows deviation [from the rule] by way of the nominative case (*paṭhamā*) when referring merely to the meaning.
Other cases should also be understood in this way, according to the tradition from other sources as well.

The exertion of ascetics is appropriate; it suffices for one, two, or three. I shall give you a simile:

a wrestler is capable of [withstanding] a wrestler; that is for his benefit; that is for his happiness; "welcome to you, Great King"—in all these cases, the genitive case is used in connection with the whole.
26. The Ablative Case:
The ablative case ending occurs after words denoting separation.
In the case of two vowels being joined, the preceding form (*pubbarūpa*) is substituted for both, except when *ya* follows.
That is called the ablative (*apādāna*); it is twofold, according to whether it is mobile or immobile.
For example: "A man running from a horse," "He fell from a cloth," and "Fruit from a tree.
In these cases, the horse is the mobile limit, for the man falls from it; the mountain is the immobile limit, for the forest-dwellers descend from it.
And that [kamma-ṭhāna] is "indicated" (*niddiṭṭha*) because a specific action regarding its object has been pointed out;

it is "taken up" (*upātta*) when it proceeds having made its object one where the action of departing (*apa-apagamana*) is employed or brought forward (*ajjhāhaṭa*); it is "inferable" (*anumeyya*) when it is exalted by some quality.
For example: "The sages depart from the village," "The king has gone out from the city," and "They restrain the mind from evil."

Fear arises from thieves; fear arises from craving; one trembles before evil. There is no sorrow, so whence could there be fear?
One receives training from an instructor (upajjhāya); one learns or hears from a teacher (ācariya). From the Buddha—
"They defeat" means that the followers of other sects are defeated; "they become vanquished" is the meaning. The Gaṅgā originates from the Himavat;
small streams originate from the Aciravatī. A son is born from the breast; a faculty is born from karma. A disciple disappears from the preceptor;
a son causes his parents to disappear—meaning he hides from them. It is very far from here because of its connection with what is distant.
The village of Naḷakāra; they say it is indeed much further than that. Not too far from the village: "Those foolish men are far removed from this Dhamma and Vinaya;
the Blessed One is far removed from them. They pay homage from afar. Seeing him approaching from afar. In the sense of proximity:
near the village, close to the village, in the vicinity of the village. In the sense of measure: four [yojanas] from Mathurā.
Regarding distance: Sāvatthī is forty-five yojanas from Rājagaha, near Saṅkassa. Regarding time:
Ninety-one aeons from now, after the passing of one hundred thousand years, a Buddha will arise in the world.

"Abhidhammā" means they ask about the Abhidhamma; having heard the Abhidhamma, he should rise from his seat. In connection with words denoting direction:

"from this [side] is that eastern direction," "from this [side] is that southern direction," from the Avīci hell up to the peak of existence, from the soles of the feet upwards, and from the hair on the head downwards.
In the sense of analysis: "there is nothing more refined or more distinguished than this," [as in the case of] one who has tamed himself.
Therefore, it is better; for although virtue (*sīla*) is superior to giving (*dāna*), I have heard much more than that—virtue is indeed better than what has been heard.
Regarding the application of abstention (*ārati*): abstaining from evil, refraining from taking life, being restrained from taking what is not given, and not refraining from false speech.
Regarding the application of purity (*suddha*): pure with respect to alluring things, and [pure] toward his mother and father.

And pure, beyond reproach. In the sense of liberation: "I declare him to be completely freed from suffering," "I am released from the bonds of Māra," "they are not released from death," "I am released from all snares. In the sense of seclusion:
"quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states. In the sense of measurement: "a league in length and breadth, and in depth..."
The measurement of Candabhāgā is one *yojana* in breadth; the Middle Country (*majjhima-deso*) is nine hundred *yojanas* in circumference.
Regarding the connection with "east" and so forth: "Monks, before my full enlightenment, prior to this, there were none; after that, there were the bordering regions;
and at a later time, [there were others]. Regarding the question: "From where are you? From where is your lordship? From Pāṭaliputta."

In the phrase *kicchā laddhaṃ*, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used for the quality (*guṇa*), meaning "obtained with difficulty. In *kicchena me adhigataṃ*, the third case (*tatiyā*) is used for the cause (*hetu*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*), as in *evaṃ thokā mutto* (thus released by little) or *thokena mutto* (released by means of little).

How is it that "it moves slightly" (*thokaṃ calati*) is expressed? Here, the second case is used for the object (*kamma*) which functions as an adverbial modifier of the action (*kriyāvisesana*). The meaning is "it performs a slight movement. It is called an adverbial modifier because "slightly" (*thokaṃ*) qualifies the action of moving.
That which is called an adverb (*kriyāvisesana*) is established by grammatical logic (*nyāyasiddha*) as being situated in the sense of either an object (*kammattha*) or an agent (*kattā*);
therefore, there is no separate rule for that purpose.

Indeed, it is established by logic because [the suffix] *-ana* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*) in the word *calana*; therefore, by logical principle, the singular number is used for both the state (*bhāva*) and the agent (*kattā*).

And [the suffix -tva] expresses oneness (*ekatta*), in the sense of a state (*bhāve*) it expresses the neuter gender (*napuṃsakatta*), and through its connection with the action of doing (*karoti-kriyā*) it expresses the status of an object (*kammatta*).
Furthermore, the verbal roots *kara-* and *bhū-*— whose meanings are expressed by the forms of *kāriya*— are all applicable to the root *satt-*.
Therefore, because it is stated, "Action (*kriyā*) and state (*bhāva*)—their commonality (*sāmañña*) is understood therein," these [terms] are appropriate.
In the sense of "a little" (*thoka*), [the suffix] *-ka* is applied.
In all cases, the ablative (*pañcamī*) is used within its own domain. Here, "that [usage] is worldly (*lokikā*) and based on speaker’s intention (*vivakkhā*)."
Because it has been stated, “It is not possible not to turn back,” there would be no undesirable consequence. In the sense of a limit (*maryādā*), “up to the mountain” means a field.
In the sense of pervasion (*abhividhi*), “the sound rises up as far as the Brahma-world” means that, excluding the mountain, it extends throughout the Brahma-world.
Here, the boundary being excluded is the limit (*maryādā*); the boundary being included is the pervasion (*abhividhi*).

27. With *apa* and *pari*, when they signify avoidance (*vajjana*), the fifth case ending occurs in construction with these two particles. For example: *apasālāya āyanti vāṇijā*, *parisālāya āyanti vāṇijā*. The meaning is: "the merchants come avoiding the hall" (*sālaṃ vajjetvā*). 28.
With *pati*, [the fifth case ending occurs] in the senses of representation (*paṭinidhi*) and giving back (*patidāna*).

When used in connection with *pati* (lord/master) in the sense of "substitute" (*paṭinidhi*) or "giving back" (*paṭidāna*), the fifth case ending occurs after a noun. *Sāriputto buddhassa pati* (Sāriputta is the substitute for the Buddha); *ghatassa telassa pati dadāti* (he gives back the master of the oil, i.e., the owner of the jar).
29. *Rite* [the second case ending and the fifth case ending occur].
When used in connection with the word *rite*, the second case ending and the fifth case ending occur after a noun. *Rite saddhammā* (apart from the True Dharma); *rite saddhammaṃ*.
30. *Vinā* and *aññatra* take the third case;

when used in conjunction with *vinā*, *aññatra*, and *aññathā*, the third, second, and fifth cases are used after a noun. *Vinā vātena*, *vinā vātaṃ*, *vinā vātasmā*. *Aññatra ekena piṇḍapātanīhārakena*, *aññatra dhammaṃ*, *aññatra dhammā*.
31. *Puthu* and *nānā* [take the same cases].

With these [words], the third and fifth cases occur. The separation of the grammatical rule (*yoga*) is for the purpose of excluding the second case. [Examples: *puthageva janena*, *puthageva janasmā*, *janena nānā*, *janasmā nānā*.
39. The sixth case occurs in relation to connection (*sambandha*).
When the sixth case occurs in relation to connection, as in the expression "the king’s man" (*rañño puriso*), because the king gives and the man receives, therefore—
He is known as "the king’s man. In the same way, whatever is dependent upon another—whether by way of being a servant and so forth, or by way of being property;
or by way of proximity, collection, part, modification, effect, state, genus, quality, action, and so on;
or by way of location, or by way of succession—that threefold meaning is called a relation (*sambandha*). For it has been said:

The meaning called "relation" (sambandha) arises from [the interaction of] action and its factors, and is caused by the state of dependence (assedaṃbha). In that case, the genitive case is prescribed.
For relation is indeed dependence (pāratantya); therefore, the genitive case occurs there.
"It is understood through the presence of an adjunct (*upādhi*), not from the perspective of a qualifier (*visesa*).
First, regarding the designation as an adjunct: "the king's man. In this context, the king is the qualifier because he excludes [the man] from those owned by Brahmins and others;
the man is the qualified (*visessa*) because he is distinguished by that [qualifier]. Regarding the connection with an object: "I have abundant wealth."
*Sakka*: a share for one; the bowl and robes of a monk. *Samīpa*: near the mango grove, not far from it; in the vicinity of Nibbāna itself.
*Samūha*: a heap of gold; a multitude of monks. *Avayava*: the head of a human being;
a branch of a tree. *Vikāra*: a transformation of gold; flour made from parched grain. *Kāriya*: [a derivative] of barley.
*Ankura*: the sound of a cloud; *puttā*: his many sons; *kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko*: the fruit and ripening of karmic actions. In the sense of a state (*avatthā*):
the manifestation of the aggregates (*khandhānaṃ pātubhāvo*), aging, or dissolution. In the sense of birth (*jāti*): the being of a human (*manussassa bhāvo*), the birth of humans.
In the sense of a quality (*guṇa*): the color of gold; the fame of the qualities of the Tathāgata, the Buddha, does not fade; the fragrance of flowers; [the taste] of fruits.
Taste; contact of the mind; there is no hundred of needles; a handful of sesame seeds; their conjunction; the release of a joint;
concerning the perfection of wisdom of the Tathāgata; "Is it well with you? Is it painful for you?"—thus a reflection arose in the mind;
the proficiency of wisdom; lightness of form, or malleability, or integration. In the context of a connection between actions: of the foot.
Lifting up, or casting down; the bending of the hand, giving, or stretching it out; the movement, standing, sitting, or lying down of the elements;
the name and clan of the Tathāgata, his cause, his mother and father, his appearing before him, to the south of the city, in the third month of the rains—there is no simile for this.
"An offering for Kuvera," and so forth. Moreover:
The birth, color, gait, horn, and name of a cow are thus established;
likewise, the birth and other qualities of grass are distinguished according to one's desire.

The suffix *ta* is elided after a word ending in *u*, as in *gottañca sabalodissa* (the lineage and the white bull) and *pākamanassa sukkatā* (the ripening of the white rice). In the case of *paṭassa siṅgaṃ meṇḍassa* (the horn of the white ram), it is distinguished from other [words]. From the standpoint of the grammatical rule (*ṭhānita*), the *e* of vowels is elided.

From the standpoint of the augment (*āgamita*), the *s* of *suña* is elided. In the construction with a genitive (*sāmiyoga*), examples are *devānaṃ indo* (the lord of the gods) and *migānaṃ rājā* (the king of beasts).

In connection with *rujā* (sickness) and so forth: *devadattassa rujati* (Devadatta is ill), *tassa rogo uppajji* (a disease arose for him), *mahāsenāpatīnaṃ ujjhāpetabbaṃ* (it should be complained against the generals), *rajakassa vatthaṃ dadāti* (he gives cloth to the washerman), *musāvādassa ottappaṃ* (shame regarding lying), and so on.

In connection with *yaja* (to sacrifice): *pupphassa buddhassa yajati* (he sacrifices to the Buddha with a flower), meaning "with a flower. Likewise: *ghatassa aggiṃ juhati* (he offers fire to the lamp). In the sense of being satisfied (*suhita*): *odanassa pattaṃ pūretvā* (having filled the bowl with rice).

The fool is filled with various kinds of impurity, filled with silver and gold; he is filled with evil. The genitive case is used here because of the frequent application of the rule for the agent (*kitaka*) and the instrument (*appayoga*).
"Appointed by the king," "honored," "venerated," "esteemed," "revered," or "respected.
"O monks, the Deathless has not been tasted by those by whom mindfulness directed to the body has not been tasted. It is esteemed as excellent by the many; it has been well-penetrated.
The Dhamma-element of the Buddhas; the wise one who guards the Dhamma. Regarding the sense of "action" (kamma), there are those who speak of him as:

one who performs actions with deliberation, a giver of the Deathless, a reconciler of those who are divided, a promoter of those who are united, an awakener of the world, one for whom there is no doer of action and no experiencer of its result, and one who does not deceive the world.
Sensitivity derived from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). In the case of the construction with *sarati* ("to remember"): "he remembers his mother"; no one else remembers them;
it is due to the karmic condition of sentient beings that he desires [something] for his son. In the case of the construction with *karoti* ("to do"):

"he attends to the water," "he attends to the wound"; the meaning is "he prepares" (*abhisaṅkharoti*). Also in the sense of the ablative case (*pañcamī*), when used in connection with the sense of fear of decline (*parihānibhaya*).
The sixth [case] occurs because of not having heard the Dhamma in its various modes; for instance: "Why indeed do I fear that happiness?
All tremble at punishment, all fear death; one who is afraid of four snakes of terrible venom," and so forth.
Alternatively, the third case is used in the sense of equality (*tulyārtha*).
In the sense of equality (*tulyattha*), when used in conjunction [with another word], the sixth case (*chaṭṭhī*) or the third case (*tatiyā*) occurs. For example: *pituno tulyo* or *pitarā tulyo*;
*mātuyā tulyo* or *mātarā tulyo*. 32.

Regarding the seventh case (*sattamī*): the locus (*ādhāra*). That which serves as the basis for the agent, the object, or the action—such as sitting, cooking, and so forth—is called the "locus factor" (*ādhārakāraka*). How so?
Devadatta sits on a mat; he cooks rice in a pot.

Because the mat and the pot sustain the actions of sitting and cooking—which are the objects of Devadatta’s agency—they are said to "sustain" those respective actions; thus, the seventh case ending occurs for them.

That [locative relation] is fourfold: pervasive (*byāpika*), contiguous (*opasilesika*), objective (*vesayika*), and locative (*sāmīpika*). Among these, that which serves as the absolute support for what is contained within it—
That which is pervasive (*byāpika*) is like oil in sesame seeds, water in milk, or clarified butter in curds.
That which exists as an adherence or clinging through the state of being contained within independently established entities is "adherent" (*opasilesika*).
For example: the Saṅgha seated on a seat; cooking rice in a pot; water in a jar; standing at a distance; or standing nearby.

That which is metaphorical by way of proximity (*sāmīpika*) is where, having applied the designation of the proximate object to that which is near it, the state of being a locus (*ādhārabhāva*) is figuratively attributed for the purpose of indicating dependence upon it;
for example, "a roar on the Ganges," meaning a roar near the Ganges. [As in: "He dwells at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove.
That [metaphor] wherein there is a conceptualization of a locus either by way of a change of state or by way of delimiting another location is...
It is enticed. Just as birds move in the sky, humans on the earth, and fish in the water;
as one who has fallen upon palaces, yet the mind delights in evil; as one who is confident in the Buddha’s teaching, excellent in wisdom, and skilled in the Vinaya;
as one who is good toward his mother and skilled toward his father.
Action (kiriyā) is that by which the agent and the object of action are supported;
that support (ādhāra) is said to be fourfold, according to its divisions such as the pervasive and so forth.
The pervasive [support] consists of sesame milk and the like; the surface-support is a mat and so forth.
But that which is proximate, such as the Ganges and so forth, is considered the object (visaya). 33.

The locative case occurs in the sense of a cause (nimitta) and in the sense of being a cause (nimittattha). A leopard is killed for its skin; an elephant is killed for its tusks. Seeing fear even in the slightest faults, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for intentional lying. In all these instances, the sense is that of a cause.
34. *Yabbhāvo bhāvalakkhaṇaṃ*:

When the state (*bhāva*) of one thing becomes the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) of another state, the locative case (*sattamī*) is used from that [first state]. For example: *kāle gāvīsu duyhamānāsu gato, duddhāsu āgato* ("At the time when the cows were being milked, he went;
when they had been milked, he returned"). Here, the act of going is characterized by the act of milking, and the act of returning is characterized by the act of having milked.

The same applies to what follows. Sāriputta, when the Bodhisatta had gone out in the morning and returned in the evening, at the very moment he was being born, this ten-thousandfold world system trembled.
Stones and pebbles, gravel, stumps, and thorns—
"All paths avoid him when the Leader of the World is walking.
"When this exists, that comes to be," and so forth. "It rains for him out of season; it does not rain for him in season"—this is the locative case used in the sense of the object (*visaya-sattamī*).
35. And the sixth case is used in the sense of disregard (*anādara*).
When the state (bhāva) of one thing becomes the characteristic (lakkhaṇa) of another state, the sixth case (genitive) and the seventh case (locative) are used when disregard (anādara) is implied.
For example: "He went forth while his parents were weeping against their will," or "while his parents were weeping. Also:
"He leads [the victim] away while striking him, even as the King of the Śivis looks on," and "Death departs taking [him] away, while the great multitude of people looks on."

“Master of cows” (*gunnaṃ sāmī*) is a genitive used in the sense of a relationship; “master in cows” (*gosu sāmī*) is a locative used in the sense of a sphere of activity. Likewise: master of cows (*gunnaṃ issaro*), master in cows (*gosu issaro*);
lord of cows (*gunnaṃ adhipati*), lord in cows (*gosu adhipati*); heir of cows (*gunnaṃ dāyādo*), heir in cows (*gosu dāyādo*);

witness of cows (*gunnaṃ sakkhī*), witness in cows (*gosu sakkhī*); surety for cows (*gunnaṃ patibhū*), surety in cows (*gosu patibhū*); skilled in dancing and singing (*kusalā naccagītassa*), skilled in dancing and singing (*kusalā naccagīte*).

In *naccagīte*, *āyutto kaṭakaraṇassa*, and *āyutto kaṭakaraṇe*, the locative case is used in the sense of the locus (*adhāra*). Likewise, the locative case is used in the sense of the object (*visaya*), as in:

*bhikkhūsu abhivādenti* (they salute among the monks), *muddhani cumbitvā* (having kissed on the head), *bāhāsu gahetvā* (having grasped by the arms), *hatthesu piṇḍāya caranti* (they wander for alms among the hands), *kadalīsu gaje rakkhanti* (they guard the elephants among the plantains), *ñāṇasmiṃ pasanno* (faithful in wisdom), and *ñāṇasmiṃ ussukko* (eager for wisdom). These are examples of the locative case in the sense of the object.
36. *Niddhāraṇa* (Selection):
Selection is the setting apart of a portion from a whole by means of genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), or action (*kriyā*). From that which it is performed, the sixth and seventh cases arise.
For example: *sālayo sūkadhaññānaṃ pathyatamā*, "Of the grains of *sūkadhanna*, the *sāli* rice is the most wholesome"; *sūkadhaññesu sālayo*.
Most wholesome. Among cows, the black cow is the one with the most excellent milk; among cows, the black cow is the one with the most excellent milk.
Among those going, the runner is the swiftest; among those going, the runner is the swiftest. 14.
[The seventh case] in the sense of superiority.

When there is a sense of "excess," the seventh case ending occurs after a word joined with *upa*. For example: *upakhāriyaṃ doṇo* ("a *doṇa* measure in excess of a *khāri*"); the meaning is that the *doṇa* is more than the *khāri*. Likewise: *upanikkhe kahāpaṇaṃ* ("a *kahāpaṇa* coin in addition"). 15. *Sāmitthe + dhinā*:

When there is a sense of lordship (*sāmibhāva*), the seventh case ending occurs after a word joined with *adhi*. For example: *adhibrahmadatte pañcālā* ("the Pañcālas are under Brahmadatta") or *adhipañcālesu brahmadatto* ("Brahmadatta is over the Pañcālas").

*Brahmadatta* means one whose lord is Brahmadatta; that is, the Pañcālas. Regarding the "superior deities" (*adhideva*), the Buddha is superior to conventional deities (*sammutideva*) and the rest; this is the meaning of "superior.
And here, among the meanings already mentioned, this is the distinction:
*Kāraka* (the agent), *sādhaka* (the accomplisher), *nibbattaka* (the producer), and *kriyānimitta* (the cause of action) are identical in meaning.

Furthermore, although it is fivefold according to the distinctions of substance (*dabba*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), name (*nāma*), and genus (*jāti*)—as in the examples *daṇḍo* (the staff), *dhavalo* (white), *pacanaṃ* (cooking), *citto* (Citta), and *goti* (cow)—it is sixfold by way of the object (*kamma*), the agent (*kattā*), and so forth.

Among these, that which possesses power is the *sattikāraka* (active agent); the substance and other factors that serve as its support are the *tatraṭṭhakāraka* (static agent), but not in a primary sense.

If these [factors] were primary, then because those powers (*satti*) and substances (*dabba*) would be mutually occupied by their respective forms, whatever serves as a locus (*ādhāra*) would be only a locus;
at certain times it would not function as an instrument (*karaṇa*) or take on the form of an agent (*kartṛ*).

Therefore, there could be no distinction between agent, instrument, and locus for a single entity, such as in the expressions "the pot cooks," "he cooks with the pot," or "he cooks in the pot. This is the case regarding the position that [the power] is the agent.

However, because grass and the like serve as the substratum for various powers (*satti*), those very things—grass and so forth—are intended as distinct factors when considered in relation to each specific power;
thus, even though there is no difference in the grass and other objects, a distinction among the grammatical factors (*kāraka*) is logical. For it has been said:
"Due to the connection with diverse agents and so forth, there is a [distinction] of factors within a single substrate."
"Multiplicity is appropriate through the distinction of the performance, as in the case of an actor.
Even if the vessel is one in terms of its substance, it undergoes differentiation through the distinction of the agent, the instrument, the object, the locus, and so forth who perform the action;
how much more so does an actor wearing the costumes of Rāma, Rāvaṇa, and others undergo differentiation by way of their names, such that he is called "Rāma" or "Rāvaṇa"?
The intention is "just like that.
Furthermore:
Just as a single cloth, when joined with qualities such as yellow dye and so forth, [becomes multicolored];
"A white cloth" or "yellow"—in this very way, that which undergoes differentiation [is understood].

And herein, the agent (*kattā*) and so forth, being of the nature of a sword and such, are the primary factors (*mukhyakāraka*); through association with them, the pot, being of the nature of a substance, is the secondary factor (*guṇakāraka*).
But how do these become factors of action (*kriyā-kāraka*)? The agent [becomes so] through the action of laughing, dancing, and so forth, which are established by himself.
It is a cause (nimitta). And in such expressions as "he cooks rice," the action itself—while performing its own established function—is the cause for the fuel and so forth that serve as its object.
In such expressions as "it is cooked by wood," the wood is the cause by virtue of being a factor (aṅga) for the cooking that is to be accomplished through the act of burning.
In such expressions as "he cuts with an axe," both the axe and the wood are [the causes] for the splitting into two.

The *nimitta* (cause/condition). And when an object (*kamma*) is connected with an action as something to be pervaded (*byāpya*), it becomes the cause of the action by way of being its condition (*nimittabhāva*).

Likewise, the recipient (*sampadāna*), the limit (*avadhi*), and the locus (*ādhāra*)—as in "he gives cows," "he leads away from the village," and "he cooks in the pot"—become causes of the action because they serve as the conditions for the actions of giving, leading away, and cooking, respectively. Of these, each according to its own...

The agent is the one who sets the action in motion; therefore, he alone receives the designation as the "primary agent" (*padhānakattā*), because although other factors such as the instrument possess the status of being agents, they do not receive that designation due to their lack of primacy.
For it was said by the Codiya:
Surely, for one who seeks the collection [of causes], tell me how the accomplishment of an action occurs,
given that there is only a single agent and no agency for all [the other factors]?
Because all [factors] such as the instrument (karaṇa) are devoid of the status of being an agent (kattutā).
"Because of the absence of instruments and so forth, the agent is indeed not sixfold.
It is said in reply:
"Even though the state of being an agent exists, [it is present] by way of its own nature within the instruments and so forth."
Even so, through the accomplishment of the action (*kriyāsiddhi*), this [agent] becomes subordinate (*appadhāna*) when it has passed over to another factor.

The intended meaning is that this [agent], while being perceived according to its own nature among the instruments (*karaṇa*) and other factors, attains the status of an instrument for the actions of others—such as burning or holding—and thus becomes subordinate.
The *kāraka* is sixfold by way of designation, but twenty-sixfold by way of its specific types.
Kamma is divided into seven ways, and the agent (kattā) is fivefold.
The instrument (karaṇa) is twofold, while the recipient (sampadāna) is considered threefold.
The point of departure (apādāna) is fivefold, whereas the locus (ādhāra) is fourfold.
The case endings (vibhattiyo),
moreover, are: the nominative (paccatta), the accusative (upayoga), the instrumental (karaṇa),
the dative (sampadāniya), the ablative (nissakka), the genitive (sāmivacana), the locative (bhummam), and the vocative (ālapana) as the eighth.
Thus ends the third section, the Section on the Kārakas, in the Payogasiddhi.
4. The Section on Compounds (Samāsakaṇḍa).
Now, because it depends upon nouns—since compounds are the mutual connection of nouns—and because it itself consists of nouns, the section on compounds is stated immediately after that on nouns.
1. It should be understood that "syādi" (beginning with *si*) refers to this [section] as the subject matter.

According to the principle of including what was stated previously regarding the inclusion of grammatical rules (*vidhi*), the term "syādi" includes those [suffixes] ending in *si*. And that which is called a compound (*samāsa*) is the state of becoming a single meaning (*ekatthībhāva*) of nouns whose meanings were previously distinct.

2. [The following words are indeclinables (*asaṅkhya*): case endings (*vibhatti*), excellence (*sampatti*), proximity (*samīpa*), totality (*sākalya*), absence (*abhāva*), "according to" (*yathā*), "afterwards" (*pacchā*), and "simultaneously" (*yugapad*).
That compound which has "pubba" (former) as its first member, "para" (other) as its last member, "añña" (another) as its last member,
or that which is neuter— this shall be called *asaṅkhyeya* here.
That which is established in other grammatical systems by the name *abyayībhāva* [is also included].
Just as in the examples *upakumbhaṃ*, *tiṭṭhagu*, and *pātameghaṃ*, so too [this occurs].

An indeclinable (*asaṅkhyam*) ending in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*), when occurring in the sense of a case-suffix (*vibhatti*) and so forth, becomes a compound with another word ending in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*).

According to the rule, “A non-compound is a permanent compound (*niccasamāsa*), provided there is no analysis involving other words,” this is a compound analyzed with other words (*padantaraviggaha*). Thus it proceeds among feminine nouns.
When a compound has been formed by combining words whose case endings have been elided (viggayha) according to rule 2.1.19:

"In a compound, there is oneness of meaning" (*ekatthatā*). That which has a single meaning—namely, a collection consisting of a base word (*pakati*), an affix (*paccaya*), and so forth—is "one in meaning" (*ekattha*). The state of being such is the ground for its occurrence (*pavatti-nimitta*), namely "oneness of meaning" (*ekatthatā*). This is the basis for the application of rules regarding the suffixes *ī* and so forth, as well as the formation of compounds. When this condition exists, the elision of the case endings (*syādi*) occurs.
9. Regarding that neuter [noun]:
In the neuter gender, when the elision of all case endings has been applied according to the rule "pubbasmā mādito," one says:
*adhitthi tiṭṭhati* (it stands), *bho adhitthi* (O, it stands), *adhitthi passa* (see it), *adhitthi kataṃ* (it is done), *adhitti carati* (it moves), *adhitthi dehi* (give it).

"Go away! Resolve is dependent; resolve is established. Thus, *adhikumāri*, [is explained as follows]: for the word *ghapa* which has become internal (*antabhūta*) and is subordinate (*appadhāna*), observe the shortening [of the vowel] in the form "ghapassa+antassa+appadhānassa.
*Sahabrahmaṃ* means "possessing the sublime" (*sampanna-brahma*). And by the method stated here and above, the compounds and so forth are formed.
Here, in the phrase "akāle satatthe," there is the substitution of *sa* for *saha*.

When the *syādi* suffixes have been applied, and the elision (*lopa*) of those *syādi* suffixes has occurred according to the rule "pubbasmā mādito," the prohibition against the fifth case ending applies via the rule "nāto mapañcamiyā.

Furthermore, from a compound whose final member is not a numeral and ends in the vowel *a*, the substitution of *am* occurs for all subsequent case endings. The same applies in the following instances as well.
*Samiddhi* (abundance) [becomes] *subhikkhaṃ* (plenty of food); here, the long vowel becomes short. "O sir, plenty of food remains; behold the plenty of food.
By the option "or *aṃ* for the third and seventh cases," there is *aṃ*: *subhikkhaṃ* (done with plenty of food) or *subhikkhena* (done by means of plenty of food);
*subhikkhaṃ* (he lives by means of plenty of food) or *subhikkhena* (he lives by means of plenty of food); give plenty of food. In the fifth case, because of the absence of *am*.
*Subhikkhāpagaccha* (depart while there is plenty of food), *subhikkhamāyattaṃ* (dependent on plenty of food), *subhikkhaṃ subhikkhe vā patiṭṭhitaṃ* (established in plenty of food).
In the sense of proximity: *upakumbhaṃ* means near a jar; likewise, *upanagaraṃ* (near a city), *bho upakumbhaṃ*, and so forth. In the sense of totality:
*satiṇaṃ* means "without leaving even a blade of grass behind"; the meaning is that one swallows what is to be swallowed without leaving even a blade of grass behind.
The remainder is equal to *sabrahma*. "Without leaving even the fire" (*aggimpi asesetvā*) means having studied it without leaving even the *Aggi* section;
this is equivalent to the inclusion of the *Vāra*.

Non-existence (*abhāva*) is manifold due to the diversity of its correlates; therein, "devoid of power" (*iddhābhāvevigata*) refers to those who lack the power of supernatural success (*iddhi*), that is, splendor (*vibhūti*).
*Dussaddikaṃ*. In the absence of a [specific] object, there is an absence of flies: *nimmakkhikaṃ*, *niddarathaṃ*, *nimmasakaṃ*.
In the absence of an excess—such as "the grass has been traversed"—there is *nittiṇaṃ*.

In the absence of the present time connected with enjoyment, such as "the light cloak has been traversed" (*atilahupāvuraṇaṃ*), the meaning is that this [present] state of being enjoyed does not exist for the light cloak.
*Yathāttha* (according to the meaning) is of many kinds; therein, *yogga* means suitable, and *anurūpa* means appropriate. *Vicchāyaṃ* (in the sense of distribution):
*anu* [with] *addhamāsaṃ* means every half-month (*anvaddhamāsaṃ*); thus it is used distributively. *Atthānativattiyaṃ* (not exceeding the meaning):

not transgressing one's capacity, i.e., according to one's capacity (*yathāsatti*). Likewise, *yathākkamaṃ* (according to sequence) and *yathābalaṃ* (according to strength). By virtue of the rule regarding frequency (*bahulādhikāra*), *yā yā parisā* means according to the assembly (*yathāparisā*).

In the sense of similarity (*sadisa*): *sakikhi*, meaning "similar to a black-spotted cow" (*kaṇhavicchitadhenu*); here, *sa-* is a substitute for *saha*. In the sense of sequence (*ānupubbiya*): *anujeṭṭha*, meaning "in order of seniority" (*jeṭṭhānukkamena*).
In the sense of posteriority (*pacchā*): *anurathaṃ*, meaning "behind the chariot" (*rathassa pacchā*).

In the sense of simultaneity (*yugapada*): *sacakkaṃ*, meaning "together with the wheel" (*cakkena saha = ekakālaṃ*); the meaning is that he deposits it at the same moment as the wheel (*cakkena ekakkhaṇe*).

3. Regarding "yathā" when it does not denote similarity: When the word *yathā* is used in the sense of similarity, it does not form a compound with a noun ending in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*). For example:

*yathā Devadattaḥ, tathā Yajñadattaḥ*. Here, the word *yathā*, functioning as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), requires the object of comparison (*upameya*), namely "Yajñadatta," [in the phrase] "tathā Yajñadattaḥ."

Therefore, if it is asked: "What is the purpose of the prohibition ‘not when [the word] has the same meaning’ (na tulye) in the case of non-compound (asamāsa), given that [a word] is dependent [on another] for its meaning"?
It is because the entire complex (samudāya) alone—namely, "yathā devadatto"—functions as the standard of comparison (upamāna), and not the word *yathā* by itself.

Consequently, since the dependence on the object of comparison (upameyya-sāpekkhatta) belongs to the complex as a whole, there is no lack of capacity (asāmatthiya) in the word *yathā* taken individually.

Therefore, this [rule] is for the purpose of prohibiting the formation of a compound with *sādissa*. Although it should have been stated as *tulyatthe* ("in the sense of equality"), since there is no "equality" (*tulyatā*) apart from that which is "equal" (*tulya*), it was not said *tulyatthe*, but rather *tulye*.
Wherever it is understood in some way that a similar thing exists, [that is the scope].
That which is called a simile (upamā) for it may become manifold through conceptual proliferation (papañca).

4. *Yāva* in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). When the word *yāva* is used in the sense of restriction, it forms a compound with a form ending in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*). Restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) means a delimitation by a specific measure (*ettakatāparicchedo*).
In the compound *yāvantāni amattāni bhājanāni*, when combined with *yāvāmattaṃ*, the remainder follows the preceding word.

*Yāvajīvaṃ* means "as long as life lasts," being the extent of the limit of a living being; in *yāvatāyukaṃ*, the suffix *-ka-* is added in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*). *Yāvadatthaṃ* means "as much as is needed" (*yattakena attho*).
5. *Pari*, *apa*, *bahi*, *tiro*, *pure*, and *pacchā* [are compounded] with a word in the fifth case.
The words *pari* and others optionally form a single compound with a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*). For example: *pari pabbatā* becomes *paripabbataṃ*.
Because the particle *vā* has the sense of an alternative in a sentence, forms such as *pari pabbatā* also occur. Examples include: *apa pabbatā* → *apapabbataṃ*; *ā pāṭaliputtā* → *āpāṭaliputtaṃ*;
*bahi gāmā* → *bahigāmaṃ*; *tiro pabbatā* → *tiropabbataṃ*; *pure bhattā* → *purebhattaṃ*; *pacchā bhattā* → *pacchābhattaṃ*.
"pacchābhattaṃ" (after the meal), "sabbaṃ upakumbhasamaṃ" (all that is equal to the vicinity of the jar)—by this [example], the compound and its distinction are shown.
It is the same in the subsequent sutta as well. The section on "vā" (or) ends here—6. In the sense of proximity and length, the suffix "anu" [is applied].
The inclusion of the term *samīpa* (proximity) in the rule beginning with *asaṃkhya* serves as an alternative (*vikappa*) for the obligatory compound (*niccasamāsa*).
The prefix *anu*, when occurring in the sense of proximity (*sāmīpya*) or extension (*āyāma*), optionally forms a single word with a noun ending in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*).

Here, because the inclusion of *samīpa* emphasizes the state of being, only proximity is understood; thus it is stated as "in the sense of proximity. *Anu-vanaṃ* = near the forest; *anu-gaṅgāya* = the length [of the river] along the Ganges.
*Anugaṅgam*, or *gaṅgāya anu*, [meaning] along the Gaṅgā; *bārāṇasī* [means] near Benares.
7. *Tiṭṭhagū* and so forth:
although words such as *tiṭṭhagu* are established by other [grammatical] means, they are fixed as *nipāta* (irregular) forms in this *asaṃkhyasamāsa* (indefinite compound). Cows stand...

In the expression *yasmiṃ kāle tiṭṭhanta-sadda-gosaddehi paṭhamāyaṃ akate*, the compound is formed by the rule *vā aññatthe*. By this rule, elision (*lopa*) is applied through a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*), and the neuter sense is also established.
Then, after the suffix *si* is added, the *u* in *gossu* (from *go*) is substituted by the rule *gossu*; subsequently, the case ending is dropped by the rule *pubbasmā mādito*.
Thus, in expressions such as *vahantī gāvo yasmiṃ kāle*, we have *vaha-ggu* and so forth. This also applies to words such as *velā*, *appakāsa*, *kapāta*, and others.
In this very context, there is a compound: *pāto nahānam* (morning bath) is a locative-tatpuruṣa compound (*sattamī-amādi-samāsa*), meaning "bathing in the morning.

Likewise, there is *sāyanahānam* (evening bath), *pātakālam* (morning time), *sāyakālam* (evening time), *pātamegham* (morning cloud), *sāyamegham* (evening cloud), *pātamaggam* (morning path), and *sāyamaggam* (evening path).
Here, by the rule *“ena-ṇa-ma vaṇṇe”* (the suffix *ena* [of the locative] becomes *a* when followed by a vowel), the *niggahīta* (anusvāra) is elided.
8. *Ora*, *pari*, *paṭi*, *pāra*, *majjhe*, *heṭṭhā*, *uddha*, *dho*, or *anto* [may be compounded] with a word ending in the sixth case (*chaṭṭhiyā*).
Words beginning with *ora* may optionally form a compound with a word ending in the sixth case. Examples: *oraṃ gaṅgāya* becomes *oregaṅgā*;
*upari sikharaṃ* becomes *uparisikharaṃ*; *paṭi mukhaṃ sotassa* becomes *paṭisotaṃ*; *pāraṃ yamunāya* becomes *pāreyamunaṃ*; *majjhaṃ*.
In the middle of the Ganges: *majjhegaṅgaṃ*; below the palace: *heṭṭhāpāsādassa*; above the Ganges: *uddhaṃ gaṅgāya*;

below the Ganges: *adho gaṅgāya*; inside the palace: *anto pāsādassa*. By means of this very rule, when the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra) and the substitution of *ekāra* (e) have been performed, forms such as *orecca* arise.
10. *A-mādi*:
Words beginning with *am* and ending in case endings (*syādyanta*) frequently become singular when combined with another word ending in a case ending (*syādyanta*).
The meaning of the subsequent word is predominant, and its gender is also that of the subsequent word.
The second [type] is a single-meaning compound (ekattha) beginning with a prefix; it is analyzed in many ways.
When combined with another word, it is further known as a *tappurisa* compound;
for example here, "rājāpaccaṃ" (the king's subordinate), or in some cases, "mitīdisaṃ" (measuring thus).
