A compound (samāsa) may optionally occur in some instances between words ending in *am* and those that are not case-endings (*akāraka*). This should be understood as being due to the rule of "frequent application" (*bahulavidhāna*).
Among these, the second-case *tappurisa* is formed with words such as *gata*, *nissita*, *tīta*, *tikkanta*, *patta*, and *panna*, following the *am*-ending.

When the compound *saraṇaṃ gato* is formed, the elision of the case-ending and so forth occurs everywhere in the subsequent sections by virtue of the principle of "identity of meaning" (*ekatthatāyaṃ*), as previously explained.
Saraṇagato, saraṇagatā; saraṇagatā, saraṇagatāyo; saraṇagataṃ kulaṃ, saraṇagatāni kulāni, and so forth.
Araññagato, bhūmigato. Dhammaṃ nissito is dhammanissito; likewise atthanissito.
Bhavaṃ atīto is bhavātīto; likewise kālātīto. Pamāṇaṃ atikkantaṃ is pamāṇātikkantaṃ; likewise lokātikkantaṃ.

One who has attained happiness is "sukhappatto"; one who has attained suffering is "dukkhappatto. One who has entered the stream is "sotāpanno"; likewise, "nirodhasamāpanno" (one who has attained cessation) and "maggappaṭipanno" (one who has entered the path).
One who has mounted a chariot is "rathāruḷho. One who is beautiful throughout the night is "sabbarattisobhaṇo," as in the case of "muhuttasukhaṃ" (momentary happiness).
A compound of non-agents occurs in the sense of absolute connection (*accantasaṃyoga*). This occurs specifically in an *upapada* compound because that [type of compound] is obligatory.
One who performs an action is a "doer of action" (*kammakāra*); a potter (*kumbhakāra*). One who desires welfare is a "well-wisher" (*atthakāma*);

one who desires the Dhamma is a "lover of the Dhamma" (*dhammakāma*). One who upholds the Dhamma is a "bearer of the Dhamma" (*dhammadhara*); one who upholds the Vinaya is a "bearer of the Vinaya" (*vinayadhara*). One who cooks for them is a "cook for them" (*sapāka*); one who weaves thread is a "weaver" (*tantavāya*).

One who brings a boon is a "boon-bringer" (*varāhara*). With suffixes ending in *-nta*, *-māna*, *-kta*, and *-vanta*, there is only a nominal sentence. [Examples: "listening to the Dhamma" (*dhammaṃ suṇanto*).
"Listening to the Dhamma," "having eaten rice"—these are examples of the third type of tappurisa compound (tatiyātappurisa).
[The following] are similar to *kitaka*, *pubba*, *sadisa*, *samo*, *nattha*, *kalaha*, *nipuṇa*, *missa*, *sakhila*, and so forth:
"the Dhamma spoken by the Buddha" (*buddhabhāsito dhammo*), likewise "taught by the Victor" (*jinadesito*); "praised by the Teacher" (*satthuvaṇṇito*).
Blamed by the wise is "condemned by the wise"; praised by the wise is "commended by the wise. Made by a lord is "lord-made"; made by oneself is "self-made.
Brought by parrots is "parrot-brought"; killed by a king is "king-killed"; oppressed by a king is "king-oppressed. Burnt by fire is "fire-burnt"; bitten by a snake is "snake-bitten";
pierced by arrows is "arrow-pierced. Fabricated by desire is "desire-fabricated"; endowed with virtue is "virtue-perfected."
Likewise: accompanied by pleasure (*sukhasahagata*); associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta*); association with friends (*mittasaṃsagga*); separation from the beloved (*piyavippayoga*);

arrogant by birth (*jātithaddha*); deficient in virtue (*guṇahīna*); increased in virtue (*guṇavuddha*); that which is to be performed by a group of four (*catuvaggakaraṇīya*); that which is to be done by a group of four and so forth (*catuvaggādikattabba*).

The river *Kākapeyyā* means "drinkable by crows. In some cases there is only an elided form (*vutti*): [it is called] *uraga* because it moves on its breast (*urasā gacchati*); [it is called] *pādapa* because it drinks with its foot (*pādena pivati*). In some cases there is only the full sentence (*vākya*):
To be cut with an axe; to be eaten by crows; to be abandoned through seeing. In the *pubbādi* (beginning with *pubba*) compound: *māsapubba* means "pus from a month" (*māsena pubbo*).
Likewise, *mātusadisa* (mother-like), *mātusama* (equal to a mother). Nineteen; deficient in virtue; a sword-fight; clever in speech;
mixed with what is for the time being (*yāvakālika*); harsh in speech. Like the Teacher, *satthusadisa*; resembling the Teacher, *satthukappa*; [equal] in merit.

One who desires is one who desires merit (*puññatthika*), one who possesses superior qualities (*guṇādhika*). Food mixed with curd is "curd-food" (*dadhibhojana*); rice mixed with molasses is "molasses-rice" (*guḷodana*).

This is a relationship between the agent and the object established through an action; even though the actions of "mixing" and so forth are not explicitly expressed in the formation, the function [of the compound] itself conveys those actions of mixing and so on, and thus there is no lack of semantic connection.
In the same way, there is "milk-rice" (*khīrodana*). [The example continues with] "by means of a horse" (*assena*).
A chariot joined with horses is an *assaratha*; the path-consciousness is *maggacitta*; the island known and marked by the Jambu tree is *Jambudīpa*;
ten plus one is eleven (*ekādasa*); one blind from birth is a *jaccandha*; naturally intelligent is a *pakatimedhāvī*, and so forth.

The fourth type of *tappurisa* compound is formed with words such as *tadattha*, *attha*, *hita*, and *deyya*. Regarding the sense of identity (*tadattha*): cloth for the *kathina* robe is *kathinadussa*.
The meaning is "of the *kathina* robe-cloth. In this same way: *cīvaradussa* (robe-material), *cīvaramūla* (the price of a robe);
*yāgutaṇḍula* (rice for the sake of rice-gruel), *bhattataṇḍula* (rice for a meal); *saṅghabhatta* (food for the sake of the Saṅgha), *āgantukabhatta* (food for guests);
likewise, *gamikabhatta* (food for those going on a journey); *pāsādadabba* (timber for a palace). And here, this is a permanent compound (*niccasamāsa*); of that—

And there is the state of having three genders: "a monastery for the sake of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus" (*bhikkhusaṅghassa attho vihāro*), "a monastery for the sake of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus" (*bhikkhusaṅghattho vihāro*);

"rice-gruel for the sake of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus" (*bhikkhusaṅghatthā yāgu*); "a robe for the sake of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus" (*bhikkhusaṅghatthaṃ cīvaraṃ*). Whatever is the purpose of someone is "for whose sake" (*yassa attho yadattho*), "for whom" (*yadatthā*), or "for which" (*yadatthaṃ*).

Likewise: "for that sake" (*tadattho*), "for those [sakes]" (*tadatthā*), or "for that [sake]" (*tadatthaṃ*). Similarly: "beneficial to the world" (*lokahito*). A flower to be given to the Buddha is "a gift for the Buddha" (*buddhadeyyaṃ pupphaṃ*).
A robe given to the Saṅgha. Here there is no [expression] "to be given to the Saṅgha.

It is a *pañcamī-tappurisa* compound by way of the meanings of departure, fear, abstention, release, and so forth. One who has departed from sexual intercourse is "one departed from sexual intercourse" (*methunāpeta*);

likewise, one who has gone to a clearing, one who has gone out of a city, one who has returned from alms-round, and one who has emerged from sensual desire is "emerged from sensual desire" (*kāmanikkhanta*).

Falling from the top of a tree is "tree-top-fallen"; one who has fallen away from the Teaching (sāsana). Rising from an offense is "emergence from an offense" (āpattivuṭṭhāna); having reached the surface of the earth is "gone to the ground.
Released from all states of existence is "released from all existences" (sabbabhavanissaṭa). In the context of fear and so forth: fear of a king is "kings-fear" (rājabhaya);

likewise, fear of thieves, fear of non-human beings, and fear of fire. One who is afraid of evil is "fearful of evil" (pāpabhīruka). Abstinence from what should not be done is "abstinence from the un-doable" (akattabbavirati).

Likewise, there is abstention from bodily misconduct and abstention from verbal misconduct. Released from bondage is "released from bondage"; released from the forest is "forest-released"; release from bondage is "bondage-release.
[The term] "arisen from karma" (*kamma-samuṭṭhita*) refers to that which is most excellent or most inferior.

In some cases it is simply a usage; "born of karma" (*kammaja*) means arisen from karma. Likewise, there are those born of mind (*cittaja*), born of temperature (*utuja*), and born of nutriment (*āhāraja*). In this context, the expression "fallen from the palace" does not occur.
The sixth case (genitive) tatpuruṣa compound: "the king’s son" is *rājaputta*;

likewise, "the king’s man" (*rājapurisa*), "one who honors the teacher" (*ācariyapūjaka*), "a disciple of the Buddha" (*buddhasāvaka*), "an image of the Buddha" (*buddharūpa*), "the word of the Victor" (*jinavacana*), "the roar of the ocean" (*samuddaghosa*), "a heap of grain" is *dhaññarāsi*, "the fragrance of flowers" (*pupphagandha*), "the taste of fruit" (*phalarasa*), "lightness of the body" is *kāyalahutā*.
"Mindfulness of death" (*maraṇassati*), "the foot of a tree" (*rukkhamūla*), "an iron bowl" is *ayopatta*.
In this context, the rule is: "The suffix *ma* is substituted for *man*, *ādi*, and *āpādi* when followed by *maye*. Thus:

*suvaṇṇakaṭāhaṃ* (golden basin), *pānīyathālakaṃ* (water bowl), *sappikumbho* (ghee jar), *devānaṃ rājā devarājā* (the king of the gods, the lord of the gods). *Pulliṅgaṃ* is the masculine gender; according to the rule "for *pum* [there is] *puṃ*," the *pum* of *puṃsa* becomes *puṃ*, with the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra) and the doubling of the *l*.

Examples are: *hatthipadaṃ* (elephant's footprint), *itthirūpaṃ* (female form), *bhikkhunisaṅgho* (community of nuns), *jambusākhā* (Jambu branch). In these cases, there is the elision of the vowels *ī* and *ū*.

The suffix *rasso* (short vowel) does not occur after [a word ending in] *-anta*, *-māna*, a noun extracted from a compound (*niddhārita*), a numeral denoting a part (*pūraṇa*), an abstract state (*bhāva*), or the sense of satiety (*titta*), due to the governing rule of frequency (*bahulādhikāra*).

Examples: *mamānukubbaṃ*, *mamānukurumāno*; "among cows, the black one is the most rich in milk" (*guṇṇaṃ kaṇhā sampannakhīratamā*); "the fifth among pupils" (*sissānaṃ pañcamo*); "the thread-nature of the cloth" (*paṭassa suttatā*).

However, it does occur in some instances, such as in the expression "present time with proximity" (*vattamānasāmīpyaṃ*). It does not occur when there is a state of expectancy (*sāpekkhatā*), as in "the Brahmin’s teeth are white" (*brāhmaṇassa sukkā dantā*).

“Satiated with fruits,” “refreshed with fruits,” “satisfied with fruits. [In the phrase] “the high house of the brahmin,” [the genitive] does not occur because of the presence of expectancy (*sāpekkhatā*).
[In the phrase] “the wealth of the king of Pāṭaliputta,” the genitive occurs as a relation to wealth;

however, [in the case of] “of the king, the cow, the horse, and the man,” it does not occur because there is no connection with “Pāṭaliputta. Furthermore, [in the phrase] “the king’s cow, horse, and man,” it is merely a sentence (*vākya*) due to the diversity of the referents.
The expression *rañño gavassapurisā* (the king’s cow-horse-men) indeed occurs because there is a state of identity (*ekatthībhāva*).
However, even though words denoting relations are always dependent [on another term], a compound is still formed because they are evocative (*gamaka*).

Indeed, evocativeness is also the basis for a compound, as in examples such as *devadattassa gurukulaṃ* (Devadatta’s teacher’s family) and *bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho* (the Blessed One’s community of disciples), and so forth.
A genitive-tatpurusa compound: perception of form is *rūpasaññā*; likewise, volition regarding form is *rūpasañcetanā*, and the suffering of saṃsāra.
Consciousness dependent on the eye is *cakkhuviññāṇa*. Delighting in the Dhamma is *dhammarato*;

delight in the Dhamma (*dhammābhirati*), inclination toward the Dhamma (*dhammaruci*), reverence for the Dhamma (*dhammagāravo*), and linguistic expression regarding the Dhammas is *dhammanirutti*. Inclination toward giving (*dānādhimutti*) is performed in another existence. In the act of seeing...
The gratification is the gratification of seeing. Dwelling in the forest is "forest-dwelling"; eating at the wrong time; rain during the [wrong] season;
wild flowers; a wild buffalo; a village pig; ocean fish; a pond tortoise; a pond frog; a well frog; a ferry-boat.
A rogue among women is a "woman-rogue," as is a gambler. One parched in the shade is "shade-parched."
*Angārapakka* (roasted on coals), *vanacāraka* (forest-dweller). In some cases there is simply a compound: one who wanders in the forest is a *vanacāraka*;

one who lies in the belly is a *kucchisaya*; one who stands on dry land is a *thalaṭṭha*, as well as a *jalaṭṭha* (standing in water) or a *pabbataṭṭha* (standing on a mountain). That which is born in the mud is *paṅkaja*, such as *saroruha* (lotus) and so forth.
Here [the suffix] does not occur, as in *bhojane mattaññutā* (moderation in eating) and *indriyesu guttadvāratā* (guardedness of the sense-doors).
Seated on a seat; one should sit on a seat.
11. Compound with an Adjective (Visesana-mekattha):
An adjective ending in a case-suffix forms a compound with a noun ending in a case-suffix that has the same referent (samānādhikaraṇa).

Where there are two words of identical meaning that express both the qualifier (*bhedaka*) and the qualified (*bhedyaka*), this is a descriptive compound (*visesana-samāsa*), because the meaning of the qualified is predominant.
Here, the gender is that of the qualified alone; beyond that [gender], it follows the subsequent word.
The *kammadhāraya* compound is known by others [grammarians] as being with a qualifier (*visesana*).

Although it was not explicitly stated in the sutta that it is "with a qualifier," because the word related to the qualifier is understood through implication (*sāmatthiya*) even when not uttered, it is stated as "with a qualifier. And it has been said:
"That which possesses a general quality is qualified by another thing."
Establishing [a subject] in a single mode is defined as a qualification (*visesana*).
A thing that possesses a single mode is called the qualified (*visessa*).
Whatever words here enter into a relationship with one another, [they constitute the sentence].
It is understood through the freedom of usage that there is a qualifier and a qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya*).
And here, since the word "lotus" (*utpala*) qualifies the "lotus-stalk" (*dabba*) by specifying it as a red lotus and so forth, the word "blue" (*nīla*) is the qualifier.

That which is qualified by it is the word "lotus," which is the qualified. Furthermore, since the commonality [of the color] found in bees, charcoal, and so forth is distinguished from the meaning of "blue," "blue" [is the qualifier].

It is not [a qualifier] of the cloth and so forth, but rather of the lotus alone; thus, because it is a qualifier (*visesana*), it is stated that "the lotus" (*uppala*) is the qualifier according to one's preference. Furthermore:
"Because it comes (*ayanti*) around (*parito*) by means of this, it is called a 'synonym' (*pariyāya*);
but when used as 'cow-speech' (*govāca*), the meaning of the word is indeed the qualifier."

"Those gender, number, and case-endings which are expressed by the qualifier (visesana) must be made identical with the qualified (visesya) when they share the same grammatical basis (tulyādhikaraṇa).

Because this has been stated, it should be understood that in examples such as *mahanto* (great), the gender and other attributes are the same. Why say "more"? [Because] in cases such as *devā pamāṇaṃ* (the gods are the authority), it is not so.

And that [compound] is sixfold: with a qualifying word as the first member (*visesanapubbapada*), with a qualifying word as the final member (*visesanuttarapada*), with a qualifying word as both members (*visesanobhayapada*), with a comparative word as the final member (*upamānuttarapada*), with a word expressing esteem as the first member (*sambhāvanāpubbapada*), and with a restrictive particle as the first member (*avadhāraṇapubbapada*).

In this regard, regarding those with a qualifying word as the first member: in the sentence *mahanto ca so puriso ca* (“he is a great man”), a compound is formed by this sutta. By the rule *“Ṭa nta+ntūnaṃ”* (the suffix *ṭa* replaces *nta* and *ntu*), there is a long vowel substitution for *nta*, resulting in *mahāpuriso*, *mahāpurisā*, and so forth.

The employment of the words *ca* and *ta* in the sentence is for the purpose of clarifying their state of having a common substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇabhāva*). However, in the *Vutti*, it is done by means of the compound alone.
Because it reveals that [state], there is no application of effort for that purpose. Likewise, in other instances where the meaning has already been stated, there is no application of effort.
Thus: *mahāvīro* (the Great Hero), *mahāmuni* (the Great Sage). That which is both great and power is "great power" (*mahābala*); likewise, "great fear" (*mahabbhaya*).

He who is both virtuous and a person is a "true person" (*sappurisa*). Similarly: *pubbapurisa* (a person of the past), *aparapurisa* (a person of the future), *paṭhamapurisa* (the first person), *majjhimapurisa* (the middle person), and *uttamapurisa* (the supreme person).
*parapurisa*, *setahatthī*, *kaṇhasappa*, *nīluppala*, *rattuppala*, *lohitacandana*.
In some instances it does not occur: *puṇṇo mantāṇiputta*, *citto gahapati*. *Pumā ca so kokilo ca* = *puṅkokila*;
when the following member (*uttarapada*) begins with a vowel, *pumassa* becomes *puṃ*. Likewise, *punnāga*.
A Kṣatriya and that maiden [form] "Kṣatriyakanyā" (a Kṣatriya maiden).
67. Regarding the rule "In the feminine, a word whose masculine form has been stated [remains] in the masculine":

when a feminine word has its masculine counterpart stated, it remains in the masculine alone; thus, by virtue of its masculine state, there is the cessation of feminine suffixes. In this way, [one forms] *rattalatā* (a red creeper).
A second alms-giving. A Brahmin woman who is also a girl is a "Brahmin girl" (*brāhmaṇadārikā*), as in "the Naga maiden.

What is meant by "a female"? For example: the maiden-jewel (*kumāriratana*) and the stone-lotus (*samaṇipaduma*). What is meant by "masculine forms"? For example: the Ganges river, the river of craving (*taṇhānadī*), and the earth element (*pathavīdhātu*).
That which is both eastern and a body is the "eastern body" (*puratthimakāya*); here, the word "body" (*kāya*) refers to a part of the body. Likewise, the "western body" (*pacchimakāya*).
The upper body, the lower body, the whole body, the nine abodes, which group, the causal condition (*hetu-paccaya*).
The "ninefold life-force" refers to the life-force nonad (*jīvita-navaka*), and so forth.
Regarding the qualifying term in the supreme position: elders, teachers, and scholars become qualifiers when placed after another word, as in *Sāriputta*.
And he is an elder, thus "the Elder Sāriputta"; likewise, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, the Elder Mahākassapa, the teacher Buddhaghosa, the teacher Dhammapāla, or the teacher Guttila.
And he is both Mahosadha and wise, thus "the wise Mahosadha";
likewise, the wise Vidhura.

Examples where both members of the compound are qualifiers (*visesanobhayapada*): *sītañca taṃ uṇhañcāti sītuṇhaṃ* (cold and that is hot, thus "cold-hot"); *siniddho ca so uṇho cāti siniddhuṇho māso* (it is both glossy and hot, thus "the glossy-hot month").
*Khañjo ca so khujjo cāti khañjakhujjo* (he is both lame and humpbacked, thus "lame-humpbacked");

likewise, *andhabadhiro* (blind-deaf), *katākataṃ* (done-undone), *chiddāvachiddaṃ* (hole-without-hole), *uccāvacaṃ* (high-and-low), *chinnabhinnaṃ* (cut-and-broken), *gatapaccāgataṃ* (gone-and-returning). In some cases, even the preceding time-element is placed last.
"Perfumed and smeared" means *littavāsita* (smeared-perfumed); likewise, *naggamūsita* (naked-clad), *sittasammaṭṭha* (sprinkled-polished), and *bhaṭṭhaluñjita* (stripped-bald).

In a compound of comparison (*upamanuttarapada*), the qualifying term that serves as the standard of comparison (*upamānabhūta*) comes last; for example, when "lion" is said, the word "sage" (*munisaddo*) qualifies the common understanding of both the metaphorical and non-metaphorical lions. And here:
"The similarity of the qualities of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison is the simile (*upamā*)."

And that [designation] occurs through the similarity of the base, the color, and the form. Just as "lion" is like a lion, he is both a sage (*muni*) and a lion, thus a "Sage-Lion" (*munisiṃha*), a Bull among Sages (*munivṛṣabha*), a Preeminent Sage (*munipuṅgava*), a Naga of a Buddha (*buddhanāga*), and a Sun of a Buddha (*buddhāditya*).
Like a ray of light is a ray of light, he is both the True Dharma (*saddharma*) and a ray of light, thus the "Ray of the True Dharma" (*saddharmaraśmi*);
likewise, [he is] the Ocean of Discipline (*vinayasāgara*). Like a white lotus is a white lotus, [he is] a recluse (*śramaṇa*).
And he is a *puṇḍarīka* (white lotus), thus a "lotus-like ascetic" (*samaṇapuṇḍarika*), a "lotus-like ascetic" (*samaṇapaduma*). Like the moon, it is the moon;
and that face is the moon, thus a "moon-face" (*mukhacanda*), a "lotus-face" (*mukhapaduma*), and so forth.
When the first member of the compound denotes esteem (*sambhāvanā*), as in *dhamma-buddhi*—where the intellect is the Dhamma—it is likewise called *dhamma-saññā*, *dhamma-saṅkhāta*, and so on.

Examples include: *dhammasammata* (agreed upon by the Dhamma), the perception of a living being (*pāṇasaññitā*), the perception of the foul (*asubhasaññā*), the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*), the perception of elements (*dhātusaññā*), the perception of self (*attasaññā*), and the view of self (*attadiṭṭhi*).

Regarding compounds where the preceding word functions as a restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*): just as "virtue alone is wealth" is *guṇadhana*, so too are *saddhādhana* (wealth of faith) and *sīladhana* (wealth of virtue).
"The jewel of wisdom" is *paññāratana*. "The eye itself is the faculty" is *cakkhundriya*; likewise, *cakkhāyatana* (eye-base) and *cakkhudhātu* (eye-element).
"The eye-door, visible-form as object," and so forth.
When used together with qualifiers and the qualified, or with a verb,
the particle that distinguishes their state functions as a delimiter.
"Non-yoga," "conception of yoga," and "absolute yoga"—
since this meaning is understood even from the word *payutta* when it is intended as a negation (*vivakkhā*),
a sentence has exclusion (*byavaccheda*) as its fruit. Therefore, Citta was the archer."
"Pāttho dhanuddharo nīluppalamattīti" is an example of this. Here, "nipāta" refers to the particles *eva* and *iti*.
Even when the word *eva* is not explicitly joined [with another word], it should be construed in this way: "Citto dhanuddharo eva" (Citta is indeed the archer).
Joined with the qualifier, it excludes non-connection; because it establishes the connection with the bow, [it is said] "pāttho eva" (Pāttha is indeed...).
The term “*dhanuddharo*” (bow-bearer) is connected with a qualification (*visesana*) and excludes other associations, because it establishes the state of being a bow-bearer specifically in Arjuna,
who is known as Pārtha. The phrase “*nīluppalamattheva*” (like a blue lotus) is connected with an action (*kriyā*) and excludes absolute non-connection,
because it establishes the existence of a blue lotus itself.
21. *Saṃkhyādi* (Numerals, etc.).
In a collective compound (*samāhāra*) expressing a single entity, numerals and so forth take the neuter gender.

For example, in the sentence "The three worlds are combined" (*tayo lokā samāhaṭā*), meaning "united by the mind," or "the collection of the three worlds"—when a descriptive compound (*visesana-samāsa*) has been formed, the neuter gender is applied by this rule.
The agent of a collective compound (*samāhāra*) takes only the singular number: *tilokaṃ*, *bho tiloka*, *tilokaṃ*, *tilokena*, and so forth. Likewise: three staffs are a *tidaṇḍa*;
three impurities combined, or the collection of the three impurities, is *timala*;

the three characteristics (*tilakkhaṇa*); the four truths (*catusacca*); the five training rules (*pañcasikkhāpada*); the six sense bases (*chaṭṭhāyatana*); seven days (*sattāha*); the eight precepts (*aṭṭhasīla*).
"Nine supramundane," "ten precepts," "one hundred yojanas. Two nights joined together is "two nights" (*dvirattaṃ*).

12. *Nañ*: It should not be said that a word ending in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*) forms a compound with another word ending in a case-suffix. The letter *ñ* in *nañ* is for the purpose of specification in the rule "*ṭa nañassā*" ("the suffix *ṭa* is added after *nañ*").

In words such as *pāmana-putta*, [the rule] "let there not be a substitution of *ṭ* for *na*" applies. In *abrāhmaṇo* (non-Brahmin), by the rule "ṭa nañassā" (*ṭ* replaces *na* when followed by *nañ*), there is a substitution of *ṭ* for *na*.
The letter *ñ* is used here specifically for the purpose of distinction.
A negation (*na*) is appropriate only when something exists; it cannot function without a restriction of place or other factors.
"Or [if you say] it is fruitless for one who is not a brahmin, therefore how can he be called a non-brahmin?"—
this is a statement of negation (paṭisedha-vidhi) by way of restating a prohibition (nisedhattha-anuvāda);
it results in the manifestation of another's wrong knowledge.
And its meaning is twofold, by way of absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) and relative negation (*paryudāsa*).
Therein, that which indicates the total absence of the meaning of the subsequent term—as in "the king’s women are not sun-eyed" (*asūriyapassā rājadārā*)—is called expressive of absolute negation.
However, that which, having set aside and rejected the meaning of the subsequent term—as in "honour those who are not Brahmins" (*abrāhmaṇaṃ māneyyāsi*)—[refers] to something similar to it...
When it establishes the action upon the substratum, that is called "expressive by exclusion" (*pariyudāsavācī*). And it has been said:
"The characteristic of a simple negation (*pasajjapaṭisedha*) is the non-existence of the substratum;
whereas that which functions apart from the substratum is the characteristic of exclusion (*pariyudāsa*)."
Where, among non-Brahmins and the like, the object [of negation] is excluded,
and one speaks of a king or similar person engaged in that activity, that is a *pariyudāsa* (presuppositional negation).
But *prasajyapratiṣedha* (absolute negation), on the other hand, does not imply another object.
In the negation of something specific, that contingency would not arise; furthermore,
another thing opposed to it, as well as its absence,
are the meanings of the negative particle.

In the sense of being other than that (*tad-aññatthe*): "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇo*) means one who is other than a Brahmin, similar to him; thus [we have] "non-human" (*amanusso*), "non-recluse" (*assa-maṇo*), and "unexpounded" (*abyākatā*) phenomena, which are not expounded.
In the sense of being opposed to that (*tabbiruddhatthe*): "not wholesome" (*na kusalā*) means unwholesome (*akusalā*), the opposite of the wholesome;

thus [we have] "non-greed" (*alobho*), "non-friend" (*amitto*). This is the method of negation by exclusion (*pariyudāsa-nayo*). In the sense of its absence (*tad-abhāve*): "not having done" (*na katvā*) means "having not done" (*akatvā*), "by not having done" (*akātuna*).
Not performing merit, one becomes non-existent. This is the method of negation by implication (*pasajjapaṭisedhanaya*).

And here, regarding both types of exclusion (*pariyudāsa*), when it is said that a "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*) is a Kṣatriya or the like who does not abide in the qualities of a Brahmin, yet is similar to a Brahmin, this is understood in the former case.
However, in the other alternative, due to some cause for doubt regarding a Kṣatriya or the like...

When it is said "a brahmin," the cessation of wrong knowledge is effected by the thought, "This is not a brahmin; he is a non-brahmin (abrāhmaṇo)," meaning that one does not persist in the state of being a brahmin.

In this context, since wrong knowledge is impossible without similarity, there is a corresponding practice due to the power of the application, and the gender and number belonging to that [referent] are employed. For this very reason, it is said:
“When joined with another word, [the negative particle] is similar to that other word in its grammatical function; for such discourse is conducive to the goal.
75. *Ana* before a vowel: the word *nañ* becomes *ana* before a vowel. For example: *na asso* = *anasso*; *na ariyo* = *anariyo*. Likewise, *anissaro*, *aniṭṭho*.

*Anāsava*: not having taken up, not having taken up; not looking at desire and so forth. Due to the predominance of the prefix *a-* [expressing] "not," it occurs with certain words that do not possess the sense of "unfitting.

Furthermore: *apuna-geyyā* (not to be sung again) refers to verses; *anokāsaṃ kāretvā* (having made no room); *amūlamūlaṃ gantvā* (having gone from root to root); *acandamullokikāni mukhāni* (faces that do not look up at the moon);
*asaddhabhojī* (one who does not eat with companions); *alavaṇabhojī* (one who does not eat salt).
13. Regarding the rule for the suffixes *nicca* and so forth:

the word *ku* and words beginning with *pāda* form a single compound with a word ending in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*) only in the scope of the rules concerning *nicca* and the other suffixes; elsewhere, they do not.

Here, by virtue of its constant association with *pāda* and the rest, *ku* is a particle (*nipāta*) alone, and not the word *ku* denoting earth. This is the scope of the rules concerning *nicca* and the other suffixes.
The word *nāma* is placed in the accusative case with respect to *pati* and others, as in the examples beginning with "lakkhaṇitthambhūtā.

Furthermore, in order that the compound *anvaddhamāsaṃ* not be treated as if it were an *asaṅkhya* (innumerable) compound, there is the prohibition [stated in the rule] "in the rule concerning *asi*, etc. An ill Brahmin is a *kubrāhmaṇo*;
because it is a permanent compound (*niccasamāsa*), the analysis is made with a non-case-ending word (*asapada*).
107. *Kad* replaces *ku* when followed by a vowel in the subsequent word.

When *ku* occurs before a vowel in the following word, the substitution of *kad* for *ku* takes place. Examples: *īsakaṃ uṇhaṃ* (slightly warm) becomes *kaduṇhaṃ*; *kucchitaṃ annaṃ* (wicked food) becomes *kadannaṃ*; *kadasanaṃ* (wicked speech). Why "when followed by a vowel"? [Counter-examples: *kuputtā*, *kudārā*, *kudāsā*, *kudiṭṭhi*. 108. *Kā* is used in the sense of "praise" (*pattha*). [Note: This rule indicates that *kā* is substituted for *ku* when it expresses praise.]
When *appa* (small) is used as a prior member, it becomes *kā* before a following word. *Appakaṃ lavaṇaṃ* (little salt) becomes *kālavaṇaṃ*. Likewise, *kāpupphaṃ* (few flowers). 109.
Or when *purisa* (man) follows, *kusa* may become *kā*. A contemptible man is a *kāpurisa*, or a *kupurisa*. *Panāyaka* is one who leads excellently; it is the preeminent leader.

*Vacana* is speech; *pāvacana* is extensive speech. *Bhusaṃ* means greatly increased; *pavaddhaṃ* means fully increased. *Samādhāna* is placing together or correctly placing. *Vimati* is various-mindedness;
*vikappa* is various or distinguished conceptualization. *Atideva* is a superior deity; likewise, *adhideva*. *Adhisīla* is higher virtue.
*Sugandha* is a beautiful fragrance; *duggandha* is a foul-smelling fragrance. *Sukataṃ* is well-done.
Well done (*sukata*); badly done is *dukkata*. "Abhisecana" means sprinkling; "abhiseka" means knowing [it as such]. Having done with excellence is "katvā";
having performed is "pakaritvā"; that which is performed is "pakata. Praised with excellence is "atitthuta"; praised beyond measure is "atitthuta.
Slightly crooked is "ākaḷāra"; well-bound is "ābaddha."
After *pāda*, etc., the first case ending is used in the sense of "gone to," etc.:
*ācariyaṃ paṭigato* becomes *pācariyo*; likewise *antevāsī*.
After *acca*, etc., the second case ending is used in the sense of "reached," etc.

*Atimañca*: having passed beyond the bed; *atimañco*. In *atimālo*, [the rule] “*gha* becomes short before *mālā*” applies; thus, the *gha* in the word *mālā* is shortened. The same applies to the subsequent *gha*s as well.
In the sense of “abandoned,” etc., [the prefix] *ava* and others [combine with nouns] in the third case:
*avakuṭṭhaṃ kokilāya vanaṃ* (a forest abandoned by cuckoos) becomes *avakokilaṃ*; likewise, *avamayūraṃ*. *Avakuṭṭhaṃ* means “completely relinquished.”
*Pari-* and its derivatives are used with the fourth case (*catutthī*) in the sense of "afflicted by" and so forth,
as in *parigilāno jjhenāya* (afflicted by exhaustion).
*Ni-* and its derivatives are used with the fifth case (*pañcamī*) in the sense of "fleeing from" and so forth.
"Departed from Kosambī" means "one who has left Kosambī. In the phrase "in the manner of eating, etc.," what is it? [It is] "it flashes toward the tree. 14. With *kriyā* (action) meanings:

A word ending in the suffix *cī* forms a compound with words ending in case-suffixes (*syādi*) that have the meaning of a *kriyā*. For example: *amalīnaṃ malīnaṃ karitvā* ("having made the unstained stained").
Having combined [the words] with the suffix *cī* applied according to the rule “*abhūtatabbhāve karā sa-bhūyoge vikārācī*,” this compound is formed.
Here, the letter *c* in *cī* serves the purpose of specification according to the rule “*cī kriyatthehi*. Then, by the rule “*pyo vā tvāssa samāse*,” *pya* is substituted;
the letter *p* in *pya* serves the purpose of specification according to the rule “*pye sissā*. Thus: *malinīkariya*.
15. *Alaṃ* [is used] in the sense of adornment (*bhūsana*) and disregard (*anādara*).
In these senses of adornment and so forth, the words *alaṃ*, *ādi*, and others have the same meaning.

When the analysis (*viggaha*) is formed as "having adorned" (*alaṃ karitvā*), "having honored" (*sakkaritvā*), or "not having honored" (*asakkaritvā*), and the compound is made, by the rule "in the case of *pye* and *sā*, there is the substitution of *sādhikarā* and *cariccā*," there is the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*). Thus: *alaṃkariya*.
*Sakkacca*, *asakkacca*. 16.

Regarding the phrase *aññecā*: when a compound is formed according to the rule [of sandhi], just as when it is said "he opens the door," one understands from the context that it refers to the "bolt," so too here, because of the presence of the particle (*nipāta*), the general term *aññe ca* is understood through the traditional authority (*āgama*) as being merely particles that correspond to case-endings (*vibhatti*).
They are cognized: having become foremost, being in front; having disappeared, being out of sight; having made oneself vanish, being concealed;
having placed upon the breast, being breast-deep; having brought to mind, being attended to;
having placed in the middle, being central; having become silent, being hushed.
17. *Vā* in the sense of "or" (*aññatthe*):
Several words ending in case-suffixes may optionally become a single unit in the sense of another word.
Whatever is the meaning of that other word, and whatever is its predominant gender, [that becomes the gender of the compound].
This compound has a meaning other than its constituent parts and is called *bahubbīhi*.

It is of nine kinds: two-word, having different grammatical bases (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*), three-word, preceded by a negative particle (*na-nipāta*), preceded by the word *saha*, preceded by a term of comparison (*upamāna*), having both members as numerals (*saṅkhyobhaya*), expressing the sense of an intermediate direction, and characterized by reciprocity (*byatihāra*).
1. Among these, the two-word compound with identical grammatical bases occurs in the six case-meanings, beginning with the accusative.

(Ka) Regarding that, first, concerning the second sense: "The monastery has come to the monks" means that the monks have arrived at the monastery; thus it is "saṅghārāma. And that [compound] is twofold, by way of being based on those qualities (*tagguṇa*) or not being based on those qualities (*atagguṇa*).
For it is said: "Based on those qualities and not based on those qualities—this compound is considered to be of two kinds."
For example: "Anīyataṃ Lambakaṇṇo" (The one with long ears is Anīyata) and "Ayaṃ Diṭṭhasāgaro" (This is Diṭṭhasāgara).
Among these, where the meaning that serves as the qualifier is understood through the inclusion of another word-meaning, that is *tagguṇasaṃviññāṇa*.
As in the example: “Bring the long-eared one. However, where it is not understood [from context], that is a designation based on the non-perception of its actual quality, as in:
“Bring the wealthy one. Here, the qualifier is placed first. And in this case, both the word *āgata* and the word *samaṇa* [retain] their own respective meanings.
They function with respect to another word—designated as a "monastery" (saṅghārāma)—which constitutes the meaning of the second case;

therefore, because the object (kamma) is already expressed by the compound itself, a further second case does not occur. Thus: *āgatasamaṇā Sāvatthi* (Sāvatthī where monks have arrived), *āgatasamaṇaṃ Jetavanaṃ* (Jetavana where monks have arrived);
*paṭipannaddhiko maggo* (a road for travelers who have set out), *abhirūḷhaṇijjā nāvā* (a boat for those who have boarded).
She is a merchant ship that has embarked.

(Kha) In the sense of the agent (*tatiyatthe*): he is one by whom the faculties have been conquered, thus a "conqueror of the faculties" (*jitindriyo*), a recluse (*samaṇo*), who has thus seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, and accomplished what was to be done.

He is a "conqueror of Māra" (*vijitamāro*) because Māra has been conquered by him; [he is] the Blessed One who has penetrated all phenomena (*paṭividdhasabbadhammo*). In the sense of the instrument (*karaṇatthe*): it is cut.

(Ga) That by which the tree was cut is the axe (*pharasu*). (Gha) He to whom a tax has been given is a king to whom tax has been given (*dinnasuṅko*); he to whom food has been given is one to whom food has been given (*dinnabhojano*).

(Ca) That from which people have gone out is a village from which people have gone out (*niggatajano*); that from which suffering (*ayo*) has gone out is a hell (*nirayo*), [as it is] free from defilement (*nikkilesa*). That from which consciousness has departed is a dead body from which consciousness has departed (*apetaviññāṇo*); one from whom fear and terror have departed is an Arahant (*apagatabhayabheravo*).
(Ṅa) Regarding the sense of the sixth case: one whose hands are cut off is "cut-handed" (*chinnahattha*). Likewise, one whose intention is fulfilled and whose taints are exhausted is [described];
one from whom passion has departed is "one free from passion" (*vītarāga*). That which has two parts is "two-parted," as in "a cloth with two hands. Regarding the term *tevijja*:

here, the suffix *ṇo* is used in the sense of the word itself (*sakatthe*), and there is a vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*). One that has four parts is "four-parted. That which has five eyes is "five-eyed" (*pañcacakkhu*).

The Blessed One, possessing the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiñña*), [is called] "Ghapassa" and so forth due to the shortening of the vowel. The Teacher’s dispensation consists of nine branches (*navaṅga*). The One of Ten Powers (*dasabala*) possesses infinite knowledge.
"Tidasā" refers to the gods, as three times ten is their measure; here, because the word for measure indicates a specific group, the word *dasa* functions in the sense of a number.
Those for whom this is the condition are "those having this as their condition" (*idappaccayā*); in the subsequent compound, [the form is derived from] *imassa + idaṃ*.
This [is the analysis] of the word "vā. What is its origin? Thus: "What is the origin of the body? (kiṃ-pabhavo kāyo). That from which impurity has departed is "stainless" (vimalo);
that which possesses a beautiful fragrance is "fragrant sandalwood" (sugandhaṃ candanaṃ). Likewise, one who is well-behaved is "susīlo," and one with a handsome face is "sumukho.

That which possesses a foul odor is "foul-smelling" (duggandhaṃ), such as a corpse; one with a bad face is "dummukho"; and one who possesses a corrupted mind is "dejected" (dummano)—thus is one "immoral" (dussīlo). Austerity itself...

One who has wealth [in the form of austerity] is a "wealthy in austerity" (*tapodhana*). One who possesses the power known as patience is "powerful in patience" (*khantibala*). One whose name is "Inda" is "Inda by name" (*indanāma*).

In compounds such as *chandajāta*, both the qualifier and the qualified may be placed first because they are desired according to one's wish; there is no purpose for deviating from the standard order.

One in whom desire has arisen is "one whose desire has arisen" (*jātachanda*); likewise, one is "born with desire" (*chandajāta*). One who has produced joy and mental happiness is "possessing joy and mental happiness" (*sañjātapītisomanassa*).
Born with joy and gladness (*pītisomanassasañjāto*). Born for a month (*māsajāto*), i.e., one month old. With a severed hand (*chinnahattho*), i.e., one whose hand is cut off (*hatthachinno*).
"One who has long shanks" is *dīghajaṅgho*; here there is masculine gender (*pumbhāvo*) and shortening (*rasso*) by the rule beginning with "ghapassā.

Likewise, "one who has abundant tongue" (*pahūtajivho*). "One who has great wisdom" is *mahāpañño*. By the absence of the suffix *vī* according to the rule "In the feminine, when the masculine has been stated, [the word] in the masculine alone [remains] in a single meaning," the suffix *va* is absent.

The substitution of *ṭ* and the shortening [of the vowel]. Why say "in the feminine"? [Example: *khamādhano*. Why say "spoken as masculine"? [Example: *saddhādhuro*. [Examples: *paññāpakatiko*, *paññāvisuddhiko*;
here, by the rule "after *l*, *tvi*, *itthī*, and *ū*, [the suffix] *ko* [is applied]. [The form] *gaṇḍīvadhanvā* is established through another grammatical tradition (*pakatantara*).
Various kinds of trees are *nānādumā*; fallen from various trees are *nānādumapatitāni*; [these are] *nānādumapatitāni*.
And those flowers are the flowers fallen from various trees; scented by them is "scented by the flowers fallen from various trees";
the mountain whose ridges are scented by the flowers fallen from various trees is "the mountain with ridges scented by the flowers fallen from various trees.
This is a descriptive (visesana) tatpuruṣa compound containing a bahubbīhi within it, where the referent of the other word (aññapadattha) is in grammatical apposition (tulyādhikaraṇa).

(Ca) That country in which crops have reached perfection is "a country with abundant crops" (*sampannasassa*). A region where alms-food is easily obtained is "a place where alms-food is easily obtained" (*sulabhapiṇḍa*).
A royal capital in which people are densely crowded is "a royal capital crowded with people" (*ākiṇṇamanussā*).

An hermitage in which there are many ascetics is "an hermitage with many ascetics" (*bahutāpasa*). One in which flesh and blood are accumulated is "one with accumulated flesh and blood" (*upacitamaṃsalohita*).
*Sarīraṃ*. A city where there are many masters is *bahusāmikaṃ*; a place where there are many rivers is *bahunadiko*—the suffix *-ka* is applied because of the final long vowel *-ī*.
Likewise, a forest with many jackals is *bahujambukaṃ*; a region where there are many agents is *bahukattuko*; similarly, *bahubhattuko*. The suffix *-ko* is applied by the rule:
"The suffix *-ko* [is added] after words ending in *l*, *u*, *itthi*, or *ū*."

2. A compound with different substrata (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*) is as follows: "one whose dwelling is for one night" is *ekarattivāsa*; "one whose dwelling is together with people of the same [kind]" is a person who is *samānavāsa*.
"One who has the characteristics of both" is *ubhatobyañjanaka* (here there is elision of the case-ending, and according to the rule *vā ññato*, the suffix *-ka* is added).
"One who has an umbrella in his hand" is *chattapāṇi*; likewise, *daṇḍapāṇi* ("staff-in-hand") and *satthapāṇi* ("sword-in-hand").

"Vajirapāṇi," "khaggahattha," "pattahattha," and "one whose inclination is toward giving" (dānajjhāsayo) means one who is intent on giving (dānādhimuttiko), such as one who is devoted to the Buddha (buddhabhattiko) or reverent toward the True Dhamma (saddhammagāravo), and so forth. 3.
The three-word [compound] is as follows: those great beings by whom prosperity has been attained through exertion are "those who have attained prosperity through exertion" (parakkamādhigatasampadā).

Thus, he has wealth acquired in accordance with the Dhamma. He is one by whom the hand has been withdrawn from the bowl; thus, he is "one who has withdrawn his hand from the bowl" (*onītapattapāṇi*). His body is like the forepart of a lion;

thus, he is "one whose body is like the forepart of a lion" (*sīhapubbaddhakāyo*). There are many elephants in rut in this forest; thus, it is a "forest with many elephants in rut" (*mattabahumātaṅgavanaṃ*).
4. When preceded by the particle *na*, as in *asama*: there is no equal to him, thus it is *assama*; according to the rule "*ṭa nañassā*," the *na* becomes *ṭa*.
Thus, [the terms] *appaṭipuggalo*, *aputtako*, *ahetuko*, and *akāraṇo* should be understood in the same way as above.
That with which there is no living together is *asaṃvāso*; that in which there is no rain is an *avuṭṭhiko* country; a monastery without monks is an *abhikkhuko* vihāra.
Likewise, *anuttaro* [is analyzed]: *ana* according to the rule "in *asare*"; thus also *anantaṃ* and *anāsavo*.
5. In the sense of "together with" (*saha*), when preceded by the word *saha*, [the suffix *ka* is added]. For example: that which exists together with a cause is *sahetuka* or *sahetu*.

According to the rule “*sahassa so aññatthe*” (the substitute *sa-* occurs for *saha* in other senses), *saha* becomes *sa-*. Thus: *sappītikā* (with joy), *sappaccayā* (with conditions), *sakileso* (with defilement), *saupādāno* (with clinging), *saparivāro* or *sahaparivāro* (with a retinue).
A tree pulled up together with its root is *samūluddhaṭo* (root-and-all-pulled-up).

6. A compound whose first member is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), joined with a word expressing the object of comparison (*upameyya*) and the connective particle *iva*, is [an *upamāna-samāsa*].
For example: "He who is as well-proportioned as a banyan tree" is *nigrodha-parimaṇḍalo*. "He is white like a conch shell" is *saṅkha-paṇḍaro*. "He is fierce like a crow" is *kāka-sūro*.
"This Blessed One has become like an eye" because he sees the ultimate truth; thus he is *cakkhu-bhūto*.
Thus, it has become meaning (attha), it has become Dhamma, it has become Brahma, and it has become blind (andha).
This wrong view is called "become like the *muñja* grass and the reed" (*muñjapabbajabhūtā*). It is called "born like a tangled skein" (*tantākulajātā*) because it has arisen like a tangled skein.

In the sense of the genitive case, he whose complexion is like the color of gold is "gold-colored" (*suvaṇṇavaṇṇo*), the Blessed One; this is a compound with the middle term elided (*majjhapadalopa*).

"Having a gait like that of an elephant, thus it is 'elephant-gait' (*nāgagati*). Likewise, 'lion-gait' (*sīhagati*), 'elephant-stride' (*nāgavikkama*), 'lion-stride' (*sīhavikkama*), and 'lion-jaw' (*sīhahanu*).
Having shanks like those of an antelope, thus he is 'antelope-shanked' (*eṇijaṅgha*). Having a voice like that of Brahmā, thus he is 'Brahmā-voiced' (*brahmassara*).
7. In the sense of the particle *vā* (or), when a numeral is used as both members [of a compound], as in *dvatti* or *dvattayo*, these are 'two or three' bowls."
And thus, *dvattipattā*; when the word *tisu* follows the word *dvi*, the latter becomes *tti*. *Dvīhaṃ vā tīhaṃ vā* becomes *dvīhatīhaṃ*; *cha vā pañca vā vācā* becomes *chappañcavācā*;
likewise, *sattaṭṭhamāsā* and *ekayojanadviyojanāni*. 8. Regarding the meaning of the intermediate directions:
that which is between the eastern and southern directions is the intermediate direction (*vidisā*) known as the southeast. In this regard—
69. *Sabbādayo vuttimatte*:

Feminine-denoting words beginning with *sabba* become masculine when expressing only the state of being (the abstract quality). Thus: *pubbuttarā*, *aparadakkhiṇā*, *pacchimuttarā*; or *pubbā ca sā dakkhiṇā ca*. 9. An example characterized by reciprocal exchange (*byatihāra*), according to the rule:
*“tattha gahetvā tena paharitvā yuddhe sarūpan”*—[where the word retains its original form when used in the sense of a mutual combat].
When a compound is formed, because they have seized each other by the hair, the battle that ensued is called *kesākesī*;
because they have struck each other with sticks, the battle that ensued is *daṇḍādaṇḍī*. And here, in the case of the suffix *cī* [in the rule] "cī vītihāre," the vowel *ā* occurs as in "cismiṃ";
thus, *muṭṭhāmuṭṭhī* is formed in the same way.
"Sobhaṇo gandho" means a pleasant fragrance; "sugandhī" is established by the suffix *ī* in the sense of possession (*atthiatthe*), meaning "one who has that [fragrance].

Furthermore, because it is stated in the Apadāna of Bhaddā Kāpilānī: "Then, having taken the bowl and cleansed it with a fragrant [substance] (*sugandhinā*)," therefore, in order to demonstrate the absence of the vowel *i* in the grammatical rule (*vutti*), there are the applications: "sugandhi" and "duggandhī."
"It is not seen," so it is said. In the case of *sugandhinā*, the vowel is shortened in the singular.

19. Regarding the sense of "and" (*ca*): A word ending in the plural or other numbers becomes singular in meaning when used with the sense of "and. The fourfold meaning of the word "and" (*ca*) consists of: conjunction (*samuccaya*), addition (*anvācaya*), mutual connection (*itarītarayoga*), and collective totality (*samāhāra*).
In this regard, there is no compound in cases of conjunction (*samuccaya*) or sequence (*anvācaya*), because the nouns, being dependent on a verb, do not have a mutually connected meaning;
for example: "He gave robes, alms-food, requisites, and lodgings," or "Give the gift and guard the virtue.
However, in cases of mutual connection (*itaretarayoga*) and collective totality (*samāhāra*), a compound does occur due to their mutual dependence.
If it is asked how a state of unity (ekatthībhāva) can occur when there is a fourfold relation of mutual exertion (ubhayatthapadhāna), it has been said:
"Even where there is mutual exertion, as if there were mutual dependence,
because of the commonality of connection with the action, that is called a 'fourfold' unity."
Since, even when there is identity of meaning, that which is predominant is what conveys the sense, therefore this is said:
"They do not qualify one another, like words in a fourfold sense;
therefore, their grammatical function (vutti) is according to the teacher, as they are employed for the predominant sense."
The *itaretarayoga* (copulative) and the *samāhāra* (collective)—this compound is of two kinds.
Others, however, know this [latter] by the name *dvanda*.
In the case of *itaretarayoga*, there is the occurrence of a distinction between the members.
The disappearance of the aggregate, as well as its gender, is like that of another [word].
That meaning in which there is the emergence of the aggregate and the parts are concealed is called *samāhāra* (aggregation); and that [meaning] occurs in the neuter gender.
Mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) is as follows: Sāriputta and Moggallāna are "Sāriputta-Moggallānā"; "O Sāriputta-Moggallānā," and so forth.
Because the individual members are predominant, only the plural number is used. Likewise: ascetics and brahmins are "ascetic-brahmins" (*samaṇabrāhmaṇā*);
similarly, brahmins and householders; kshatriyas and brahmins; gods and humans; moon and sun.
64. Regarding those related by knowledge (*vijjā*) and those related by birth (*yoni*):

in this case, *ā* is substituted for the vowel *u* when there is a connection by knowledge or a connection by birth. Thus, *hotā* (sacrificer) and *potā* (reciter) become *hotāpotāro*. Likewise, *mātā* (mother) and *pitā* (father) become *mātāpitaro*. 65. Regarding "sons" (*putta*): [the rule applies here as well].

When *putta* follows as the second member of a compound, the substitution *mā* does not occur for words such as *pitā* when they signify the sense of "son. Thus, *pitā ca putto ca* becomes *pitāputtā*;
likewise, *mātāputtā*. 78. *Jāyā* becomes *jayaṃ* before *pati*.

When *pati* follows, *jāyā* becomes *jayaṃ*. Thus, *jāyā ca pati ca* becomes *jayampatayo*. The form *jānipati* is established by another grammatical rule (*pakatantarena*); thus, *jāni ca pati ca* becomes *jānipati*. Similarly, *jampati* and *dampatī*.

In some cases, that which has fewer syllables is placed first, as in *canda* and *sūriya* (moon and sun), *candasūriyā*; and in *nigama* and *janapada* (market towns and provinces), *nigamajanapadā*. Likewise, [the same applies to] *sura*, *asura*, *garuḷa*, *manuja*, *bhujaga*, and *gandhabba*.

In some cases, there is the prior placement of words ending in the vowels *i* and *u*, as in *aggi* and *dhūmā* (fire and smoke), *gati*, *buddhi*, *bhujapaṭha*, *harakara*, and *sayā*, and in the case of the *dhātuliṅgāni* (grammatical roots and gender signs).

In some cases, that which begins with a vowel and ends in the letter *a* is placed first, as in *attha* and *dhammā* (meaning and phenomena), *attha* and *saddā* (meaning and sounds), or *sadda* and *atthā* (sounds and meanings).

A collective compound (*samāhāra*) is that which consists primarily of a whole whose internal distinctions of parts are concealed, while the members themselves remain mutually dependent; for example, "an umbrella and sandals" (*chattupāhanaṃ*).
20. "In a collective compound, [the word] is neuter.
In all cases of a collective compound, the gender is neuter; because it expresses a single aggregate, it takes only the singular number.
23. *Syādīsu rassoti*:

In the case of neuter nouns, when the suffixes beginning with *si* (the nominative) are present, the vowel is shortened. For example: *bho chattupāhana*, *chattupāhanaṃ*, *chattupāhanena*, and so forth.

These [compounds]—whether they are collective (*samāhāra*) or mutually connected (*itaretarayoga*)—are generally prescribed as having restricted domains (*niyatavisaya*). In this regard, the following is the classification of their domains as found in the *Niruttipiṭaka*: [they apply to] hands, musical instruments, equipment, and the limbs of an army.

The formation of a single compound through constant conjunction occurs for: enemies, numerals and measures, small creatures, outcaste cooks, those who share a common practice, those whose scriptural recitation is identical, gender distinctions, various conflicting things, directions, and rivers. For example, among the members of the body:
*cakkhu* (eye) and *sota* (ear) become *cakkhusota*; *mukha* (mouth) and *nāsikā* (nose) become *mukhanāsika*. [This applies] in the case of *si* and so forth.
"Short vowel" refers to the short vowel occurring in a neuter noun. Jaw and neck = jaw-neck; ear and nose = ear-nose;
hand and foot = hand-foot; skin, flesh, and blood = skin-flesh-blood;
name and form = name-and-form; aging and death = aging-and-death.
The *tūriyaṅga* (fourfold musical ensemble) consists of the *alasa* and the *tālambara*, thus forming *alasatālambara*; the *muraja* and the *gomukha*, thus forming *murajagomukha*;

the conch (*saṅkha*), the *paṇava*, and the *deṇḍima*—or alternatively, the conch, the *paṇavas*, and the *deṇḍimas*, thus forming *saṅkhapaṇavadeṇḍima* (where both *paṇava* and others are specific types of *bheri* drums);
the *maddavika* and the *pāṇavika*, thus forming *maddavikapāṇavika*; and song (*gīta*).

Instrumental music and vocal music are "instrumental and vocal music" (*vāditañca gītavāditaṃ*). Cymbals and drums are "cymbals-and-drums" (*sammañca tāḷañca*); here, *samman* refers to bronze cymbals (*kaṃsatāla*) and *tāḷa* refers to hand-clapping (*hatthatāḷa*).
Ploughshares and harrows are "ploughshares-and-harrows" (*phālo ca pācanañca*). Yokes and ploughs are "yokes-and-ploughs" (*yugañca naṅgalañca*). Among the components of an army:
elephants and horses are "elephants-and-horses" (*hatthino ca assā ca*); chariots and infantry are "chariots-and-infantry" (*rathā ca pattikā ca*); swords... [and so forth].

*Satti* is a spear, *tomara* is a javelin, and *piṇḍa* is a club; thus, *asisattitomarapiṇḍa* means a sword, a spear, a javelin, and a club. *Asi* is a sword and *camma* is a shield; thus, *asicamma*.
*Camma* refers to a shield made of the hide of a rhinoceros. *Dhanu* is a bow and *kalāpa* is a quiver; thus, *dhanukalāpa*. *Kalāpa* means a quiver.
*Paharaṇa* is a weapon and *āvaraṇa* is armor; thus, *paharaṇāvaraṇa*.

*Ahinakulaṃ*: for those who are constant enemies, such as the snake and the mongoose, or snakes and mongooses—thus it is *ahinakulaṃ*. Likewise, *biḷāramūsikaṃ*, where there is shortening of the final vowel. *Kākolukaṃ*, *sappamaṇḍūkaṃ*, *garuḷasappaṃ*, *nāgasupaṇṇaṃ*.
Regarding numerals, measures, and names: *ekakañca dukañca* becomes *ekakadukaṃ*. Likewise, *dukatikaṃ*, *tikacatukkaṃ*, *catukkapañcakaṃ*. *Dasakañca ekādasakañca* becomes *dasekādasakaṃ*;
and in the case of "thirty-four" (*tettālīsa*), by the rule of elision of the *ka*-portion, the letter *ka* is dropped.
"Small creatures" refers to insects and winged insects; "insects" refers to creatures such as beetles and cockroaches.
Likewise, "kunthas and ants"; "gadflies and mosquitoes"; "flies and ants";
and "insects and reptiles. In this context, "kunthas" are tiny ants.
Whether they be small creatures without bones, or even those that are tiny;
whether they be a hundred or a thousand, those which are not weighed [on a scale]—such are they.
The slaughterers of dogs, the sheep-slaughterers, and the pig-slaughterers constitute the "sheep-and-pig" group; likewise for the bird-catchers and the cowherds.
*Sapāko ca caṇḍālo ca* means "the *sapāka* and the *caṇḍāla*," thus *sapākacaṇḍālaṃ*; *pukkusachavaḍāhakaṃ*, *venarathakāraṃ*.
In this context, *vena*s are woodworkers (*tacchakā*), and *rathakārā*s are leather-workers (*cammakārā*).
Regarding those who share a common practice: *Atiso ca bhāradvājo ca* means "Atisa and Bhāradvāja," thus *atisabhāradvājaṃ*; *kaṭṭho ca kapālo ca* means "Kaṭṭha and Kapāla," thus *kaṭṭhakapālaṃ*.

Virtue and wisdom are "virtue-and-wisdom" (sīlapaññāṇaṃ); serenity and insight are "serenity-and-insight" (samathavipassanaṃ); true knowledge and conduct are "true-knowledge-and-conduct" (vijjācaraṇaṃ).
Likewise: name-and-form; moral shame and moral dread; mindfulness and clear comprehension; greed-and-delusion; hatred-and-delusion;
lack of moral shame and lack of moral dread; sloth-and-torpor; restlessness-and-worry, and so forth.

The *Dīgha* and the *Majjhima* among the discourses (*pāvacana*) taught in single recitation sessions are "long-and-middle" (*dīghamajjhima*). Likewise, the *Ekuttara*, the *Saṃyuttaka*, the *Khandhaka*, and the *Vibhaṅga*.
As for the distinction of gender: "woman and man" is *itthipuma*; "female slave and male slave" is *dāsidāsa*;
"robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick" is *cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāra*.

“Grass, wood, branches, and foliage” means grass, wood, branches, and foliage (*tiṇakaṭṭhasākhāpalāsa*). It is also seen [in the texts] as: “He is a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.

“Various opposites” refers to the wholesome and the unwholesome (*kusalākusala*), and likewise the blameworthy and the blameless, the inferior and the sublime, the dark and the bright, the mean and the noble, pleasure and pain, the low and the supreme, aversion and attraction, and shade and sunlight.

Light and darkness. Regarding *rattindivaṃ*: from *ratti* (night) and *divā* (day), when the suffix *apaccaya* is applied according to the rule “*rattindivadāragavacaturassā*,” the augment *numa* is inserted.

Regarding *ahorattaṃ*: from *aho* (day) and *ratti* (night), when the suffix *apaccaya* is applied according to the rule “*dīghā+hovassekadesehi ca ratyā*,” the vowel *o* is substituted by the rule “*manādyāpādīna+mo maye ce*.”
Of directions: the east and the west—east-west; likewise, the north and the south, the southeast, the northeast, the southwest, and the northwest.
Of rivers: the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā—the Gaṅgā-Yamunā; likewise, the Mahī and the Sarabhū.
Or [the compounds] of grasses, trees, cattle, birds, wealth, food, condiments, and countries. Of specific types of grass: *usīrāni*.
And *bīraṇa* grasses and *usīra* roots are "usīra-bīraṇa," or "usīra-bīraṇā. Likewise, *muñja* reeds and *pabbaja* grasses are "muñja-pabbaja," or "muñja-pabbajā";
*kāsa* and *kusa* grasses are "kāsa-kusa," or "kāsa-kusā.
Of various kinds of trees, *assattha* and *kapiṭṭha* are "assattha-kapiṭṭha," or "assattha-kapiṭṭhā"; likewise...
Ambapanasa and ambapanasā; khadirapalāsa and khadirapalāsā; dhavāssakaṇṇa and dhavāssakaṇṇā;
pilakkhanigrodha and pilakkhanigrodhā; sākasāla and sākasālā. Among the various kinds of animals:
gajas and gavajas are "gajagavaja" or "gajagavajā"; ajas and eḷakas are "ajeḷaka."
Goats and sheep, elephants and cows, horses and mares—this is "elephants, cows, horses, and mares," with shortening of the vowel.
Likewise: *gomahisaṃ* and *gomahisā*; *eṇeyyavarāhaṃ* and *eṇeyyavarāhā*; *sīhabyagghataracchaṃ* and *sīhabyagghataracchā*;
*kukkuṭasūkaraṃ* and *kukkuṭasūkarā*; *eṇeyyagomahisaṃ* and *eṇeyyagomahisā*.

Regarding specific types of birds: *haṃsā* (swans) and *bakā* (cranes) form the compound *haṃsabakaṃ* or *haṃsabakā*. Likewise, *kāraṇḍava* (ruddy geese) and *cakkavāka* (ruddy sheldrakes) form *kāraṇḍavacakkavākaṃ* or *kāraṇḍavacakkavākā*; *mayūra* (peacocks) and *koñca* (herons) form *mayūrakoñcaṃ* or *mayūrakoñcā*; *suka* (parrots) and *sālika* (mynahs) form *sukasālikaṃ* or *sukasālikā*;

*baka* (cranes) and *balāka* (egrets) form *bakabalākaṃ* or *bakabalākā*. Regarding wealth: *hiraññaṃ* (silver) and *suvaṇṇaṃ* (gold) form the compound *hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ* or *hiraññasuvaṇṇāni*. Likewise, *jātarūpa* (gold) and *rajataṃ* (silver) form *jātarūparajataṃ* or *jātarūparajatāni*; *maṇi* (gems), *saṅkha* (conch shells), *mutta* (pearls), and *veḷuriyaṃ* (cat's eye gems) form *maṇisaṅkhamuttaveḷuriyaṃ* or *maṇisaṅkhamuttaveḷuriyā*.

Of grains: *sālī* and *yavā* become *sāliyavaṃ* or *sāliyavā*. Likewise, *tila*, *mugga*, and *māsa* become *tilamuggamāsaṃ* or *tilamuggamāsā*; *nippāva* and *kulattha* become *nippāvakulatthaṃ* or *nippāvakulatthā*.

Of condiments: *sāka* and *sūpa* become *sākasuvaṃ* or *sākasuvā*. Likewise, *gavya* and *māhisaṃ* become *gabyamāhisaṃ* or *gabyamāhisā*; *eṇeyya* and *varāhaṃ* become *eṇeyyavarāhaṃ* or *eṇeyyavarāhā*; *miga* and *mayūraṃ* become *migamayūraṃ* or *migamayūrā*.
Of countries: *Kāsi* and *Kosalā* become *Kāsikosalaṃ* or *Kāsikosalā*; *Vajjī* and *Mallā* become *Vajjimallaṃ*.
The Vajjis and the Mallas are the "Vajji-Mallas"; Aṅga and Magadha are "Aṅga-Magadha"; likewise, Cetī and Vaṃsā are "Cetī-Vaṃsā";

Maccha and Sūrasena are "Maccha-Sūrasena"; Kuru and Pañcāla are "Kuru-Pañcāla. As for "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*), although it should be expressed according to the fourfold or fivefold planes as "name and form and name-and-form," by virtue of the rule of frequent usage (*bahula-adhikāra*), there is a single-remainder compound (*sarūpa-ekasesa*) [where the first member alone remains].
Having done so, it is stated as "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
In this section on synonymous terms, that which was mentioned first is placed first, because there is no purpose for deviating from the sequence.
In some instances, however, there is an inversion due to the governing principle of usage (*bahulādhikāra*), as in "the king of teeth" (*rājadanta*) [meaning] "the tooth-king."
In the *Catu-samāsa*, the rule "of an assembly and a gathering" (*sabhā-parisāya*) serves as an indicator that in certain instances the neuter gender does not apply;
thus, "sovereignty and retinue" (*ādhipacca-parivāra*). Likewise, there is "zeal and purification" (*chanda-pārisuddhi*) in the context of rebirth and the course of existence.
40. [End of] the section on compound endings.
The following is treated as a governing rule (adhikāra).
41. Regarding "pāpādīhi bhūmiyā":

when *bhūmi* follows *pāpa* and so forth, the suffix *a* is applied at the end of the compound. In the sense of "that in which there is a sinful ground," it is *pāpabhūmaṃ*; a ground characterized by birth is *jātibhūmaṃ*.
42. Regarding "by number" (saṃkhyāhi):
it does not exist for a stage beyond [the limit of] numbers. If it has two stages, it is "two-staged" (dvibhūmaṃ). Likewise, it is "three-staged" (tibhūmaṃ).
43. Regarding the rivers Godāvarī and Varī...

The suffix *a* occurs at the end of a compound when preceded by numerals (*saṃkhya*) or the word *nadīgodhāvarī*. For example, the collection of five rivers is *pañcanadaṃ*; likewise, [the collection] of seven *godhāvarī* rivers is *sattagodhāvaraṃ*.

44. The suffix *a* also occurs at the end of a compound with the word *aṅguli* when preceded by non-numerical (*asaṃkhya*) or numerical (*saṃkhya*) words, provided they do not have other numerical meanings. For example, that which has emerged from fingers is *niraṅgulaṃ*.
Two fingers joined together are *dvaṅgula*. Regarding the phrase "in the sense of not being other": what is it? Five fingers are in this hand, thus it is *pañcaṅguli*;
near to a finger is *upaṅguli*. 45. [The suffix *ka* is used] after long [vowels], *aho*, *vassa*, and *eka*, and after *ratti* [to form adverbs].
The suffix *a* is applied after words beginning with *dīgha* followed by *rattī*. Thus, "that which is long and is a night" is *dīgharattaṃ*.
"Day and night" is *ahorattaṃ*, where *o* is substituted for *āpāditta*. "Night during the rains" is *vassārattaṃ*. "That which is the former and is a night" is *pubbarattaṃ*.
Likewise, *apararattaṃ*, *aḍḍharattaṃ*, and "having passed the night" is *atiratto*. Two nights combined are *dvirattaṃ*.
In the sense of "unknown" (*anaññāta*) and "number" (*saṅkhya*), however, [the rule applies]: *dīghā ratti asmiṃ* becomes *dīgharatti*, meaning "winter. *Uparatti* means "near to night.

Due to the provision for abundance (*bahula*), it occurs in some cases even without elision; thus, according to the measure of the night, we have *yathāratta*. 46. Also in the sense of "cow-ness" (*gotva*) and when there is elision (*lopa*).
In the domain of *alopa* (non-elision), the word *go* becomes *a* when forming a compound, provided it is not a compound ending in the fourth case (*catthādi*) and so forth.
*Rañño go*: *rājagavo* (the king’s bull). *Paramo ca so go ca*: *paramagavo* (the supreme bull). The collection of five bulls is *pañcagavam*;
here, *avaṅ* is substituted according to the rule "of *go*, *avaṅ*. *Tam dhanam assa*: *pañcagavadhano* (one whose wealth consists of five bulls). *Dasagavam* (ten bulls).
47. *Rattindiva*, *dāragava*, and *caturassa*: these words ending in *-a* are formed as *nipātta* (irregular) compounds.

*Ratti* (night) and *divā* (day) form *rattindivaṃ*; by this very rule, the suffix *num* is added. *Dārā* (wife/women) and *gavo* (cows) form *dāragavaṃ*. He who has four mares (*assiyo*) is *caturasso*.
48. In the sense of length, *anugavaṃ* [is formed].

*Anugavam* is formed when *āyāma* (length) is understood in relation to a cow. A cart whose length is that of a cow is called *anugava*; this is a compound with an uncountable number (*asaṅkhyasamāsa*). 49.
After *akkhi*, the suffix *a* is added to form a compound when it denotes something other than its own meaning. One who has large eyes is *visālakkho*.
50. *Dārumya-aṅgulyā aṅgulantā*:

when the word ending in *aṅguli* is compounded with another word meaning "wood" (*dāru*), the suffix *a* is applied. For example, that which has two fingers as its parts is *dvaṅgulaṃ dāru* (two-finger wood); likewise, *pañcaṅgulaṃ* (five-finger wood). Wood that has parts resembling fingers and is used for scattering grain and so forth is called *aṅgulantā*. 54. *Uttarapade* (in the case of a following word).
This [rule] is to be applied everywhere.
55. *Imassidanti uttarapade*:
in the case of a subsequent word, "of this" becomes *idaṃ*; "the meaning of this" is *idamattho*; *tha* becomes *ṭha*; "this meaning belongs to him" is *idamattho assa atthi*.

This is *idaṃ*; the state of being this is *idamaṭṭhitā*. These are the conditions; thus, *idappaccayā* [is formed], with the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra) and the doubling of the following consonant.
57. *Ṭa ntantūnaṃ*:

The suffix *ṭa* is substituted for the genitive plural ending *ntantūnaṃ* when followed by a subsequent word (*uttarapada*). *Bhavantaṃ patiṭṭhā amhaṃ* becomes *bhavaṃpatiṭṭhā mayaṃ*, with the insertion of the *niggahīta*, the substitution of the final consonant of the group (*vagganta*), and the change of *yossa* to *ṭā*. *Bhagavā mūlaṃ etesaṃ* becomes *bhagavaṃmūlakā* our doctrines.
Thus, because there is no other [support] for me than these threads, I am one who has the virtuous as my support (*guṇavantapaṭṭho*). 60.
The mention of another’s number.
In the context of numbers, *para* becomes *o*; *para* plus one hundred (*sata*) is *parosataṃ*.

(61) Regarding *puthujjana*: in the phrase "among people who are diverse" (*puthassa jane*), *u* is substituted [for the final vowel]. Since this person is indeed diverse among people, he is a *puthujjana*; for this word, the doubling of the consonant occurs.

62. When *cha* is the first member [of a compound] and *āyatana* or *aha* is the final member, *so* optionally replaces *cha*. Thus: *sāhaṃ* or *chāhaṃ*; *saḷāyatanaṃ* or *chaḷāyatanaṃ*. (End of Sambara. 63.
In the case of *ltu*, *pitā*, etc., *māra* is the substitute for *varaṅa*.

In the case of words ending in the *ltu*-suffixes and words such as *pitā* (father), etc., when they stand as prior members (*pubbapada*), they optionally become *māra*, *vara*, and *aṅga* respectively, provided a subsequent word (*uttarapada*) follows. For example: *satthu-dassanaṃ* becomes *satthāra-dassanaṃ*; this is a designation of the agent (*kattāraniddeso*). [Similarly: *mātāpitaro*. Or rather: *satthudarśanaṃ*, *mātujāyā*. 68. *Kvaci paccaye*:
In the case of a suffix (*paccaya*) expressing the masculine gender, there is an intensification: *byatta* becomes *byattara*, *byattatama*. [Examples: *tassaṃ*, *tatra*; *tāya*, *tato*.

At that time, in the meantime: “… in this interval, according to the opinion of the Elder Ācariya Saṅgharakkhita Mahāsāmi, these forms are established by this very sutta, ‘kvaci paccaye’; for that reason, they are cited in this sutta.

However, according to the opinion of the Elder Ācariya Moggallāna Mahāthera, they are established by the sutta, ‘sabbādayo vuttimattā,’ because suffixes such as *to* and so forth are prescribed in the sense of case endings (*vibhatti*).”
And because the suffixes beginning with *ṇa* are prescribed for both [the preceding and following words], the opinions of both Elders (*thera*) are not contradictory.
71. *Saññāya+mudo+dakassa*: When *muda* or *udaka* follows as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) after a word ending in *saññā*, the substitution of *uda* occurs. Examples: *udadhi*, *udapānaṃ*.

72. Or, when *udaka* precedes words such as *kumbha*, there is optionally a substitution of *uda* for *udaka*. Thus: *udakumbho* or *udakakumbho*; *udapatto* or *udakapatto*; *udabindu* or *udakabindu*. This is a class of words defined by their form (*ākṛtigaṇa*). 73.
In the case of *sota* and similar words, [the final vowel] is elided.
In the subsequent compounds beginning with *sota*, there is the elision of the *ussa* (genitive) of *udaka*. Examples: *dakasotaṃ* (a water-stream), *dakarakkhaso* (a water-demon).
26. *Itthiyam matvā*: The suffix *āp* occurs after a feminine noun ending in the vowel *a*. Example: *dhammadinnā*.
27. *ṅī* after *nadādi*:
The suffix *ṅī* occurs after words beginning with *nadi* when denoting a female. Examples: *nadī*, *mahī*, *kumārī*, *taruṇī*, *vāruṇī*, *gotamī*. [The suffix *ṅī*] may also occur after *gota*.

*Gāvī* means "cow. This is a class of words based on their form (*ākṛtigaṇa*). The letter *v* is for the purpose of specification, as in the rule: "For *nt*-ending stems, *to* optionally replaces [the suffix] before *vī*.
28. *Yakkhāditv-inī ca*: After *yakkha* and other such words, the feminine suffix *inī* occurs, and *vī* also occurs. Thus: *yakkhinī*, *yakkhī*; *nāginī*, *nāgī*; *sīhinī*, *sīhī*.
29. From *ārāmika* and so forth, the suffix *-inī* is applied in the feminine sense. Examples: *ārāmikinī*, *anantarāyikinī*.
In the case of a name, from *mānusa* it becomes *mānusinī*, but otherwise it is *mānusī*.
30. *Yuvaṇṇehi nī*:

After [stems] ending in a young vowel (*yuvaṇṇa*), the suffix *nī* occurs frequently. Examples: *sadāpayatapāṇinī*, *daṇḍinī*, *bhikkhunī*, *khattabandhunī*, *paracittavidunī*. Why does it not occur after *mātṛ* and so forth? Because femininity is expressed even without the feminine suffix. 31. *Ttimhā ññatthe*: [The suffix *nī* occurs] after [stems ending in] *ti* when another meaning [than that of the base] is intended.

In other instances, *nī* is frequently used for the word *itthī* (woman). "I am she who delights in non-violence" (*ahiṃsāratinī*); [this is said] of her whose mindfulness is lost (*muṭṭhassatiniyā*). "She is the cow greedy for her calf" (*vacchagiddhinī*). [The question] "In other instances" (*aññattha*) refers to what?

[For example: "one who delights in the Dhamma" (*dhammarati*). 32. **Gharaṇy-ādayo**: Words beginning with *gharaṇī* are correct when ending in the suffix *nī*. "He has a house" (*gharo assa atthi*): by adding the suffix *īm*, and then applying the rule "after *yu* and *vaṇṇa*, *nī* [is substituted]," we get *gharaṇī*. By this [rule], *na* becomes *ṇa*, and *ī* becomes *attā* (the long vowel *ī*).
Because it is restricted by the *gaṇa*-sutta "Ācariyā vā yalopo ca," there is both the feminine suffix *nī* and the elision of *ya* by this very rule:
*ācarinī*, *ācariyā*. 33. Regarding "Mātulāditvā + nī bhariyāya":
the suffix *mānī* is applied after words beginning with *mātula* when expressing "wife. Thus: *mātulānī*, *varuṇānī*, *gahapatānī*, *ācariyānī*.
Because [the word] *bhariyā* is restricted by the rule for groups (*gaṇasutta*) as "either *abhariyā* or *khattiyā*," [the suffix] *ī* is applied by this [rule], resulting in *khattiyānī*.
