29. The suffix *ṇika* is applied after roots such as *kṛ* (to do) in the sense of "done by that" (*tena kataṃ*), and so forth.
[Examples: *kāyena kataṃ* becomes *kāyikaṃ* (bodily), *vācasikaṃ* (verbal), *mānasikaṃ* (mental); here there is the addition of the augment *sakā*.

*Vātena kato ābādho* becomes *vātito* (caused by wind), *semhiko*, *pittiko* (caused by phlegm or bile). *Satena kītaṃ* becomes *sātikaṃ* (bought for a hundred), *sāhassikaṃ* (bought for a thousand); [and] *vatthena*...
*Kīta* means "bought," as in *vatthika*, *kumbhika*, *sovaṇṇika*, and *ghātika*.

Because it is not possible for something to be bought by Devadatta without a root price (*amūlavācittā*), the term does not apply [to the person]; this is because the meaning of that [price] is not understood.
*Vārattika* means "bound for a rope" (*varatthāya*), as in *āyasika*, *pāsika*, and *suttika*. *Ghātika* means "prepared with or mixed with ghee" (*ghatena*); likewise, *goḷika* and *dadhika*.
*Mārīcikaṃ*. One who kills with a net (*jāla*) is called *jālika*, that is, a fisherman (*bālisika*). Wealth won by dice is *akkhika*; likewise *sālākika*, *tindukiko*, and *ambaphaliko*.
One who wins or plays with dice is *akkhiko*. One who digs with a spade (*khaṇitti*) is *khāṇittiko*, that is, a digger (*kuddāliko*).
[The suffix does not apply] in cases such as "won by Devadatta" or "digs with a finger," because the intended meaning is not understood there.
One who crosses by means of a raft is an *oḷumpika*; the suffix *-ika* is used here as in *uḷumpika*. Likewise, *kullika*, *gopucchika*, and *nāvika*.
One who travels by cart is a *sākaṭika*, and a *rathika*; the suffix *-ika* is used here as in *parappika*. One who carries on the shoulder is a *khandhika*;

the suffix *-ika* is used here as in *aṃsika* and *sīsika*. One who lives by wages is a *vetanika*, a *bhatika*, a *kayika*, a *vikkayika*, or a *kayavikkayika*; the suffix *-ika* is used here as well.
30. It conduces to that.
Regarding the meaning "it conduces," the suffix *ika* is applied. That which conduces to renewed existence is *ponobbhavika*;
in the feminine, it is *ponobbhavikā*. That which conduces to the world is *lokika*. That which is truly the highest is *sagga*; that which conduces to heaven is *saggika*.
*Sovaggika* is derived from the reading *sassa-vagga-tad-aminādī*. That which leads to wealth (*dhana*) is called *dhañña*.

31. Regarding the suffix *-ika* after words ending in the fifth case (ablative) in the senses of "originated from" (*sambhūta*) and "come from" (*āgata*): [the example is] "originated from or come from the mother" (*mātito sambhūtam āgatam vā*).

Here, in the phrase "from the mother and from the sister," the word *mātito* is a sentence [ending] with the suffix *ussa*. In the case of short vowels followed by a double consonant, we have *māttikaṃ* and *pettikaṃ*.
The suffixes *ṇya*, *riyaṇa*, and *rya* are also seen. That which is produced from *surabhi* is *sorabhyaṃ*. In the case of *yamhi*, it is *thaññaṃ*.
In both instances, there is elision according to the rule "elision of vowels and semi-vowels" (*lopo vaṇṇi-vaṇṇānaṃ*). From *pitṛ* with the suffix *riyaṇa*, we have *pettiyo*.

In the case of *mātṛ*, by the rule “*rānubandhe’ntasarādissa*,” there is elision [of the suffix], resulting in *mattiyo*. When followed by *ryam*, there is elision, and through the substitution of the *cavagga* sounds and the prior form (*pubbarūpa*), it becomes *macco* or *vā*.

32. The suffix *ṇika* occurs after words ending in the locative case when used in such senses as “dwells there,” “is known there,” “is devoted there,” or “is appointed there. For example, one who dwells at the foot of a tree is called a *rukkhamūlika*.

A forest-dweller (*āraññika*); one from Rājagaha (*rājagahika*); one from Magadha (*māgadhika*); a charnel-ground dweller (*sosānika*). Known in the world, he is worldly (*lokika*). Those who have the Four Great Kings as their food (or support) are the Cātummahārājika [gods].

Appointed at the gate, he is a gatekeeper (*dovārika*); *dassoka* is from such readings as these. A storekeeper (*bhaṇḍāgārika*). An overseer of new works (*navakammika*), one who performs the first work (*ādikammika*).
Belonging to a certain caste (*jātikiya*), he is an Andhaka (*andhakiya*).

33. After these [stems ending in] the sixth case, the suffix *ṇika* occurs in the sense of "belonging to this. For example: *saṅghassa idaṃ* becomes *saṅghikaṃ* ("belonging to the Saṅgha"), *puggalikaṃ*, *sakyaputtiko*, *nāṭaputtiko*, *jenadattiko*.
In the sense of "his own," it is *sakiyo*; in the sense of "another's," it is *parakiyo*. In the sense of "one's own," it is *attaniyaṃ*.
*Ke-sako*: this royal property belongs to the king. 34. *Ṇo*:

after words ending in the sixth case, the suffix *ṇo* occurs in this sense [of belonging]. *Kaccāyanassa idaṃ* = *kaccāyanaṃ*, the grammar; *sogataṃ*, the teaching of the Buddha; *māhisaṃ*, beef and so forth.

35. After words such as *go*, etc., when they end in the sixth case (*chaṭṭhīvibhatti*), the suffix *ya* occurs in this sense of "belonging to" (*idaṃ*). This belongs to cows (*gavānam*) is *gavyam*; [here] *avaṅ* [substitution] applies, and [the word] consists of meat, etc. When the *i* is elided, it is a poetic form (*kabbaṃ*). This belongs to wood (*dunānam*) is *dabbaṃ*. 36.
After the word *pitā*, the suffix *reyyaṇa* occurs in the sense of "brother."

“From the father’s side” (*pitito*) and “from the mother’s side” (*mātito*): these are derived from those very same *Sutta-nipāta* verses. From the word *pitu*, the suffix *-eyya* is applied to denote his brother; thus, the father’s brother is *petteyyo*. 37. Regarding the sister on both the mother’s and the father’s side:

after the words *mātu* and *pitu*, the suffix *-ccha* occurs when denoting their respective sisters. The mother’s sister is *mātucchā*; the father’s sister is *pitucchā*. As for the expression “the mother’s brother is *mātulo*,” the suffix *-la* is applied by means of the rule of irregular derivation (*nipātanā*) beginning with “*mātula-ādi*.”

38. "The great festival for mother and father": this refers to the great festival for their respective mothers and fathers. The mother’s mother is the maternal grandmother (*mātāmahī*); the mother’s father is the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*).

The father’s mother is the paternal grandmother (*pitāmahī*); the father’s father is the paternal grandfather (*pitāmaha*). This is not according to numerical order, because each term is connected individually and separately.
Through the words "mother" and "father," there is a condition for the welfare of those parents.
39. Regarding welfare and reverence:
There is welfare and reverence toward one's mother and father. One who is beneficial to his mother is filial toward his mother; one who is beneficial to his father is filial toward his father.
40. Regarding the suffixes *nindā*, *aññāta*, *pa*, *paṭibhāga*, *rassa*, *dayā*, and *saññā*:
what [suffix] occurs after a noun when these meanings such as "blame" (*nindā*) are present? In the sense of blame (*nindā*): *nindita*, *muṇḍa*, *muṇḍaka*;

likewise, *samaṇaka*, *paṇḍitaka*, *brāhmaṇaka*, *veyyākaraṇaka*. In the sense of "unknown" (*aññāta*): *kassa ayaṃ asso* = *assako* (this horse belongs to whom?). This is due to the power of the grammatical application (*payoga-sāmatthiya*).
The non-understanding of a specific relationship is thus understood. In the sense of "little" (*appattha*): *appakaṃ telaṃ* becomes *telakaṃ*, *ghatakaṃ*.
In the sense of "resemblance" (*paṭibhāgattha*): like an elephant, it is *hatthikaḥ*; likewise *assakaḥ*, *balībaddhakaḥ*.

In readings such as "These are our elephants, horses, and oxen," it should be understood either through the elision of the suffix *ka* (by the rule "elision") or by metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*). And these are forms made from wood and other materials.

In the sense of "quick," *mānusa* becomes *mānusaka*, *rukkha* becomes *rukkhaka*, and *pilakkha* becomes *pilakkhaka*. In the sense of "dear," *dayita* becomes *dayita* (as it is), *putta* becomes *puttaka*, and *vaccha* becomes *vacchaka*.
In the sense of "perception," *mora* becomes *moraka*, *katara* becomes *kataka*, and *bhataka* becomes *bhataka*.
41. The suffix *-ika* expresses its measure (*parimāṇa*).

The suffixes *ṇika* and *ka* occur after a word ending in the nominative case (*paṭhamantā*) in the sense of "this belongs to this," provided that the nominative-ending word is a measure (*parimāṇa*).
Because it is the instrument for measuring rice and other grains by means of measures such as a *doṇa*, it is called "measure" (*parimāṇa*) in the sense of "that by which something is measured.
Thus: "A *doṇa* is his measure" is *doṇiko vīhi*; *khārasatiko*, *khārasahassiko*; "eighty years" (*āsītiko vayo*); "half a body" (*upaḍḍhakāyo*).
A half-body pillow for its measure. [The groups] five and six.
42. *Yādīhi* with initial *ya* etc., ending in the nominative case, the suffix *ttaka* occurs in the sense of the genitive (*chaṭṭhī*), provided that the nominative form is a measure.
Whatever its measure may be, to that extent it is "ettaka," meaning "of this much.
In the case of *yāvataka*, whatever its measure may be, to that extent it is *yāvataka*. 43.
And all [these] as far as... (*sabbā cāvantu*).

After all [words] ending in the nominative case, the suffix *āvan* occurs in the sense of the genitive (*chaṭṭhyatthe*), provided that the nominative-ending word expresses a measure (*parimāṇa*). Thus, for one whose measure is "all," there is *sabbāvantaṃ*;
by the rule “*aṃ* in the neuter,” the suffix *aṃ* is applied.

Likewise, *yāvantaṃ* and *tāvantaṃ*. 44. After the word *kiṃ* ending in the nominative case, the suffixes *rati*, *rīva*, *rīvataka*, and *rittaka* occur in the sense of the genitive. Of what number? (Of how many?)

The measure of these [words] is as follows: because they have *r* as an *anubandha*, there is elision of the following portion (*iṃbhāgalopa*). Thus: *kīva*, *kīvatakaṃ*, *kittakaṃ*. By its very nature, *rīvanta* is innumerable. 45.
Regarding the suffix *ita* in the sense of "having arisen" (*sañjāta*), according to the rule for the group beginning with *tāraka*:

it is applied in the sense of having arisen. For example: *tārakitaṃ gaganaṃ* (the sky in which stars have arisen), *pupphito rukkho* (a tree in which flowers have arisen), *pallavitā latā* (a creeper in which sprouts have arisen).
46. In the word *māne*, the suffix *-mat* occurs in the sense of "measuring" (*mānavuttito*) based on the first [rule]. A *pala* is the measure of this; thus, *palamattaṃ*.
A *hasta* is the measure of this; thus, *hatthamattaṃ*. A hundred is the measure of this; thus, *satamattaṃ*. A *doṇa* is the measure of this...
A *doṇa*-measure. Through metaphorical treatment (*upacāra*) as non-different [from the object], it is also called "the *doṇa*. That by which something is measured is a "measure" (*māna*);
because it relates to a measure, the rule applies only to those words ending in the sixth case (genitive).
And here: "But *ummāna* is measurement upwards; *parimāṇa*, however, is from all sides."
The term *pamāṇa* signifies length (*āyāma*), while *saṅkhā* and *sesa* signify it from all sides.
(47) *Taggha*, *cu*, and *uddha*:

because they denote measurement (*māna*) and height (*uddha*), *taggha* is used in the sense of "measured" (*matto*). *Jaṇṇutaggha* means having the knee as its measure, i.e., "knee-high" (*jaṇṇumatta*).
48. *Ṇo ca purisa*:
"Purisā" becomes "ṇo," as in "mattādayo. "Puriso" is the measure (*parimāṇa*) of a man; thus it is "porisaṃ," meaning "the measure of a man" (*purisamattaṃ*) or "worth a man" (*purisatagghaṃ*).
49. *Ayubhaddvitīhaṃ se*.
The suffix *aya* occurs by means of two dual functions. That which has both parts (*ubho aṃsā*) is *ubhaya*, *dvaya*, or *taya*.

If it is argued that because the rule applies to the whole through its connection with the parts, there should not be a plural form from *ubhaya* and the others, [we reply: plural forms certainly do occur, as in the case of "the head of Rāhu" (*rāhuno sira*), where a plural is used even when there is no actual plurality, due to the intention to express a distinction.

50. After a numeral [ending in] -tī, -sā, -sa, -dasanta, followed by *adhika* (more), *satasahasse* (in a hundred thousand), or *ḍo*, [the suffix] *ḍo* occurs in the sense of the locative case (*sattamī*) when the word *satyantāya*, *utyantāya*, *īsantāya*, *āsantāya*, *dasantāya*, or a numeral ending in *-paṭhama* follows, provided that the numeral is *adhika*.
[The form] *yadasminti* refers to "that which is in this," namely a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand (*satasahassa*).
Or it is so. "In this there are twenty more than a hundred," thus it is *vīsaṃsataṃ*.
139. When *ḍe* follows, there is the elision of the letter *ti* in the word *sati*. For example: *ekavīsaṃsataṃ*, *sahassaṃ*, or *satasahassaṃ*.
"Thirty more than this hundred, etc. means three hundred, one thousand three hundred, and so forth.
"Ninety more than this hundred, etc. means nine hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand.
"Forty more than this hundred, thousand, or hundred-thousand" means four hundred, and so forth. It is the same for those ending in *ā*: "fifty more than this hundred," and so forth.
"Dasantāya-ekādasaṃsataṃ" and so forth. 51.

In the sense of completion, the suffix *ḍo* optionally occurs after a numeral beginning with *ekādasa* (eleven) that ends in the sixth case, when it expresses the meaning of completion. That number is completed [by the person].
That by which it completes is *pūraṇa*. The completer of eleven is *ekādasa*; except for the rule "after *pañca* and the following numerals, [the suffix] *ma* [is used]," it is *ekādasama*.

The completer of twenty is *vīsa* or *vīsatima*; [likewise] *tiṃsa* or *tiṃsatima*. Because the particle *vā* has a restricted optionality (*vavatthita-vibhāsā*), [the forms] *cattālīsa* and *paññāsa* are always [used].
52. *Ma-pañcamādikatīhi*:
with the suffix *ma*, [the forms] *pañcamo*, *pañcamī*; *sattamo*, *sattamī*; *aṭṭhamo*, *aṭṭhamī*; *katimo*, *katimī*, and so forth, are formed. 53. *Sathādīnam i cati*:
for *sa* and the others, *i* is substituted before *cati*.

In the case of *sata* and other numerals, there is the substitution of *anta* and the addition of *i*. Thus, the one completing a hundred is *satima*, and [the one completing a thousand] is *sahassima*.
54. Regarding *chaṭṭha* and *ṭṭhamā*:
from the word *cha*, in the sense of completion, the forms *ṭṭha* and *ṭṭhamā* arise. The one completing six is *chaṭṭha*; [in the feminine] it is *chaṭṭhamī*. In the feminine, it is *chaṭṭhī*.

The sixth [case]. By the rule of grammatical derivation (*nipātana*), “*catuttha-dutiyesu esaṃ tatiya-paṭhamā*,” for the sense of ordinal numbers (*pūraṇatthe*): from *dvi*, *tiyo* is substituted and *du* is also substituted;

from *tri* and *catur*, *a* is substituted for *ti*; and from *tiya* and *ttha*, they are respectively *dutiyo*, *tatiyo*, and *catuttho*. 55. *Ekā kā + kya sahāye*: [The suffix] *kā* or *kya* is used in the sense of a companion (*sahāye*).

“An adjective is purposeful when there is a possibility of confusion”—according to this principle, the word “asahāye” (without a companion) is stated in order to specify [the meaning]. The suffixes *ka* and *ākī* optionally occur after the word *eka* in the sense of being without a companion (*asahāya*).
Thus: *ekova ekako*, *ekākī*, or simply *eko*. 56.

After words such as *vaccha*, the suffix *tara* occurs in the sense of the attenuation of their inherent nature (*sabhāva-tanutte*), that is, when only a small remnant remains. That which is one’s own nature is *sabhāva*.
The cause for the occurrence of the notion of "belonging to oneself" (*attaniya*). In the case of the diminution of a well-bred cow, there is *vacchataro* (a young bull);

in the case of a female, *vacchatarī*. In the case of the diminution of youth, there is *okkhataro*. *Okkhā* refers to a bull in his second stage of life. In the case of the diminution of horse-nature, there is *assataro*.
In the case of the diminution of the capacity of the genus "cow," there is *usabhataro*. Here, "diminution" (*tanutta*) means weakness.
57. Regarding selection (*niddhāraṇa*):
the words *kiṃ*, *katara*, and *katama* are used for selection. For example: "Which one among you is Devadatta? Which one among you is Kaṭṭha? Or:
"Who among the Bhāradvājas are you, O Brahmā? (In these cases, *kiṃ* becomes *ko*, *kataro*, and *katamo* respectively when followed by the particle *eva*.)
58. *Tena datte liyāti*:

when "given by him" (*tena datte*) is the meaning to be expressed, the suffixes *la* and *iya* occur frequently by virtue of the general rule (*bahulādhikārā*) in the sense of a human being (*manussasaññāyaṃ*). For example: *devena datto* becomes *devalo* and *deviyo*;

*brahmalā* becomes *brahmalā* and *brahmiyo*. *Sīvalā* becomes *sīvilā* and *sīviyo*. The long vowel (*dīgho*) occurs after the word *sissa*. *Deva*, *brahma*, and *siva* refer to humans who bear those names.
(Rattam-icc-ādi-aneka-attha-taddhitaṃ). 59. *Tassa bhāva-kammesu sutta-tā-tta-na-ṇya-ṇeyya-ṇi-ya-ṇiyā*:

After a word ending in the sixth case, the suffixes *tā* and the others—namely *tta*, *na*, *ṇya*, *ṇeyya*, *ṇi*, *ya*, and *ṇiya*—are frequently used in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*) or object (*kamma*). Not all suffixes occur after every [base], except for *atta* and *tā*. That from which a verbal notion arises is the "abstract state" (*bhāva*), which is the cause for the occurrence of a word. And it has been said:
"There was indeed for us the cognition of sound; that state [arises] from the occurrence of that sound.
And the name, which serves as the cause, consists of genus, substance, action, and quality.

The state of a blue cloth is "blueness" (*nīlattam*) or "blueness-ness" (*nīlatā*); this is a quality (*guṇa*), a state (*bhāva*). Here, by way of the quality of blueness, the word "blue" [applies] to the cloth.
The state (*bhāva*) that serves as the cause for the application of a word through a quality is called "state" (*nimitta*). The state of the quality blue is "blueness" (*nīlattam*);
it is the genus of the quality blue (*nīlaguṇajāti*). Here, the genus of the quality blue, acting as the cause, is the cause for the application of the word "blue" through a quality.
"Cowness" (*gottam*), "cowness" (*gotā*), or "the genus of cows" (*gojāti*): here, when words denoting a genus are applied to a substance, the genus is the cause.
The state of being a cooker (*pācaka*) is "cooker-ness" (*pācakatta*); thus, "state" (*bhāva*) is the quality of being connected with an action.

Here, the state is the quality of being connected with the action of cooking. Stick-ness (*daṇḍitta*), horn-ness (*visāṇitta*), and king’s-man-ness (*rājapurisatta*) are the states of being connected with the substances—the stick, the horn, and the king—respectively, because they serve as the grounds for the application of such terms as "one who has a stick" (*daṇḍī*) and so forth.
The state of Devadatta is *devadattattaṃ*; "moon-ness" (*candattaṃ*) and "sun-ness" (*sūriyattaṃ*) are the commonalities of specific states.

The distinction between Devadatta’s various states such as childhood and so forth, the distinction between the moon’s various states such as its phases and so forth, and the distinction between the sun’s various states such as its dullness or brilliance and so forth, constitute the commonality;
this is the "sign" (*nimitta*) here. Here, it refers to the existing referents—the words for perceptions that have become objects.

The "occurrence-characteristic" (pavattinimitta) has been stated. Regarding "the state of space" (ākāsatta) and "the state of non-existence" (abhāvatta): therein, the commonality of distinctions—such as the space within a jar (ghaṭākāsa) and the space within a pot (pīṭharākāsa), or the absence of a cloth (paṭābhāva) and the absence of a jar (ghaṭābhāva)—is a "state" (bhāva). [Similarly,] there is the state of an ordinary person (puthujjana), which is the state of an ordinary person (puthujjanatta).
The state of feeling (vedanā) is the state of feeling (vedanatta); [here] the vowel is shortened. Likewise, there is the state of being born (jāyatta) and the state of being an elder (jāratta).

The state or action of one who is lazy (*alasassa*) is *ālasyaṃ*; here, after the elision of the vowel *a* according to the rule "elision of vowels following a vowel" (*lopo vaṇṇi vaṇṇānaṃ*), the vowel *ā* is substituted by the rule "the first of vowels" (*sarānam ādissa*), and so it is in the subsequent cases as well.
The state of a Brahmin (*brāhmaṇassa*) is *brahmaññaṃ*, with the double *ñ* resulting from the prior form (*pubbarūpa*). [Likewise:

*cāpalyaṃ* (restlessness), *nepuññaṃ* (skillfulness), *pesuññaṃ* (slander); the state of a king (*rañño*) is *rajjaṃ* (kingship), *ādhipaccaṃ* (sovereignty), *dāyajjaṃ* (inheritance), *vesammaṃ* or *vesamaṃ* (unevenness).
The suffix -ṇa [is applied]. The state of being a friend is *sakhyaṃ*; likewise: *vāṇijjaṃ*, *ārogyaṃ*, *odagyaṃ*, *ānaṇyaṃ*, *dubbalyaṃ*, *balyaṃ*, *paṇḍiccaṃ*, *bāhussaccaṃ*, *porohiccaṃ*.
The state of one who is forgetful is *muṭṭhassaccaṃ* (with the elision of the vowel *i*).
Likewise: *kosallaṃ*, *vepullaṃ*. The state of being common is *sāmaññaṃ*; likewise: *perissaṃ*, *somanassaṃ*, *domanassaṃ*, *sovacassaṃ*.
*Do-vacassaṃ*: the state of being ill-behaved; *ne-pakkaṃ*: the state of being prudent (*nipaka*); *ādhikkaṃ*; *dobhaggaṃ*:
the state of being unfortunate (*dubhaga*); *sāruppaṃ*: the state of being suitable (*sarūpa*); *opammaṃ*; *sokhummaṃ*; *tacchaṃ*: the state of being true (*tatha*); *dummejjhaṃ*:
the state of being dull-witted (*dummedha*); *bhesajjaṃ*: the state of being a remedy (*bhesaja*); *veyyāvaccaṃ*: the work of one who is occupied (*byāvaṭa*), just as in the case of *veyyākaraṇa*.

The state of one who is pure (*su-cina*) is purity (*soceyya*); sovereignty is *ādhipateyya*; the state or action of one who is a monkey (*kapi*) is monkeyishness (*kāpeyya*). The state or action of one who is crafty (*saṭha*) is craftiness (*sāṭheyya*).

The state of those who possess the suffix *-ṇa* is reverence (*gārava*), with *u* substituted for *ava*. Proficiency is *pāṭava*; straightforwardness is *ajjava*; gentleness is *maddava*; and by [the rule] beginning with "from *kusīta*," there is the substitution of *ussa* and the doubling of the consonant. The state of supreme beings (*parama*) is perfection (*pāramī*), with the suffix *-vī*. The state of those who are harmonious is concord (*sāmaggī*). The state of one who possesses mastery (*adhipati*) is mastery (*adhipatiya*);
likewise, wisdom (*paṇḍitiya*), erudition (*bahussutiya*), nakedness (*naggiya*), and heroism (*sūriya*).
The state or action of one who is lazy (*alasa*) is *ālasiya*, *tālusiya*, *mandiya*, *dakkhiya*, *porohitiya*, or *veyyattiya*. How is it that *rāmaṇīyaka* is formed?

The suffix *ka* (from *kantā*) is established by the addition of *ṇa* in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*). Action (*kamma*) means activity (*kriyā*); therein, the action of one who is lazy is laziness (*alasatta*), laziness (*alasatā*), laziness-ness (*alasattana*), *ālasya*, or *ālasiya*.
122. "In the sense of identity" (*sakatthe*).
In the case of *saka* as well, *ttā* and so forth occur according to the appropriate application. *Yathābhūtaṃ* itself is *yathābhuccaṃ*; *kāruññaṃ*; *pattakallaṃ*.

*Ākāsānantam* itself is *ākāsānañcaṃ*; here there is the elision of the vowel *a*, and when the single-substitute rule (*pubbarūpa*) has been applied, by the rule "tadaminā" etc., there is the replacement of *n* with *ñ* and the elision [of the following vowel], as in *kāyapāguññatā*.

60. *Bya*, *vaddha*, and *dāsa*—with the addition of *cha* and *ṭṭhi* at the end—become *byo* when used in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*) or action (*kamma*). The state or action of an elder (*vaddha*) is *vaddhabbyaṃ* or *vaddhatā*. The state or action of a slave (*dāsa*) is *dāsabyaṃ*, *dāsyaṃ*, or *dāsatā*. How does one say "the state of being an elder"? [The suffix] *ṇa* is added as an augment (*āgama*). 61.
*Nasa* [is substituted for the final vowel of the stem], and *yu* is substituted for *va*. The suffix *bo* is also applied to *va*.

After words ending in the sixth case (genitive) that denote youth, *naṇ* optionally occurs in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*) or action (*kamma*), and *vassa* or *bo* also occur. The state of being young is *yobbanam*, *yuvattam*, or *yuvatā*.
62. *Aṇvādito ti-mo*:

this suffix *ti-mo* optionally occurs in the sense of abstract state. The state of being minute is *aṇimā*; the state of being light is *laghimā*; the state of being great is *mahimā*; the state of being thin is *kasimā*.
133. *Kisa-mahata-mime kasa, mahāti*:
In these cases, for both "great" (*mahato*) and "small" (*kisassa*), there is the substitution of the word *kasa* [for the suffix].
63. [The suffix] *bhāva* is produced by that.
From a word expressing an action (*kriyāvācaka*), this suffix [is applied]: *pākimaṃ* (cooked), *sekimaṃ* (sprinkled).

127. From the words *kosajja*, *ajjava*, *pārisajja*, *sohajja*, *maddava*, *arissa*, *sabhā*, *jañña*, *theyya*, and *bāhusacca*, these words are derived with the suffix *ṇa* as an unattached marker (*anubandha*).
The state of one who is indolent is "indolence" (*kosajja*); here, the suffix *ṇya* occurs in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), by which the *ī* of *kusīta* becomes *a*.
And that which is done toward him, whose prior form is *kosajja*. In the sense of "straightness" (*ujju*), [the suffix] *ṇya* is applied by the rule "for *ujju*, *ajjava*";

by this, *u* is replaced, and by the rule "for *u-vaṇṇa*, *avaṅ* before a vowel," there is the substitution of *avaṅ*, whereby the doubling of *j* occurs. In the phrase "one who is good among assemblies" (*parisāsu sādhu*), the suffix *ṇya* is applied by the rule "the suffix *ṇya* in the sense of 'good therein'";
by this, *j* is inserted as an augment (*jāgama*), and by the rule "long and short vowels before a consonant," there is the shortening of *ā*. When these have been performed...
*Yassa pubbarūpaṃ pārisajjo*: by this very sequence of words, the grammatical derivation (*saddasiddhi*) is to be understood.

*Suhadayo va suhajjo*; its state is *sohajjaṃ*, by which [rule] there is the elision of the *ya*. *Muduno bhāvo maddavaṃ*; by this [rule], the substitution of *ussa* for *attaṃ*. *Isino idaṃ bhāvo vā ārissaṃ*;

with the suffix *ṇya*, by this [rule] there is the augment *āra*, and by the rule "elision of the final vowel and the following consonant" (*lopo vaṇṇī vaṇṇānaṃ*), there is the elision of the final letter *a*.
*Usabha*: the state of being a bull (*usabha*) is *āsabha*; by this rule, the vowel *u* is elided. *Ājānīya*: the state of being a thoroughbred is *ājañña*;

by this rule, when *ya* is elided, the vowel *ī* is dropped according to the rule "there is elision of vowels following a consonant" (*lopo vaṇṇi vaṇṇānaṃ*). *Thena*: the state of being thievish is *theyya*; by this rule, the letter *na* becomes *ya*. *Bahussuta*:

the state of being one who has heard much is *bāhusacca*; by this rule, the vowel *u* becomes *a*, and there is elision of the first member of the conjunct (*saṃyogādilopa*). (This concludes the section on secondary derivatives [taddhita] expressing state.)

64. *Tara*, *tama*, *issa*, *ka*, *ya*, *iṭṭha*, and *atisaya*—these suffixes are called *atisaya-paccayas* because they function to express excellence (*atisaya*). For example: *pāpatara* (more wicked), *pāpatama* (most wicked), *pāpissita*, *pāpiya*, *pāpiṭṭha*;
and in the feminine: *pāpatarā*, and so forth. Those suffixes ending in *atisaya* are also termed *atisaya-paccayas*.
Exceedingly wicked: *pāpiṭṭho*, *pāpiṭṭhataro*, *pāpiṭṭhatamo*. Likewise: *paṭutaro*, *paṭutamo*; *paṭissiko*, *paṭiyo*, *paṭiṭṭho*, *varataro*, and so forth;
as well as *paṇītataro*, and so forth. 135. [The suffix] *jo* is used before words ending in *vuḍḍha*, *assi*, *yi*, and *ṭṭha*.

That which is "vuddha" (grown) regarding the [suffixes] *iya*, *iṭṭha*, etc., is called *jeṭṭha* (the eldest/greatest). In the substitution of *ja*, when the preceding vowel is elided, the vowels [of the suffix] undergo the *ekāra* change after *issa*, and there is doubling of the *ya*.

136. For the words *bāḷha*, *antika*, and *pasattha*, the substitutes *sādha*, *neda*, and *sa* respectively occur before the [suffixes] *iya*, *iṭṭha*, etc. Thus, one who is exceedingly *bāḷha* (intense/strong).

*sādhiya* becomes *sādhiṭṭha*. *Antika* with the suffix *iya* becomes *nediyo*; with the superlative suffix *tama*, it becomes *nediṭṭha*. *Seyya* and *seṭṭha* are formed from *praśasta* with the suffix *iya*;
when the preceding vowel *ra* is elided, there is doubling of the following consonant (*dvitta*).
137. [The suffixes] *kaṇa*, *kana*, *ppa*, and *yuvan*.

In the case of *iya* and *iṭṭha*, the suffixes *vī*, *mantu*, and *vantu* become *kaṇa* and *kaṇā* respectively. *Kaṇiya* means "one who is exceedingly young," and *kaṇiṭṭha* means "the youngest. *Kaniya* means "one who is exceedingly young," and *kaniṭṭha* means "the youngest.
138. Regarding the rule "there is elision of *vī*, *mantu*, and *vantu*":
in the case of *iya* and *iṭṭha*, there is elision of *vī*, *mantu*, and *vantu*. *Medhiya* means "one who is exceedingly wise," and *medhiṭṭha* means "the wisest. Exceedingly...

*Satimā* means possessed of mindfulness (*sati*), established in mindfulness (*satiṭṭha*). *Guṇiyo* means exceptionally virtuous (*guṇavā*), established in virtue (*guṇiṭṭha*). Here, in the sense of expressing possession (*mantvatthe*), the suffixes *-vī*, *-mantu*, and *-vantu* occur respectively.
65. The suffix *-llo* occurs when [the quality] is dependent upon that.

The suffix *lla* is applied after a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyanta*) in the sense of dependence upon that. That which depends upon knowledge (*veda*) is *vedalla*. That which is badly dependent is *duṭṭhulla*. *Veda* means satisfaction. That which depends upon formations (*saṅkhāra*) is *saṅkhārilla*. 66.

The suffixes *ṇa*, *ṇika*, *ṇeyya*, and *maya* are applied after a word ending in the sixth case (*chaṭṭhiyanta*) in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*) or a part (*avayava*). A modification is a state different from the original nature (*pakati*). After a noun ending in the sixth case, the suffixes beginning with *ṇa* are applied in the sense of a modification or a part.

[The suffix] *Ṇa* occurs frequently. A derivative (*vikāra*) of iron (*ayasa*) is *āyasa*, meaning an iron bond; [here] the augment *sakāga* is applied. A part or a derivative of the *udumbara* tree is *odumbara*, such as ash or a leaf.
*Kāpota* refers to the flesh or the bone of a pigeon (*kapota*). [With the suffix] *Ṇika*: a derivative of cotton (*kappāsa*) is *kappāsika*, meaning a cotton cloth.
[With the suffix] *Ṇeyya*: a derivative or a part of the eni-deer (*eṇi*) is *eṇeyya*. A derivative of cocoons (*kosa*) is *koseyya*, meaning silk cloth.
"Made of" (*maya*) means a transformation of grass; thus there is a chariot made of grass, made of wood, made of reeds, made of clay, made of gold, or made of silver.
"In another" (*aññasmiṃ*) [is used] with *maya*; cow-dung is "cow-made" (*gomaya*).
67. From *jatu* comes *jatuma*. Or: *ssaṇa*.

In the case of derivatives (*vikāra*) and parts (*avayava*), the suffix *ssaṇ* optionally occurs after the word *jatu*. Here, although the rule applies to both "derivatives" and "parts," due to the governing principle of "frequently" (*bahulādhikāra*), it occurs only in the sense of a derivative. A derivative of *jatu* is *jātussaṃ* or *jatumayaṃ*. 123. *Lopa*:
Generally, there is also the elision (*lopa*) of a suffix. [For example: "The fruit of a tree that has borne fruit is both a part and a derivative; likewise for one that has sprouted..."
Because it is stated [in the grammatical rule] as "pallavaṃ" (the shoot), the fruit and so forth are both modifications (*vikāra*) and constituent parts (*avayava*). Therefore, this is said:
among the modifications and constituent parts—namely, the fruits of the *piyāla* tree are *piyālāni*, the flowers of the *mallikā* are *mallikā*, and the root of the *usīra* is *usīraṃ*.

Alternatively, by means of that word, there is a designation of that [object] through the metaphorical transfer of identity (*abhedopacāra*); therefore, the formation is established even without the elision of the suffix.
68. *Kaṇa-ṇa-ṇika* for a collection.
The suffixes *kaṇ*, *ṇa*, and *ṇika* occur after a word ending in the sixth case when denoting a collection. From a clan-suffix (*gotta-paccaya*), the collection of *rājaññas* is *rājaññakaṃ*;

[the collection] of humans is *mānusakaṃ*. From *ukkha* and others: the collection of *ukkhas* is *okkhakaṃ*; the vowel *o* occurs by the rule “in some cases after a conjunct consonant. [The collection of] *oṭṭhas* is *oṭṭhakaṃ*.
A collection of *urabbhas* (rams) is *orabbhakaṃ*. Likewise: *rājakaṃ*, *rājaputtakaṃ*, *hatthikaṃ*, *dhenukaṃ*, *māyūrakaṃ*, *kāpotakaṃ*, *māhisakaṃ*.
With the suffix *-ṇa*: a collection of crows is *kākaṃ*; [a collection] of alms is *bhikkhaṃ*. With the suffix *-ṇika*: a collection of apūpas (cakes) that are not made by mind is *āpūpikaṃ*;
a collection of *saṃkulis* is *saṃkulikaṃ*.

69. *Tāti* [is used] after *jana*, etc., in the sense of a collection (*samūha*). A collection of people is *janatā*; likewise *gajatā*, *bandhutā*, *gāmatā*, *sahāyatā*, and *nāgaratā*. Those ending in *-tā* are feminine by their very nature.

The form *madanīya* is established by the suffix *-anīya* in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). The forms ending in *-itatta* and *-itta* are derived from nominal roots (*nāmadhātu*).

By that, it is established: because it behaves like smoke, the suffix *ktvā* is applied according to the rule "after [roots] having the sense of going, being intransitive, or denoting a locus" (*gamana-tthā-kammaka-ādhāre ca*), and with the addition of the augment *ū*, the abstract state of that which has behaved like smoke is "smokeness" (*dhūmāyitattaṃ*).
70. "The suffix *iya* is added after *hi*."
The suffix *iya* is used in the sense of "beneficial. That which is beneficial for the objects of clinging (*upādāna*) is called *upādāniya*.
71. The suffix *ssa* is used after words such as *cakkhu* in the sense of "beneficial. That which is beneficial for the eye is *cakkhussaṃ*; likewise, *āyussaṃ*.

72. *Ṇyo*: The suffix *ṇya* occurs in the sense of "skilled in" (*tattha sādhu*) when following a word ending in the locative case (*sattamyanta*). "Skilled" (*sādhu*) means competent, suitable, or beneficial. In *sabhāyaṃ kusalo* (skilled in the assembly), the suffix *ṇya* becomes *ya*, and there is the elision of the vowel *ā*.

Thus, *sabhāyaṃ* becomes *sabha*. In *parisāyaṃ sādhu* (skilled in the assembly), the suffix *ṇya* becomes *ja*; by the rule beginning with "kosajjā," there is the strengthening (*vuddhi*) of the vowel *a*. Thus, *parisāyaṃ* becomes *pārisajja*.

*Mejjhaṃ* (marrow) is beneficial for intelligence (*medhā*); *pajjaṃ* (foot-ointment) and *telaṃ* (oil) are beneficial for the feet (*pāda*). The suffix *-nya-* occurs in the sense of "another," as in *racchā*, which means "that which carries a chariot" (*rathaṃ vahati*).
73. From the word *kamma* [the suffixes] *-niya-* and *-ñña-* occur in the sense of being suitable (*sādhū*): that which is suitable for action (*kamme sādhu*) is *kammaniyaṃ* or *kammaññaṃ*.
74. After *kathā* and others, the suffix *ika* is applied.
One who is skilled in discourse (*kathā*) is a *kathika*. A preacher of the Dhamma (*dhammakathika*), a warrior (*saṅgāmika*), one living abroad (*pavāsika*), and one observing a fast (*upavāsika*).
75. After *patha* and others, the suffix *neyya* is applied.
*Ṇeyya*. That which is beneficial for a journey is *pātheyya*; that which is beneficial for a master (*sapati*) is *sāpateyya*, meaning wealth. *Padīpeyya* means oil. 76.
[The suffix] *ṇeyya* is applied in the sense of "one who is worthy of" (*arahaṭṭhe*). One who is worthy of a gift (*dakkhiṇa*) is *dakkhiṇeyya*.

77. *Rāyo tumantā*: [The suffix] *tum* occurs after verbal roots (*rā*) in the sense of "one who possesses" (*tumantā*), or it is a root (*rā*) itself. In *ghātetāyaṃ*, [the word is analyzed as] "one who is worthy to be killed" (*ghātetuṃ arahati*). Here, by the rule "after a vowel (*a*), the *u* of *uṃ* is elided when followed by *rā*, *anu*, *bandha*, *nta*, *sa*, or *ra*", there is the elision of *uṃ*. [Similarly: *jāpetāyaṃ*, *pabbājetāyaṃ*. Why [is the word] *vā* mentioned? [To exclude cases such as] *ghātetuṃ*. (This concludes the section on miscellaneous secondary derivatives. 78. *Taṃ ettha assa atthīti mantu*:
[The suffix] *mantu* is applied [to a noun] in the sense that "this belongs to that" (*taṃ ettha assa atthi*).

The suffix *mantu* occurs in these senses when there is "something belonging here" (*paṭhamantā ettha assa atthīti*). When it is said, "Cows belong to this place or to this person," one says *gomā* (possessor of cows) or *gomanto*; such forms are equal to those ending in the possessive suffix *-vant*.
Because the word *atthi* (is) specifies the present tense, one does not say *gomā* [based] on cows that are past or future.

How then can one say, "He was a possessor of cows" (*gomā āsi*) or "He will be a possessor of cows" (*gomā bhavissati*)? Even then, he is a possessor of cows based on cows that are [conceptually] present; the words *āsi* and *bhavissati* are merely other words [expressing time].
“Kālantaraṃ. From the word *iti*, there is a restriction of the object (visayaniyama).
For it is said: “The particles *me*, *mantu*, and so forth, occur in connection with abundance, praise, blame, excess, constant association, and contact.”
134. In the word *mantu*, there is the substitution of *āyu* for *āya*.

Thus, one who possesses life (*āyu*) is called *āyasmā*. Because words denoting genus (*jāti-sadda*) have the capacity to denote the individual substance (*dabba*), suffixes such as *manta* do not apply;
likewise, this is not the case for words denoting qualities (*guṇa-sadda*), as in the example "the white cloth. However, for those quality-words...
There is no capacity for the designation "dabba" [in those cases], yet they do indeed exist; thus, one who has intelligence (*buddhi*) is "intelligent" (*buddhimā*).

Regarding "having abandoned the qualities" (*vantavaṇṇā*): it means possessing form, possessing taste, possessing smell, and possessing sound. Regarding "the suffixes *ika* and *ī* after *daṇḍa* and so forth": [the suffixes] *ika* and *ī* [are applied];
thus, one who possesses taste is *rasī* or *rasika*, one who possesses form is *rūpī* or *rūpika*, and one who possesses smell is *gandhī* or *gandhika*.
79. One who has vomited out [faults] is *vanta*.
One who possesses praised virtue (*sīla*) is *sīlavā*. One who possesses abundant or praised wisdom (*paññā*) is *paññavā*.
80. According to the rule "after *daṇḍa* etc., there is *tva*, *ika*, or *ī*."

The suffix *ika* occurs in the sense of possession (*mantatthe*). Because of the rule of frequent application (*bahulavidhāna*), two forms arise from the word *kuto*: *kutoci* and *kuto*; however, when followed by *ce*, only one form occurs. When *daṇḍa* is permanently joined [to the suffix], it becomes *daṇḍika* or *daṇḍī*, meaning "one who has a staff. Similarly, *gandhika* or *gandhī* means "one who has fragrance. But when the suffix *vā* is used, it is simply *daṇḍavā*.
According to the grammatical rule (*gaṇasutta*) "the suffix *ika* alone after *uttama* and *dhana*," we have *dhanika* (wealthy);

otherwise, it is *dhanī* or *dhanavā*. In the sense of "not present" (*asannihite atthā*): "one who has wealth not present" is *atthika* or *atthī*; when the wealth is present, it is *atthavā*. And [the suffix applies] to words ending in *ta* (*tadantā ca*): "one who has merit as their object" is *puññatthika* or *puññatthī*.
“*Vaṇṇantā īyeva*”: One who possesses the color of a Brahmā is *brahmavaṇṇī*, meaning one with the appearance of a deity (*devavaṇṇī*).

“*Hatthadantehi jātiyaṃ*”: One who has hands is a *hatthī* (elephant), and one who has tusks is a *dantī*; [these apply] specifically to those belonging to the elephant species, not to anyone else who merely possesses hands or tusks.
“*Vaṇṇato brahmacārimhi*”: One who possesses beauty is a *vaṇṇiko* celibate student (*brahmacārī*).
“In the sense of ‘beginning with *pokkhara*’. That which has water (*pokkhara*) or lotuses (*paduma*) is called *pokkhari*.
By the rule “after vowels [the suffix] *nī*,” there is the suffix *nī*; by the rule “*gharaṇī* and others,” there is the substitution of *ā* for *ī*, and *ṇ* for *n*.
Thus: *pokkharaṇī*, *uppalinī*, *kumudinī*, *bhisinī*, *mulālinī*, *sālukinī*.

“*Kvacādesopi*” (sometimes there is substitution). One who has lotuses is *padumī*; [the feminine forms are] *paduminī* and *paduminīpaṇṇaṃ*. From place (*desato*), other than that, it means a lotus pond; [from *hatthi*] it means an elephant. “*Nāvāya iko*” (after *nāvā*, the suffix *ika* is added):
*nāviko* (boatman). *Sikhī*, *bālī*, *sīlī*, *balī*.
“*Sukhadukkhā ī*” (after *sukha* and *dukkha*, the suffix *ī* is added): *sukhī*, *dukkhī*. “*Balā bāhūrupubbā ca*” (also after *bala* preceded by *bāhu* or *ūru*): *bāhubalī*, *ūrubalī*.
81. *Ssī* [is a suffix] after *tapas*, etc.
One who possesses *tapas* is a *tapassī*; likewise, a *yasassī*, a *tejassī*, a *manassī*, and a *payassī*. But when it is appropriate, it becomes *yasavā*.
82. After *mukha*, etc., the suffix *ro* [is applied].
One who has a censured mouth is *mukharo*. One who has a hole or cavity (*susi*) is *susiro*.
That which has saline soil (*ūsā*, i.e., alkaline earth) is *ūsaro*. Sweet is sugar, sweet is gravel, sweet is milk.
One who has a neck-hole (*khaṃ*) is *kharo*, a donkey. One who has a jaw (*kuñjo*) is *kuñjaro*. A city (*nagaro*).
Regarding the rule "dantassa ca unnatadante": by means of the *gaṇasutta*, *u* is added after *danta*; since he has protruding teeth (*unnata-danta*), he is *dantura*. 83.
After *tuṭṭhi* and so forth, the suffix *bho* or *bha* is applied. Since he has contentment (*tuṭṭhi*) as his nature, he is *tuṭṭhibho*; likewise *sālibho* and *vālibho*.
84. *Saddhāditva*:
the suffix *itva* is optionally replaced by *a*. One who possesses excessive faith is *saddho*; likewise *pañño*, *paññavā*, *saddhā kaññā*, and *saddhaṃ kulaṃ*.
85. *Ṇo tapā*: [the suffix] *ṇo* is applied after the word *tapa*.
The suffix *ṇo* is added after the word *tāpas*, forming *tāpasī*.

86. Regarding "by covetousness (*abhijjhā*) and so forth": the suffix *ālu* is also used. One who has covetousness is *abhijjhālu*; likewise *sītālu*, *dhajālu*, *dayālu*, and *dayāvā*. One who is simply covetous is *abhijjhāluka*.
87. Regarding "picchāditvā illo vā":

that which has *piccha* (slime) is called *picchila*, meaning "slimy" (*picchavā*). Similarly, *pheṇila*, *jaṭila*, and *tuṇḍila*. One who possesses censurable speech is called *vācāla*; here, there is elision of the subsequent vowel (*parassa-ra-lopo*). 88. Regarding "sīlādito vo": [the suffix] *va* follows words such as *sīla*.
It becomes *vā*. *Sīlavant* becomes *sīlavā*; *kesavant* becomes *kesavā*.
From *anna* with the suffix *nicca*, *annava* (ocean). With the suffix *vī* after *gaṇḍī* and *rājī* in the sense of a name: *gaṇḍīvā* is a bow because it has a *gaṇḍī* (a ram’s horn);
*rājīvā* is a lotus. 89. After *māyā* and *medhā*, [the suffix *vī*].
Vī: *māyāvī*, a wise man; *medhāvī*, a wise man. In the feminine: *medhāvinī*. [In the compound] *medhāvīkulaṃ*, the vowel is shortened before the suffix *si* by the rule "ekavacanayosva-ghonaṃ.
Likewise for *māyāvī*. 90. *Si+ssare āmyu-vāmī*:

When the word *issara* (lord) is the referent, the suffixes *ām* and *uvām* are added after the word ending in *sa* (the possessive suffix *-sa*) in the sense of the suffix *-mant*. *Sāmī*: one to whom wealth is attached (*saṃ = āyattaṃ assa atthi*). *Suvāmī*: a good lord. *Suvāminī*: a noble lady.

91. After the word *lakkhī*, the suffix *no* is used in the sense of possession (*mantvattha*), and the final vowel *a* is replaced by *a*. Thus, one who possesses *lakkhī* is called *lakkhaṇo*. 92. After the word *aṅga*, the suffix *no* is used in the sense of "beautiful" (*kalyāṇa*).
Thus, one whose limbs are beautiful is called *aṅgaṇo*.
She has limbs; thus, "aṅgasmā no hoti. Because she possesses limbs that are beautiful and lovely, she is called *aṅganā*.
93. Regarding "she has hair":
*lomā so*. Because she possesses abundant hair, she is *lomaso*; [thus] a girl with hair is *lomasā*.
94. *Ima* becomes *ima*;

*ima-ya* becomes *imaya*. [The suffixes] *-puttima*, *-kittima*, *-puttiya*, *-kappiya*, *-jaṭiya*, *-hānabhāgiya*, and *-seniya* [are added after a word ending in the sixth case], provided that the taddhita suffix expresses the sense of possession (*atthi*). (Taddhita expressing the sense of "having").
95. From the fifth case, the suffix *to* [is applied].
The suffix *to* frequently occurs after a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyantā*). Words formed with suffixes such as *to* are indeclinables (*nipāta*);

when these follow, there is elision of all case endings according to the rule "after numerals and indeclinables, all [case endings] are elided. For example: *gāmato āgacchati* (he comes from the village) becomes *gāmasmā āgacchati*;
*corato bhāyati* (he fears the thief) becomes *corehi bhāyati*; *satthato parihīno* (fallen away from the caravan) becomes *satthā parihīno*. Likewise: *purisato*, *rājato*, *aggito*.

From the hand (hatthito), from the cause (hetuto), from the connection (yuttito), from the woman (itthito), from the nun (bhikkhunito), from the sacrifice (yāguto), from the rose-apple tree (jambuto), from the mind (cittato), from the income (āyuto).
From all (sabbādito), from everywhere (sabbato), from which (yato), from there (tato), and so forth.
96. *Ito* + *te* = *itto*; *kuto*.

The suffix *ṭi* is substituted for *imassa*; [the suffix] *ṭa* is substituted for *etassa*. From what do these words *kuttaṃ* and *kiṃ* derive? *Ita* means "from this"; *ato*, *etto*, and *etasmā* mean "from that";
*kuto* and *kasmā* mean "from what. 97. [The rule] "after *abhi-* etc. [is applied]. *Abhito*, *parito*, *pacchato*, *heṭṭhato*.

(*sabbādito*). The remaining substitutes (*sesādesā*) and suffixes (*paccayā*) are likewise derived as indeclinables (*nipaccanti*) by this very rule. By this—
The *ka* and *ku* of *kissam* become *te* and *ṭe*; in the suffix *vap*, there is the elision (*ilopa*) of *i*;
and in the suffixes *ha* and *dha*, *ṭi* is substituted for *ima*. [Thus: *kasmiṃ*, *kattha*, *kuttra*, *kva*; *etasmiṃ*, *ettha*, *atra*; *imasmiṃ*, *iha*, *idha*. 101.
*Dhi* is optionally [substituted] for all [of these].
*Sabbasmā* means from all; *sabbasmiṃ*, *sabbadhi*, and *sabbattha* mean in all.

*Hiṃ*, *haṃ*, *nipaccante*, *kissa*, *ku* and *kā*. *Kuhiṃ*, *kahaṃ*. *Kuhiñcanaṃ* is another form of the particle (*nipāta*). 105.
With *sabba*, *eka*, *añña*, *ya*, and *ta*, the suffix *dā* is optionally used to denote time. For example:

106. *Kadā*, *kudā*, *sadā*, *adhunā*, and *idāni*—these words are declined [as follows]:
at what time? *kadā* or *kudā*; at all times, *sadā*; at this time, *adhunā* or *idāni*. 107.
*Ajja*, *sajja*, *parajje*, *itarahi*, *karahā*.
The base form (*pakati*), the suffix (*paccaya*), the substitute (*ādesa*), and the specific time (*kālavisesa*)—all of these are obtained through grammatical convention (*nipātana*).

When the suffixes *ṭo* and *jjo* are applied to this [base *ima*], it becomes *ajja* (today); that is, on this day, *ajja*. When the suffixes *sa* and *jju* are applied to *samāna*, it becomes *sajju* (immediately); that is, on the same day, *sajju*. From *apara*, with the suffix *jju*, it becomes *aparajju* (yesterday);
that is, on the previous day, *aparajju*. When *eto* is applied to this [base *ima*] and *rahi* is added for the time, it becomes *etarahi* (now); that is, at this time, *etarahi*.
What is the suffix *tha* used for in the word *sadda*, and what is its meaning? At what time is it employed?
(108) The suffix *tha* occurs after words such as *sabba* when expressing a manner (*pakāra*).
A specific quality that differentiates a general category is "manner"; the suffix *tha* is applied in that sense. For example: *sabbathā* (in every way), *yathā* (as/how), *tathā* (thus).
109. *Katha* and *itthaṃ*:
the suffix *thaṃ* is added to *ki* and *ime*. *Ka* and *ittaṃ* are their respective substitutes. In what manner? *Kathaṃ*. By this manner? *Itthaṃ*. 110.
*Dhā* [is used] after numerals.

In the sense of "manner" (*pakāra*), *dhā* becomes *dhā*. By means of two manners, or making two manners, one makes it twofold (*dvidhā*), or makes it manifold (*bahudhā*); one makes a single heap fivefold (*pañcappakāra*), that is, one makes it five ways (*pañcadhā*).

One makes the fivefold manner into a single manner, that is, one makes it oneway (*ekadhā*). 111. Regarding *ve*, *kā*, and *jjha*: after the word *eka*, *jjha* may optionally occur in the sense of "manner. By means of one manner, or making one manner, one makes it together (*ekajjhaṃ*), or one makes it oneway (*ekadhā*).
112. From *dvi* comes *dvedhā* or *edhā*.
By means of two ways (*pakāra*), one makes two ways; thus: *dvedhā*, *tedhā*; [also] *dvidhā*, *tidhā*. 113.
[The suffixes] *-vat* and *-jāti* [are added].

Words that denote a genus through their various forms are *jāti*. For example: *paṭujātiko* (of a clever nature), *mudujātiko* (of a soft nature). 114. **The suffix *kkhattum* is used after a numeral connected with a turn.** The suffix *kkhattum* occurs after a numeral related to a turn (*vāra*).

Examples: *dvikkhattum bhuñjati* (he eats two turns); *dvikkhattum divasassa bhuñjati* (he eats twice a day). Why is "turn" mentioned? [Counter-example: *pañca bhuñjati* (he eats five times)—here it refers to the number of meals, not turns. Why is "numeral" mentioned? [Counter-example: *pahūte vāre bhuñjati* (he eats many turns)—here it is not a specific numeral.
115. *Katimhā* means "how many times. It refers to how many times one eats; *katikkhattuṃ* means "for how many times.
116. After *bahu*, [the suffix] *dhā* is used when proximity (*paccāsatti*) is intended.
The suffix *dhā* and the word *kkhattum* are used after a plural number associated with a time-period (*vāra*), provided that there is a close succession of those periods. For example:
*bahudhā bhuñjati* (he eats many times), *bahudhā divasassa bhuñjati* (he eats many times during the day), or *bahukkhattum*. Why is it said "provided there is a close succession"? [Consider:
*bahukkhattum māsassa bhuñjati* (he eats many times in a month).
117. What does *sa* mean?

It is the suffix *kiṃpacca*, and the substitution of *sā* for *eka* is prescribed. One eats once; he eats once (*sakiṃ*), or one time. 118. *So* [is used] in the sense of repetition and manifestation.

It becomes [used] in the sense of "dimness" (vichchāya) and "manner" (pakāra). *Khaṇḍaso* means he makes it into pieces, piece by piece (*khaṇḍaṃ khaṇḍaṃ*). *Puthuso* means by way of various manners (*puthuppakārena*). *Sabbaso* means by every manner (*sabbena pakārena*).

119. When there is a connection with the suffixes *ka*, *ra*, *sa*, or *bhū* in the sense of the becoming of that which has not yet come to be (*abhūtatadbhāve*), the suffix *ci* is added after a word denoting a state (*avatthāvato*) when there is a relation with *ka*, *ra*, *sa*, or *bhū* signifying the becoming of that state into another state (*avatthantarena abhūtassa tāyā avatthāya bhāve*).

It occurs after a word expressing a modification (*vikāra*). *Dhavalīkaroti* means "he makes white what was not white. *Dhavalī siyā* means "it may become white" (what was not white). *Dhavalī bhavati* means "it becomes white" (what was not white).
What is the purpose of the rule regarding the transformation into something else that did not previously exist (*abhūtatadbhāve*)?

[Examples: *ghaṭaṃ karoti* ("he makes a pot"), *dadhi atthi* ("there is curd"). Why is the condition "in connection with the root *kṛ*" (*karāsabhūyoge*) stated? [Counter-example: *adhavalo dhavalo jāyate* ("one who was not white is born white"). Here, since the state of being white arises naturally, the suffix is not applied.
What is the point of these modifications? Let them not exist by way of their original nature; one fashions gold into an earring. (Particles and Taddhita suffixes.

120. Other suffixes are also seen: other suffixes are seen besides those already mentioned. "Vividha-mātaro" and "vimātaro" are descriptive compounds (*visesanasaṃāsa*); their sons [are called *vaimātarā*].

*Vemātiko*: because of the suffix *ika*, the elision of *ra* due to its connection with *rā*, and the application of the *vṛddhi* vowel, it becomes *vemātiko*. *Pathāvino*: they go on the road (*patha*);
[the suffix] *āvin* is applied. *Issukī*: one who has envy (*issā*) is *issukī*; [the suffix] *ukī* is applied. *Dhorayhā*: they bear the burden (*dhura*); [the suffix] *yhaṇa* is applied.
The general and the particular, that which is derived from a verbal root (*bhāvaja*) and that which is derived from an indeclinable (*nipātaja*).
Thus it is to be understood by the wise; the derivative suffixes (*taddhita*), however, are fourfold.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, beginning with *ṇa*, in the section on the accomplishment of grammatical operations (*payogasiddhi*). 6. The Chapter Beginning with *tya* (*tyādikaṇḍa*).
Now, *ty-ādi* (the verbal suffixes beginning with *ti*) are expressed by verbal roots (*dhātu*) that denote action.

"It declares an action" (*ākhyāti kriyam*); thus, *ākhyāta* is the designation for a verb according to the ancient teachers. That which indicates tense, grammatical relation (*kāraka*), and person, possesses the characteristic of action, ends in *ty-ādi*, and is devoid of gender (*aliṅga*).
And this has been stated: "That which [expresses] the three tenses, the three persons, denotes action, and possesses the three relations..."
The dual number is called *atiliga* (without gender), and it is termed *tadākhyāta*.

The phrase "mostly having action as its meaning" (*kriyatthā bahulaṃ*) applies everywhere. That which has action as its meaning is a root (*dhātu*); and that is of two kinds, according to whether it is transitive (*sakammaka*) or intransitive (*akammaka*).
In this context, that verbal root for which an object is sought when a meaning of action expressed by an agent is considered is *sakammaka* (transitive). The other is *akammaka* (intransitive).
Among these, transitive roots express an action that requires an object, such as "he makes a mat" (*kaṭaṃ karoti*), "he goes to the village" (*gāmaṃ gacchati*), or "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*).
Intransitive roots express an action independent of an object, such as "he sits" (*acchati*), "he lies down" (*seti*), or "he stands" (*tiṭṭhati*).

Action (*kriyā*)—such as going, cooking, and so forth, which is considered non-existent—is said to be the meaning of a word established in either the agent or the object, and accomplished by a collection of factors (*kāraka*). Moreover:
"Both 'acting' (*karaṇa*) and 'becoming' (*bhavana*) are expressed by the verbal roots *kṛ* and *bhū* respectively."

Then, how could "cooking" and so forth be the denotable meaning (*vācyatva*) [of the roots]? By the verbal roots *kṛ* (to do) and *bhū* (to be), "doing" and "being" are expressed; it is therefore being asked: how can "cooking," "going," and so forth be the denotable meanings of those actions and states of being? Furthermore:
"Indeed, for cooking and the like to be the denotable meaning is not logical in the case of the roots *kṛ* and *bhū*."
That state of having a more predominant meaning is not applicable in the case of *pāka* (cooking) and so forth.
For it has been said:
"The meanings of verbal roots (*dhātu*) are indeed forms of action (*kāriya-rūpa*), and they are all connected with existence (*sattā*)."
From that, both action (*kriyā*) and state (*bhāva*) are understood as their commonality.
1. *Vattamāne*: *anti*, *si*, *tha*, *mi*, *ma*, *te*, *ante*, *se*, *vhe*, *e*, *mhe*.

In the sense of the present tense—whether begun but not yet completed—the suffixes beginning with *tya* (the personal endings) occur after verbal roots (*kriyattha*) when expressing the present. Because this is a section concerning action (*kriyā*), it is stated as "verbal roots" (*kriyattha*). Regarding their specific application: [The following rules apply: *aniyame*... [etc.]

14. Regarding the six preceding [suffixes] and the six following [suffixes], there are two each for the middle, the highest, and the first persons, whether singular or plural, in the case of *tumha* and *amha*, and in the case of the remaining [pronouns].

When the referents of the words *tumha* and *amha*—whether singular or plural—and the referents of other words are the agents (*kāraka*), there are two each of the middle, highest, and first persons for both the six preceding and the six following suffixes, respectively. "Therein" (*tattha*) means "among those."
*Paṭhamapuriso* (the first person) is so called because it is indicated at the beginning. *Si* and *tha* are the second person (*majjhimapuriso*) because they are indicated in the middle.
*Mi* and *ma* are the third person (*uttamapuriso*). This word *uttama* (highest/last) refers, by its very nature, to the endings beginning with *ti*.

In the subsequent group of six as well, it should be applied in the same way, starting with "those two are the endings" (*te ante*), and so forth. The same should be applied to the remaining seven rules for the formation of suffixes, such as *bhavissati*, and so on.
Now, regarding the eighteen groups of roots beginning with *bhū* (the *bhū-vādī* group), the suffixes beginning with *ti* are applied after the first root, *bhū*, meaning "existence" (*sattā*).

In that context, according to the rule "when expressing a single [object], the singular number is used," when the suffixes beginning with *ti* follow, the *ky* and *la* affixes occur only in the cases of the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*kamma*), and the impersonal state (*bhāva*).
Thus: "In the impersonal state and the passive (*bhāva-kamma*) when not in the immediate past, and in the *māna*, *anta*, and suffixes beginning with *ti*; in the active (*kattari*)."

Because these affixes (*vikaraṇa*) are prescribed by [rules] such as "lo" and so forth, the *ty*-affixes are understood to occur only in the senses of agent (*kattṛ*), object (*karman*), and impersonal action (*bhāva*);
thus, *ti*, *mhi*, and *lo* occur in the sense of the agent. What are those affixes?
They are: those occupying the preceding and following positions, and those distinct from the verbal roots and case-endings (*vibhatti*).
Dependent upon [the base], there are conditions; these may be suffixes (*vikaraṇa*). 5.82. *Yuvaṇṇānam me*:
for verbal bases ending in *i* or *u*, *e* and *o* respectively become the suffixes *e* and *o*; thus, the vowel *ū* becomes *ūs*.

5.89. When *e* or *o* are followed by a vowel (*sara*), they become *ay* or *av* respectively; thus, there is the substitution of *oss*. "That man becomes good," "that woman becomes good," "the mind becomes good.
[The suffix] *-tā* occurs after the agent (*kartr*) in a verb (*ākhyāta*), but the third case does not occur for the agent.
The nominative case (paṭhamāvibhatti) occurs indeed by depending on the mere meaning.
Even when there is a single action, because there is a plurality of agents, the plural ending (anti) is used according to the rule: "The plural is used when plurality is to be expressed. 161.
In some instances, [the plural ending is used] for the verbal suffixes (vikaraṇa).

In some instances, there is the elision of the *vikaraṇa* suffixes; thus, there is the elision of the *la*-vikaraṇa. The remainder is similar to what precedes. Those men become (*te purisā bhavanti*).
The second person singular ending is *si*: you are (*tvaṃ bhavasi*). The plural ending is the suffix *tha*:
you (all) are (*tumhe bhavatha*). The first person singular ending is the suffix *mi*.
57. Before *him* suffixes, the long vowel occurs for the letter *a*. *Ahaṃ bhavāmi* (I am). The plural suffix is *mapaccaya*:
*mayaṃ bhavāma* (we are). Likewise in the second person: *bhavase*, *bhavavhe*; *bhave*, *bhavamhe*. Some [grammarians] [prescribe] the long vowel...
Having done so, they recite: "In the case of a consonant, there are long and short [vowels]," thus [we] become *bhavāmhe*.
And here—shame, beings, stability, and wakefulness—
Increase, decrease, living, and dying;
play, liking, and delighting—
all these are stated to be intransitive roots.
Because it has been stated thus, the second case ending is not used for the verb *kamma*.

In the root *paca* (meaning "to cook"), the letter *a* is for the sake of pronunciation; the same applies to the subsequent cases. When *paca* stands [as the base], the *la*-vikaraṇa suffix is applied, and the elision of the vikaraṇa and so forth is the same as before.
Thus: he cooks rice (*so odanaṃ pacati*), they cook (*te pacanti*). You cook (*tvaṃ pacasi*), you all cook (*tumhe pacatha*). I cook (*ahaṃ pacāmi*).

We cook. In the second person plural: *pacatha*, *pacanti*. In the second person singular: *pacasi*, *pacavho*. In the first person singular and dual: *pace*, *pacāmhe*. 1.22. *Vippaṭisedha* (Negation).
Negation (*vippaṭisedhana*) is the mutual negation of one another; this is *vippaṭisedha*. [It applies] to the two, namely the first and middle persons.

In a case where there is a possibility for multiple persons (*ekattha-pasaṅge*), the suffix *tha* is used for the plural of the middle person (*majjhimapurisa*). Thus: *so ca pacati, tvañca pacasi, tumhe pacatha*.

For when there is a conflict between [suffixes] of equal strength, according to the rule "the negation of the three—first, middle, and highest persons—[occurs in the case of equal force]," in a situation where multiple persons are possible, the plural of the highest person (*uttamapurisa*) is employed: *so ca pacati, tvañca pacasi*.
"I cook" and "we cook"—thus it occurs.
*Ama-gama* = in the sense of going—5,173.
*Gama*, *yami* + *sā* + *sa*; or *disānaṃ* with *cchaṅ*.
For these roots, *chaṅ* optionally occurs before suffixes such as *nta*, *māna*, and *ti*. He goes to the village (*so gāmaṃ gacchati*).
Regarding *anti*: 74. After a short vowel preceded by a heavy syllable, *re* optionally occurs before *nta* and *ntī*.
The restriction of syllables constitutes *chandas*;
the restriction of heavy and light [syllables] constitutes *vṛtti*;
a long vowel preceded by a conjunct consonant [is likewise regulated].
The short vowel *u* becomes short *r*.
[Examples: *gacchare*, *gacchanti*; *tvaṃ gacchasi*, *tumhe gacchatha*; *ahaṃ gacchāmi*, *mayaṃ gacchāma*.

In the alternative where there is no substitution of *chā*, by the rule “*ū lasse*,” it is changed to *e*: *gameti*. When the following syllable is elided, it becomes *gamenti*. [Further forms: *gamesi*, *gametha*.
*I go*, *we two go*, *we go*. In the future tense (*paracchakka*): *he will go*, *they two will go*, *they will go*; *you will go*, *you all will go*; *I will go*, *we two will go*, *we will go*.

The expression "the unrighteousness prevails before" (*pure adhammo dibbati*) and "before I die" (*purā marāmi*) are present-tense forms used figuratively (*tabbohārūpacārena*) in proximity to that [future event].
For it is said: "A task begun but not yet finished is called 'present' (*vattamāna*)."
And that which is in proximity to the present is called "present. How so?
Just as the Ganges and its vicinity are both known as "the Ganges."

"Come to protect the Ganges," and "The sound on the Ganges"—thus it occurs in two ways according to the distinction between primary and non-primary meanings. For that which has attained conventional usage (ruḷhi) is primary;
the application [of a term] by superimposing [a quality] onto that [primary object] is the non-primary.

Alternatively, by means of the words *pure* and *purā*, the state of being future (*anāgatatā*) is understood, because at that time [the action] is present (*vattamānatā*). Or rather, this is a transposition of time (*kālabyattiyo*);

for by way of general rule (*bāhulaka*), the suffixes *-ti* and so forth occur even at another time, as in: “While they exist, I conceal them”; “After the breaking up of the body, in the life hereafter, he goes to the companionship of Vāsava”;
and “I shall pay homage excessively. “From where indeed do you come?”
In phrases such as “I am coming from Rājagaha,” however, the present tense is used to denote proximity to the present.

5.175. In place of *gama*, *vada*, *dāna*, *ghamma*, and *vajja* before suffixes such as *-nta*, *-māna*, and *-tya*, the forms *ghamma* and so forth may optionally occur. For example: *ghammati*, *ghammanti*, etc.
Regarding the object (kamma): by the influence of a prefix, even that which is without an object may become one with an object;
as in the example: "Lust is overcome by the ascetic of great psychic power."
Because they have already been stated [as intransitive], the forms *bhū*, *dhātu*, and so forth, occur in the sense of the object (*karman*) when used as transitive verbs. 5.17.

*Kyo* occurs before suffixes such as *māna*, *anta*, *ti*, and others prescribed for the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), provided they belong to the aorist (*parokkhā*) and are not themselves the aorist. This applies to roots whose meaning is that of an action (*kriyārtha*).

The letter *ka* is for the purpose of making it an *anubandha*. Due to the prohibition in the rule “*na te kānubandhanāgamesu*,” there is an absence of the vowel *o*. Devadatta experiences pleasure (*anubhūyati*).
And here—because it is not expressed by the verb, the third case is used for the agent, and not otherwise.
The second person occurs [for the agent], and because it has been stated, the first person also occurs here. "Sampattiyo anubhūyanti tayā" (Prosperities are experienced by you).

"Anubhūyasi tvaṃ devadattena" (You are being experienced by Devadatta). "Anubhūyatha tumhe" (You two are being experienced). "Ahaṃ anubhūyāmi" (I am being experienced), "mayaṃ anubhūyāma" (We are being experienced). In the dual, "anubhuyyati," etc. Thus it is for the other six persons.

In the impersonal passive (*bhāve*), because the state (*bhāva*) expressed as a non-concrete thing is singular, there is only the singular number. And that occurs only in the third person singular, not otherwise, because of the rule of frequent application (*bahulavidhāna*). "Bhūyati" or "Bhūyate" (it is being); the meaning is "existence at this very moment."
After the verbal root *pac*, the suffix *kyo* is used in the sense of the object (*kamma*). 37. Regarding *kyo*:

after a verbal root expressing an action, the suffixes *ī* or *ñā* optionally follow *kyo*. The suffix *ñā* has the meaning of the first part of the word (the base). By Devadatta, rice is being cooked (*odano pacīyati*) or is cooked (*paccati*).
In the present tense (*reātade*), [the forms] *pacīyare* and *pacīyanti*, *paccare* and *paccanti* occur. [These involve] the substitution of *ca* for *pa* and the prior form (*pubbarūpa*).
In the second person: *tvaṃ pacīyasi* and *paccasi*; *tumhe pacīyatha* and *paccatha*. In the first person: *ahaṃ pacīyāmi* and *paccāmi*; *mayaṃ pacīyāma* and *paccāma*.
In the third person plural, it is *devadattena odano pacīyate*, and so forth.

When the suffix *chaṅ* is applied after the root *gam*, and the augment *īṅ* is added, it becomes *gacchīyati*; [in the plural] *gacchīyanti*. [In the second person singular] *gacchīyasi*; [in the second person plural] *gacchīyatha*.

[In the first person singular] *gacchīyāmi*; [in the first person plural] *gacchīyāma*. It is the same in the passive voice (*paracchakka*). [In the passive singular] *gamīyati* (or *gammati*); [in the plural] *gamīyanti* (or *gammanti*).

[In the second person singular] *gamīyasi* (or *gammasi*); [in the plural] *gamīyatha* (or *gammatha*). [In the first person singular] *gamīyāmi* (or *gammāmi*); [in the plural] *gamīyāma* (or *gammāma*).
The same applies to the sixth case (paracchakka). Likewise, one finds forms such as *ghammīyati* and *ghammīyanti*.

[The rule] "after verbal roots meaning 'action' (*kriyattha*), the suffixes *tyādi* are used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*)," and so forth, applies to transitive verbs (*sakammaka*) in the sense of the object (*kammasmiṃ*). Alternatively, intransitive verbs (*akammaka*) are used in the sense of the state (*bhāve*); however, when there is a desire for the expression of the object, they are considered [to function] like transitive verbs.
For even when an action exists, if there is no desire to speak of it, this is said:
"Even though it exists, there is no intention to express it; and even though it does not exist, that [intention] may arise.
This is like a maiden who has no hips, or like one who has grown from a barren woman."
This is a worldly way of speaking, which it is impossible for one’s own intellect to transcend;
how could there be such a reversal [of meaning] here? Only the world itself would find this improper.
(The method of the present tense suffix).

*sambhāvemi saddahāmi bhavaṃ paceyya*, "I consider it possible, I believe that you might cook [it]"; *bhavaṃ pacissati*, "you will cook [it]"; *bhavaṃ apaci*, "you have cooked [it]."

9. Regarding the rules for questions (*pañha*), aspirations (*paṭṭhāna*), and procedures (*vidhi*): in the case of questions and so forth, the suffixes *eyya* and others are used in the sense of the action (*kriyattha*).
A question (*pañhā*) is an inquiry; there are two types of aspiration (*paṭṭhāna*): wishing for what is desired and requesting.
*Patthanā*, *bhatti*, or *byāpāraṇā* is the method [of expressing] desire.
In a question: "What would he cook—rice, or perhaps curry? In *patthanā*: "Oh, if only he were to cook! In *vidhi*: "May you cook rice. (The system of suffixes beginning with *eyya*). 10.
*tu*, *antu*, *hi*, *tha*, *mi*, *ma*, *taṃ*, *antaṃ*, *ssu*, *vho*, *e*, *āmase*.

These [forms] are used in the sense of the imperative (*kriyāttha*) within the procedure for posing questions (*pañhapaṭṭhānavidhi*). In the sense of wishing (*āsīsana*): “May he be happy,” “May they be happy. 48. *Hissato lopo*:

There is optionally the elision of *hi* following *a*. Thus: “May you be happy,” “May you be” (*bhavāhi*). When *hi* follows, there is lengthening of the vowel. By [the rule beginning with] *eyyātha*, etc.
Vhoka: *tumhe sukhitā bhavathavho bhavatha*. Ahaṃ sukhī bhavāmi, mayaṃ sukhino bhavāma.
In the parasmaipada: *bhavataṃ*, *bhavantaṃ*; *bhavassu*, *bhavavho*; *bhave*, *bhavāmase*. In the kamma-vacana:
*tayā anubhūyatu*, *anubhūyantu*, etc. In the bhāva-vacana: *bhūyatu*, *bhūyataṃ*.
In the sense of command (*āṇattiya*): *devadatto dāni odanaṃ pacatu*, *pacantu*, etc.
In the passive sense (*kamme*): *tena odano paccatu*, etc.; likewise *so gāmaṃ gacchatu*, etc. Regarding the suffix *-ū* when followed by the suffix *-lassa*:
*gametu*, *gamentu*, etc. In the formation of the imperative (*ghammatādesa*): *ghammatu*, *ghammantu*, etc. In the passive sense: *gacchīyatu*, etc.; likewise *gamīyatu*, etc.
When there is elision of the suffix *lassa* (the optative marker) following a rule (*vidhimhi*), there is vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*).
Here: *pabbato hotu*. In the sense of an invitation (*nimantane*): *adhivāsetha tumhe bhante bhagavā bhojanaṃ*. Regarding *vasati*: by the rule "from *cur* etc., *ṇī*," the suffix *ṇi* is applied;

by the rule "for *assā*, [there is] *ā* when followed by a suffix without a consonantal marker (*anubandha*)," *ā* is substituted; and by the rule "for semi-vowels (*yuvaṇṇānaṃ*), *e* and *o* occur before a suffix," *e* is substituted. Here: *nissīdatu bhavaṃ*.

In the case of *sadassa*, [the suffix] *īma* is applied according to the rule "after *sad*, [there is] *īma* optionally. Because of the following consonant (*manu*), by the rule of internal sandhi (*antasarato*), *īma* is substituted.
In the sense of requesting instruction: "May the Blessed One teach the Dhamma, O Bhante," here [the suffix] is the same as the preceding one due to belonging to the *curādigaṇa*.
In the sense of permission: "Ask me a question, Vāsava; may your honor enter [the assembly]. Here there is elision (*lopo*) of the [suffix] *pucchato*. "Sit down in this manner."

*Patthanā* means "requesting"; *tatrada* means "in giving. [Examples: "Give me five excellent villages" (*dadāhi me gāmavarāni pañca*); "Having given, give me one eye" (*dāto lassa ekāre ca ekaṃ me nayanaṃ dehi*). *Pattakāle* means "the time has arrived":
"The time has come for you to perform the funeral rites" (*sampatto te kālo kaṭakaraṇe*); "May your honor perform the funeral rites" (*kaṭaṃ karotu bhavaṃ*).
Here, by the rule "after *tan* etc., *i* becomes *o*," the suffixes beginning with *tvā* become *eyya* etc., expressing the present, the immediate, and the future.

The future tense, beginning with *parokkhā*, along with the four past tenses (*tītakālika*), [are formed]. (5,173) The suffixes *ya*, *mi*, *sā*, and *sa* are substituted for these [roots], or *cchaṅ* is added to them, before endings such as *honti*, *māna*, and *ty-*.
For example: *so saggaṃ gacchati*, *gameti*, *gacchanti*, and so forth.

*Kamme* means "it is gone to" or "it is traversed," and so forth. The root *yama* (to cease) takes its forms for the past tense (*parokkhā*) and the non-recent past (*anajjatana*) everywhere, which should be applied by following the usage.
Preceded by *ni*, it becomes *niyacchati* (he restrains) or *niyamati*; *niyacchanti* (they restrain) or *niyamanti* (they restrain).

Preceded by *saṃ*, there is the change [of *ya* to *jja*] as in "ye *saṃssa*"; thus, *saññamati* (he restrains) or *saññamanti* (they restrain). In the passive voice (*kamme*), it is *niyacchīyati* or *niyamīyati*.
It is restrained (*niyammati*) or is checked (*saññamīyati*). Likewise: it will restrain (*niyacchissati*), it will check (*saññamissati*);

it restrained (*niyacchi*), it checked (*saṃyami*); it would restrain (*niyacchissa*), it would check (*saṃyamissa*); it may restrain (*niyaccheyya*), it may check (*saṃyameyya*); let it restrain (*niyacchatu*), let it check (*saññamatu*). The root *isa* (with *siṃsa*) signifies desire; thus:

he desires heaven (*saggaṃ icchati*), they desire (*icchanti*), and so forth. According to the rule "for the short [vowel] before *u* and *paṇ"* (*lahussupantassā*), in the sense of seeking: he seeks (*esati*), they seek (*esanti*), and so forth.
*Kamme* (in the sense of action): *icchīyati*, or in the sense of increase (*vuddhimhi*), *esīyati*. In the case of the preceding form (*pubbarūpe*), there are forms such as *issati* and *issate*.
[Future: *icchissati*, *esissati*, etc. [Aorist: *icchi*, *esi*. [Conditional: *icchissa*, *esissa*. [Optative: *iccheyya*, *eseyya*. [Imperative: *icchatu*, *esatu*, etc.
*Āsa* = "to sit down" (*upavesane*); e.g., *so āsane acchati* ("he sits on the seat"), etc. By the rule "long and short vowels [are substituted] for a consonant," the vowel is shortened.
With *upa* as a prefix, it is likewise *upāsati*. [The forms are: *acchissati*, *upāsissati*; *acchi*, *upāsi*; *acchissa*, *upāsissa*; *accheyya*, *upāseyya*;
*acchatu*, *upāsatu*, and so forth. *Disa* = "to look"; *dicchati*, *dicchanti*, and so forth—all are the same as the previous [root].
*Labha* = "to obtain. Hereafter, we shall explain only the points of distinction; all other modes follow the pattern already stated.

It should be understood as follows: *labhati*, *labhanti*, and so forth. When the preceding form of the passive suffix (*ky*) is applied, it becomes *labbhati*, and so forth. 73. *Labhā iṃ īnaṃ thaṃ thā vā*:

After the root *labh*, the suffixes *iṃ* and *īnaṃ* optionally become *thaṃ* and *thā*. Thus, *so alabhittha*, *labhittha*, *alabhi*, *labhi*; with the suffix *iṃ*, *alatthaṃ*, *alabhiṃ*, and so forth.
26. *Labha*, *vasa*, *cchida*, *bhidā*, *rudānaṃ*:
after *labha* and the others, the suffix *cchaṅ* occurs together with *ss*. [Examples: *lacchati* (he will obtain), *labhissati*; *lacchanti* (they will obtain), *labhissanti*, and so forth.

In the conditional mood (*kriyātipatti*), when *cchaṅ* is substituted for the portion beginning with *ss*, [the forms are] *alacchā* (he would not have obtained), *alabhissa*, and so forth. *Vasa* = dwelling; [in the future tense: *vacchati*.

It will remain (*vasissati*). Due to the predominance of the *kamma*-suffix, there is the vowel *u* in *assū*; in the case of the original form, there are examples such as *vussati* (he dwells) and *vussissati* (he will dwell).

Likewise, *avacchā* and *avasissā*. The root *chid* means "to split" (*dvedhākaraṇe*): *checchati* (he will cut) and *chindissati* (he will cut). [In the latter,] by the rule "for *rudh* and so forth, *maṃ* is substituted for *lo*," *lo* is replaced by *maṃ*, and there is the elision of *la*.
The root *bhid* means "to break apart" (*vidāraṇe*): *bhecchati* (he will break) and *bhindissati* (he will break). *Abhecchā* and *abhindissā*.
*Ruda* means weeping; *rucchati*, *rodissati*. *Aruccā*, *arodissā*, and so forth.

Even with other suffixes (*aññapaccaya*), by the rule "for *chida*, [substitute] *cchaṅa*" through the division of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*), there is *cchaṅa*; with the past suffix (*ūṃpaccaya*), *acchecchuṃ*, *acchindiṃsu*.
And for other roots than those mentioned: *gama* = going, *gacchaṃ*, *gacchissaṃ*. Even with other suffixes...

In *vaca-byattavacane* and so forth, because of the governing rule for the frequentative suffix (*bahulādhikāra*), even when [suffixes] such as *tya* follow, there is, according to the tradition, the substitution of *va* for *vac* and so on.

By the rule *“vacādīnaṃ vassuṭa vā”* (for *vac* etc., *va* is substituted and *uṭ* optionally follows), in the sense of the object (*kamma*), *uṭ* is applied; and by *“assū”* (and *assu*), *a* and *s* are added.
Thus, one says *dhammo uccati vuccati* (the Dhamma is spoken) or *vuccanti*, and so forth, and there is also the prior form (*pubbarūpa*) of that [suffix].
27. In the case of *bhuja*, *muc*, *vac*, and *viṣ*, the suffix *kkaṅ* is applied after these roots along with the suffix *ss*.
For example: *vakkhati*, *vacissati*, *vakkhanti*, *vacissanti*, and so forth. 21. After the root *vac*, [the suffixes] beginning with *ī* [are applied].

In forms such as *ī*, there is elision (*oma*) of the speech-sound [the vowel]. Because of the suffixing of the letter *m*, by the grammatical rule (*paribhāsa*) "that which has *m* as its suffix follows the vowels," it is followed by a vowel.
Examples include *avoci*, *avocuṃ*, *avoco*, and so forth. In the non-present tense (*anajjatanatthe*), examples include *avaca*, *avacā*, *vacā*, and so forth.

In the conditional mood (*kriyātipatti*), examples include *avakkhā*, *avacissā*, *avakkhiṃsu*, *avacissiṃsu*, and so forth. In the optative, examples include *vaceyya*, and so forth. In the passive voice (*kamme*), examples include *vucceyya*, and so forth. Likewise...
*vacatu*, *vuccatu*, and so forth.
