Because the formation is extensive (*bahulavidhānā*), it also occurs with the object: one who is carried by the feet is a *pādahārako*. From *cupa* (meaning “slow movement”), one who moves slowly in the throat is a *galacopako*.

In the case of *siddha* and so forth, as in "He is indeed worthy of being chosen by the maiden," [the girl] was chosen (*pariggahitā*). Regarding the sense of moral conduct (*sīla*): one who takes up virtue is a "taker" (*upādātā*).
One who goes well is a "goer" (*gantā*). Those whose nature is to shave and whose practice is shaving are "shavers" (*muṇḍayitāro*);

here, according to the rule "a noun occurs in the sense of a verbal root," when the augment *ū* is applied, the substitution of *e* for *ay*, and the substitution of *āraṅ* for the word *muṇḍayitu*, the *y* of the suffix *ya* becomes *ṭ*.
34. *Āvī* is substituted for *kriya* and *attha* predominantly when the agent (*kattari*) is expressed. In the case of *disassa passa+dassa=dasa+da+dakkhā*, there is a substitution of *dassa*.

Thus, one who sees fear is a *bhayadassāvī*. With the feminine suffix *-ī*, it becomes *bhayadassāvinī*. [The form] *bhayadassāvi* [is used] for the purpose of indicating that the mind (*citta*) is the object of limited scope (*appavisayatā*).
The suffix *aka* is used to denote a distinct action (*bhinnayogakaraṇa*). Because it is prescribed as a general rule, it also occurs in relation to virtue (*sīla*) and so forth.
35. **Āsiṃsāyam +ako**:

When a wish (*āsiṃsā*) is implied, the suffix *aka* is added to a verbal root to denote the agent (*kattari*). *Jīva* (in the sense of "maintaining life"): "May he live" (*jīvatūti*) is a *jīvaka*. *Nanda* (in the sense of "prosperity"): "May he rejoice" (*nandatūti*) is a *nandaka*. *Bhava* (in the sense of "becoming"): "May he be" (*bhavatūti*) is a *bhavaka*.

36. The suffix *ṇa* is not substituted for *ṇana* when it occurs in the sense of the agent (*kattari*). That which performs is "the cause" (*kāraṇaṃ*). Why say "in the sense of the agent"? [Because] that by means of which one acts is "the instrument" (*karaṇaṃ*). 37. After the root *hā*, [the suffix *ṇa* is used] with the exception of the future tense (*vīhi*) and the tenses expressing time (*kālesu*).

In the words *hāta* and *vīhi*, the suffix *ṇa* occurs. By the rule beginning with “*āssa*,” the suffix *yu* is applied; those which abandon (*jahanti*) water are *hāyanā* (rice). When the sense of the verbal root refers to the state of being (*bhāve*), it is *hāyana*, meaning a year. [The commentary asks: Why say “in the time of rice” (*vīhikālesu*)? [Because otherwise] one who abandons is simply a *hātā* (an abandoner). 38. *Vid* with *kū*:

after the root *vid*, the suffix *kū* occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). The letter *k* is for the purpose of forming the qualifier “*kūto*. One who knows is a *vidū*, such as a knower of the world (*lokavidū*).

39. After the [verbal root] *vi-pubb* (meaning "to know"), the suffix *kū* occurs when expressing the agent (*kattṛ*). [Thus: one who knows is *viññū*. 40. After a verbal root denoting an action (*kamma*)...

After a verbal root, the suffix *ñā* becomes *kū* when denoting the agent. One who knows everything is *sabbaññū*. Likewise: *mattaññū*, *dhammaññū*, *atthaññū*, *kālaññū*, *kataññū*, and so forth. (The word *bhikkhu*, however, is established by the rule for *bharādi* and *ṇvu* suffixes. 41. *Kvac-aṇa*:
After a verbal root meaning "to do" (*kriyārtha*), the suffix *aṇ* optionally occurs after an object to denote the agent. One who makes a pot is *kumbhakāra*; this is an *amādi* compound.

In the case of *itthiyam*, [the suffix] *-ī* is applied to form *kumbhakārī*. Likewise, one forms *kammakāro*, *māsākāro*, *kaṭṭhakāro*, *rathakāro*, *suvaṇṇakāro*, *suttakāro*, *vuttikāro*, and *ṭīkākāro*.
Regarding *saralāvo*: from the root *lū* (to cut) preceded by *sa-*, the substitution of *o* for *ava* occurs, hence *saralāvo*. Regarding *manthajjhāyo*:

from the root *jjhā* (in the sense of reciting/studying), preceded by the prefix *adhi*, the substitution of *e* for *aya* occurs, hence *manthajjhāyo*; furthermore, the *y* of *adhi* is replaced by *ya*, and the *ca*-group (palatal group) and so forth are substituted.

Because of the governing rule of *bahula* (diversity), [the suffix] does not occur here in cases such as: “He sees the sun,” “He hears the Himalayas,” “He goes to the village. What is the purpose of [specifying] “in some instances”?

[It is to show that] in the case of *kammakaro*, there is no suffix here. 42. *Gamā rū*: After a direct object (*kamma*), the suffix *rū* is added to the root *gam* when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed. Because *ra* is a *anubandha* (indicatory letter), the portion following *am* is elided. One who goes to the Vedas is a *vedagū*; likewise, one who has gone to the other shore is a *pāragū*.

It occurs with regard to virtue (*sīla*) and so forth by way of common designation (*sāmaññavidhāna*). One who goes to the further shore of existence (*bhava*) by means of virtue is a "crosser to the further shore of existence" (*bhavapāragū*). One whose nature is to go to the end is an "end-goer" (*antagū*); likewise for a "wayfarer" (*addhagū*). 43.
*Samāna*, *ñña*, *bhavanta*, *yādi*, *tū*, *pamāna*, *disā*, *kamme*, *rī*, *rikkha*, *kā*.

The words *samāna* and so forth, as well as those beginning with *yādi* (starting with *yathā*) used in the sense of comparison (*upamāna*), when followed by the word *disā*, take the suffixes *rī*, *rikkha*, and *kā* in the sense of the object (*kamma*). “*Syādi syādine katthan*” (the word *syādi* [meaning ‘like this’] is used in the sense of ‘like that’).

In a compound (*samāsa*), according to the rule *“when a suffix with *r* as its indicatory letter (*rānubandha*) follows, the final vowel and the following consonant are elided”* (*ntasarādissā*), there is the elision of the final syllable of the word ending in *dis*. Furthermore, by the rule *“before *rī*, *rī*, and *rikka*”* (*rīrikkhakesu*), there is the substitution of *sā* for *samāna*.

Thus, because it appears as if it were *samāna*, it is called *sadī*; hence *sadikkha*. As for *ke*: by the rule *“there is no [elision] of the final vowel when followed by a suffix with *k* as its indicatory letter or in the case of an augment”* (*na te kānubandhanāgamesu*), the absence of the elision of the final vowel occurs; thus, it is *sadisa*. 125.
*Samānā ro rī + rikka + kesu* (The *ro* substitute occurs for *samāna* before *rī*, *rikka*, and *ke*).

From the word *samāna*, when followed by another word ending in *disa*, the substitution *ra* occurs optionally before the suffixes *rī*, *rikkha*, and *kesu*. Thus, with the substitution of *ra* for *da*, we have *sarī*, *sarikkho*, and *sariso*.

(3, 86) In the case of the group beginning with *sabba*, the substitution *mā* occurs before the suffixes *rī*, *rikkha*, and *kesu*. Because it is seen as something other (*añña*), it is called *aññādī*; thus we have *aññādikkho* and *aññādiso*.

3.87. *Nta*, *kiṃ*, and *māna* [are replaced by] *ṭā*, *kī*, and *ṭī* respectively when followed by *rī*, *rikka*, and *kesu*. The letter *ṭ* serves the purpose of indicating a complete substitution (*sabbādesa*).
Thus: *bhavādī*, *bhavādikkho*, *bhavādiso*; *kīdī*, *kīdikkho*, *kīdiso*; and that which is seen as "like this" (*ayamiva dissati*) is called *īdī*, *īdikkho*.

*Īdiso*. In the case of *yā*, etc., there are *yādikkho*, *yādiso*; *tyādi*, *tyādikkho*, *tyādiso*, and so forth. (3.88) In the singular, for the forms *tumhāmhānaṃ*, *tāma*, *eka*, *sma*, *Rī*, *rikkha*, and *kesu*, the forms *tumhāmhānaṃ*, *tāma*, and *ā* occur respectively when followed by *honte*. For example:

"He is seen like you" (*tvaṃ viya dissati*) and "He is seen like me" (*ayaṃ viya dissati*) result in *tādī* and *mādī*, and so forth. Why is it specified "in the singular"? [To exclude the plural: *tumhādiso* ("like you all") and *amhādiso* ("like us all").

3,89. In the case of *taṃ* and *maṃ*, when followed by the word *añña* (other), or by the word *uttara* (subsequent), or by the word *tumhaṃ* or *amhaṃ* (you or we) in the singular, they become *taṃ* and *maṃ* respectively. For example:
*tvaṃ dīpo etesaṃ*, *ahaṃ dīpo etesan*—in the sense of another word (*aññapadatthe*), these become *taṃdīpā* and *maṃdīpā*. *Tvaṃ saraṇaṃ etesaṃ*.

"They seek refuge in me" (*ahaṃ saraṇaṃ esanti*) becomes *taṃsaraṇā*; "having me as their refuge" (*maṃsaraṇā*). In the compounds *tayā yogo* and *mayā yogo*, there is the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra) according to the rule for *am-ādi-samāsa* [Kacc 3.90].
[Furthermore,] by *ve tassa ṭa* [Kacc 3.91], the suffix *ṭa* is applied to that [word].
The suffixes *rī*, *rikka*, and *kesu* are applied after this [base] *eta*. Thus: *edī* becomes *etādī*; *edikkho* becomes *etādikkho*; *ediso* becomes *etādiso*. 44.
Regarding the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the agent (*kāraka*):
the suffixes *sva*, *ghaṇ*, *gha*, and *kā* are frequently applied to verbal roots (*kriyattha*) in the sense of the abstract state and the agent.
*Apaccaya* (prefix) + *paggaṇhanaṃ* (grasping) = *paggaho* (exertion). Similarly, *niggaho* (restraint). One who holds the Dhamma is a *dhammadharo*; similarly, a *vinayadharo*.
Likewise, one who does that [action] is a *takkarō*; there is a doubling of the vowel (*dvittaṃ*). Similarly:
*hitakaro*, *divasakaro*, *dinakaro*, *divākaro*, *nisākaro*. One who takes a bow is a *dhanuggaho*. Similarly, a *kavacaggaho*. From the root *dada* = giving; one who gives all desires is...
The giver of all desires, the giver of everything. Regarding the word *anna*, by the inclusion of the particle *ca* in the rule "also in the case of the *parokkhā* [tense]," there is doubling;

and by the rule "the first member becomes short," there is shortening. Thus: one who gives food is an *annada*; likewise, a *dhanada*. The root *dhā* preceded by *sam* means "to hold"; one who holds together everything is a *sabbasandha*.
The root *nī* means "to lead away" (*pāpane*), preceded by *vi*: that by which one leads away (*vineti*), has led away (*vinesi*), or will lead away, or wherein one leads away, is *vinaya*.
The substitution of *e* for *aya*. *Naya* means leading (*nayana*). *Si* means service; preceded by *ni*, that from which one leans out is *nissaya*. *Si* means to lie down;
that which has lain down, lies down, or will lie down is *anusaya*. *I* means going; preceded by *pati*, that depending on which the fruit proceeds is *paccaya*.
Preceded by *sam* and with the augment *u*, it becomes *samudaya*. *Ci* means accumulation; that by which one discerns, or the act of discerning, is *vinicchaya*.
“*Nito cissa cho*”: for this [root], *cho* is the substitute. *Ucc* = to heap up; heaping up is *uccaya*, which is *saṃcaya*. *Khi* = destruction; destroying is *khaya*. *Ji* = victory;
conquering is *vijaya*, which is *jaya*. *Kī* = bartering goods; selling is *vikkaya*, which is *kaya*. *Lī* = clinging;
that to which they cling is *ālaya*, which is *laya*. (These end in *ivaṇṇ*).
*Āsuṇanti* means "they obey," thus *assavā*; the vowel *a* is short. *Paṭissavanaṃ* is "responding," thus *paṭissavo*. The root *su* means "to flow";

they flow as far as the peak of existence (*bhavagga*), thus *āsavā*. The root *ru* means "sound"; it resounds, thus *ravo*. It comes into being, thus *bhavo*. It originates from this, thus *pabhavo*.
The root *lū* means "cutting"; the act of cutting is *lavo*. (These end in the suffix *-u*).

*Car* means "to move"; *saṃcaraṇaṃ* (moving together) is *saṃcara*. *Dar* means "to split"; *ādaranaṃ* (taking up) is *ādara*. It comes (*āgacchati*) or it is a coming (*āgamanaṃ*), thus it is *āgama*.

*Sapp* means "to go"; it goes (*sappati*), thus it is a *sappa* (snake). It shines (*dibbati*), thus it is a *deva* (god). The act of departing (*pakkamanaṃ*) or he departs (*pakkamati*), thus it is *pakkama*;
likewise for *vikkama*. *Car* means "to move"; he moves in the forest (*vanaṃ carati*), thus he is a *vanacara* (forest-dweller). Desire (*kāma*) moves about therein, thus...
The world belongs to the sense-sphere; wisdom belongs to the sense-sphere; the mind belongs to the sense-sphere. That wherein cows graze is a "pasture" (*gocara*).

That which drinks with its foot is a "tree" (*pādapa*). So too is a tortoise (*kacchapa*). That which grows on the head is "hair of the head" (*siroruha*); [the suffix] *o* is added because it begins with the word *mana*.

That which lies in a cave is a "cave-dwelling" mind (*guhāsaya*), just as there are "abdomen-dwelling" winds (*kucchisayā vātā*). A person who stands on a mountain is a "mountain-dweller" (*pabbataṭṭha*).
A river situated on a mountain, ashes situated on a mountain; likewise, [water] situated on dry land, [fire] situated in water.

In the sense of difficulty (*kiccha*), when combined with the prefixes *du-*, *akiccha-*, *su-*, *īsa-*, *sukha-*, and *upapada-*, it forms *dukkara*—that which is done with difficulty, or the act of doing with difficulty.
Likewise, *dussaya*; that which is carried with difficulty is *dubbhara*, meaning one who has great desire (*mahiccha*). Likewise, the mind is *durakkha* (difficult to guard).
The Dhamma is difficult to see; the Dhamma is difficult to awaken to. It lies down slightly, thus it is *īsaṃsayo*; likewise, [it is] *sukhasayo*.
It is performed slightly, thus it is *īsakkaraṃ* karma. It is easily performed by a fool, thus it is *sukaraṃ* evil.
Likewise, [there are terms such as] *subharo*, *appiccho*, *sudassaṃ* (the faults of others), *subodhaṃ*, and so forth. In all these cases, there are compounds beginning with *pādika* and others.

"Bhāva" means "it becomes dense" (ghana-bhavati); there is the substitution of *o* for *ā*. "Aya" is a root from the *daṇḍaka* group; because one goes (*ayati*), it is "āya. Because one brings forth (*āharati*), it is "āhāra. Because it strikes down (*upahanati*), it is "upaghāta";

by the rule "for *han*, there is the substitute *ghā* when followed by a suffix with a nasal consonant as its marker," there is the substitution of *ghā*. Because one colors (*rañjati*), it is "rāga";

by the rule "for *j* and *c*, there is *g* when followed by a suffix with a nasal consonant as its marker," there is the substitution of *g* for *j*. Or, that by which they color (*rañjanti*) is "rāga. By the rule "for *s*, there is [substitution] when followed by a suffix with a nasal consonant as its marker..."
It is called *pāda* because one goes (*pajjati*) by means of it. *Tuda* means to pierce; it is called *patoda* because one prods (*patujjati*) with it.

It is called *jāra* because one grows old (*jarīyati*) by means of it; likewise for *dāra*. It is called *bhāga* because it is shared (*bhajīyati*). Likewise for *bhāra*. It is called *lābha* because it is obtained (*labbhati*). Preceded by *vi-*, it is called *vohāra* because one transacts (*voharīyati*) by means of it.
It is called *dāya* because it is given (*diyyati*). It is called *vighāta* because one is afflicted (*vihaññati*) by it. It is called *vihāra* because they dwell (*viharanti*) therein.
That in which they delight is an *ārāma*. "Cooking" is *pāka*; its suffix is *ko*. "Giving up" is *cāga*. "Sacrificing" is *yāga*. "Coloring" is *rāga*. 127.
With the suffixes *ana*, *ghaṇ*, *sva*, and *āpa*, there is *ḷo*.

With the suffixes *ā* and *āpa*, there is *ḷo* for the root *dah* (to burn) when preceded by *para*, *an*, *ghaṇ*, and *su*. "Burning all around" is *pariḷāha*. Thus [is] *dāha*. "Breaking" is *bhañjana*.
Attachment (*saṅga*). Thus, attachment. Forming is *saṅkhāra*; [it is derived from] "he forms," for what indeed? Thus, equipment (*parikkhāra*).

"Before" (*purasmā*) is [from] "he places before" (*purakkharoti*); thus, precedence (*purekkhāra*). These are the readings beginning with *etthaṃ*, *tadaminā*, and so forth. Thus, assistance (*upakāra*), grasping (*gāha*). He speaks with a *gha*-sound, thus a *vaka*.
*Sica* means to flow; the act of sprinkling is *seka*. Thus, sorrow (*soka*), and the vowels *e* and *o* undergo lengthening. Joining is *yoga*.

*Kapī* means "to drink. That which drinks is *pīya*; because of the suffix *kā*, there is no *vṛddhi* [vowel strengthening], and by the rule "for semi-vowels (*yuvaṇṇa*), *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* occur before a vowel," *iyaṅ* is applied.

*Khipa* means "to throw"; that which throws is *khipa*. *Bhuja* means "that by which they eat. *Yudha* means "in combat"; that by which they fight is *āyudha*. 45. [The roots] beginning with *dā* are verbal roots (*dhātu*).
The suffix *a* is frequently applied to the root *dā* in the senses of the action (*bhāva*) and the agent (*kāraka*). *Dā* means "giving. Thus, one who takes [it] is called *ādī* (the beginning).

Similarly, *upādī*. *Dhā* means "holding. That which holds water is *udadhi* (the ocean); here, by the rule "for the word *udaka*, there is the substitution of *uda* when followed by a technical suffix (*saññā*)," *udaka* is replaced by *uda*.
That in which water is held is *jaladhi* (the sea). That in which hair-tufts are held is *vāladhi* (the tail). That which is joined together or joins is *sandhi* (a joint or junction).

It is called *dhi* because it is held (*dhīyati*). It is called *vidhi* because it is enjoined (*vidhīyati*), or it performs (*vidhāti*), or it is an injunction (*vidhāna*). It is called *samādhi* because it places the mind rightly (*sammā*) or evenly (*samaṃ*). 46. Regarding *vamathu* and others:

the suffix *-thu* occurs after roots such as *vama* when they denote a state or an agent. *Vama* means to vomit; vomiting, or that which is vomited, is *vamathu*. *Vepa* (from *vep* = *kamp*, to shake) means trembling; trembling is *vepathu*.

47. The suffix *kvi* frequently becomes *kvī* in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the agent (*kāraka*). The letter *k* serves as an indicatory marker (*anubandha*) for the purpose of [triggering] the *kā* operation.
159. Of *kvī*.
When the suffix *kvip* follows a verbal root (*kriyāttha*) denoting an action performed for another, there is elision (*lopa*) of the suffix.

Thus: from *sambhavati*, *sambhū*; likewise, from *vibhavati*, *vibhū*; from *abhibhavati*, *abhibhū*; from *sayambhavati*, *sayambhū*. Similarly: from *dhu* (to shake), *sandhunāti*, thus *sandhū*; from *vibhāti*, *vibhā*; from *pabhāti*, *pabhā*.
From *saṃgamma bhāsanti ettha* (they speak together here), *sabhā*. [In this case], by the rule "when *kvip* follows, there is elision of the final consonant," the final consonant is elided.

Elision (*lopa*). One who goes by means of arms is a *bhujaga* (serpent). Likewise, an *uraga*. One who goes swiftly is a *turaṅga* (horse). One who goes through the sky is a *khaga* (bird). One who goes in the atmosphere is a *vihaga*;
here, due to the recitation of the root *vi-hā*, there is the substitution of *vihā* [for *vihāyas*]. One who does not go is a *naga* (mountain/tree). Likewise, an *aga*.
According to the rule “*nago vā pāṇinī*,” in an optional negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), the substitution of *ṭā* [for the feminine suffix] is prohibited. The root *jana* means "to be born."

"Born from karma" (*kammajo*) means born of karma; this is an *amādi*-compound (a compound beginning with *am*). There is "karmic-born fruition" (*kammajo vipāko*), "karmic-born rebirth-linking" (*kammajā paṭisandhi*), and "karmic-born matter" (*kammajaṃ rūpaṃ*).
Likewise, there are "mind-born," "temperature-born," and "nutriment-born. A son born of oneself is "self-born" (*attajo*); one born in water is "water-born" (*vārijo*).

Likewise, there are "land-born" (*thalajo*), "mud-born" (*paṅkajaṃ*), "water-born" (*jalajaṃ*), "egg-born" (*aṇḍajaṃ*), and "lake-born" (*sarasijaṃ*). In these cases, because the rule for the addition of a secondary member (*upapada*) is applied extensively, the case ending is not elided.

In the phrase beginning with “manādīhi,” there is the substitution of *si* (the genitive suffix). One born twice is a *dvija*; in the expression “*tadaminā*,” etc., there is the elision of *kkhattum*.
Born after is *anuja*. It perceives, thus it is *saññā*. It understands, thus it is *paññā*. It stands firm in this way, thus it is *patiṭṭhā*. *Jhā* means thinking;
one covets the prosperity of others, thus it is *abhijjhā*. Having established a desire for the welfare [of others], one meditates (*jhāyati*), thus...
Upajjhā. That very person is the *upajjhāya*. [The suffix] *ya* is used here in the sense of identity (*sakatthe*). It is called *saṃjhā* because they meditate rightly (*sammā jhāyanti*) therein.
Verbal roots ending in *kvip* do not abandon their original meaning; rather, they convey the sense of gender.

The suffix *ano* occurs after verbal roots (*kriyāttha*) when expressing the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the agent (*kāraka*). In the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*): *nanda* [becomes] *nandanaṃ*, meaning "that which is delighted" (*nandiyate*). In the sense of the object (*kamme*):

*anandīyittha*, *nandīyati*, *nandīyissati*, or "that which is to be delighted" (*nanditabbaṃ*) is called a *nandana-vana* (a grove of delight). *Gahanaṃ* means that which is to be grasped (*gahanīyaṃ*) or the act of grasping (*gahaṇaṃ*).

By the rule beginning with "tathanarā," the *na* is replaced by *ṇa*. Thus, it is also *gaṇhanaṃ*; here, the *niggahīta* is replaced by *no*. *Caraṇaṃ* means that which is to be practiced (*caritabbaṃ*). It is derived from the root *bhū*.
*Bhavanaṃ* means that which is to be cultivated; it is called *havanaṃ*. It is that which is to be obstructed, thus *rundhanaṃ* or *rodhanaṃ*.
It is that which is to be eaten, thus *bhuñjanaṃ* or *bhojanaṃ*. It is that which is to be awakened to, thus *bujjhanaṃ*; the suffix *-yu* is applied according to the rule “*kvaci* after *pada*, etc.
Alternatively, it is *bodhanaṃ*. *Suti* is that which is heard, or *savanaṃ*. It reaches, thus *pāpuṇanaṃ*; the augment *ku* is added by the analysis of the grammatical rule “*sakāpānaṃ kuka + kū*”.
And in the case of *nāga*, it is not [the same]. "It protects" (*pālīyati*) thus [is derived as] *pālanaṃ* (protection), and so forth.

In the sense of the agent: "it carries away dust" (*rajaṃ harati*) thus [is] *rajoharaṇaṃ* (a water-strainer). "It cognizes" (*vijānāti*) thus [is] *viññāṇaṃ* (consciousness). *Ghā* in the sense of grasping fragrance (*gandhopādāne*):

"it smells" (*ghāyati*) thus [is] *ghānaṃ* (the nose). *Jhā* in the sense of contemplation (*cintāyaṃ*): "it contemplates" (*jhāyati*) thus [is] *jhānaṃ* (meditation). "That by which one acts" (*karoti anena*) is *kāraṇaṃ* (cause); [here] the vowel is long.

It is called *byākaraṇa* because by means of it things are explained (*viākarīyanti*). It is called *pūraṇa* because by means of it something is filled (*pūrati*). It is called *dāna* because by means of it something is given (*dīyate*).

It is called *pamāṇa* because by means of it something is measured (*pamīyate*). It is called *vacana* because by means of it something is spoken (*vuccate*). It is called *panudana* because by means of it one drives away (*panudati*) or is driven away (*panujjate*).

It is called *sūdano*: the root *sūda* means "to prepare"; thus it is that by which one prepares (*sūdati*) or is purified (*sujjate*). It is called *savana* because by means of it one hears (*suṇāti*) or is heard (*suyate*). It is called *luyati* because by means of it something is cut off (*luyati*) or is cut off (*luyate*).
Or, it is *lavanaṃ*. Likewise, *nayanaṃ*. That by which one purifies or that which is purified is *pavanaṃ*. One who comes together (*sameti*) is a *samaṇo*, or it is *samanaṃ*.
Similarly, that which develops, is developed, or is brought forth by this is *bhāvanaṃ*. Likewise, *pācanaṃ*, *pācāpanaṃ*, and so on.
By the rule "after *ana* and *saṇa*, *ḷo* [is substituted]," there is *ḷo*; thus, *āḷāhanaṃ*.

*Adhikaraṇe*: That in which one stands is *ṭhānaṃ*. Likewise, it refers to lying down (*sayanaṃ*), an army (*senaṃ*), or a seat (*āsanaṃ*). It is called *adhikaraṇaṃ* because that wherein something is placed (*adhikarīyati*) is the locus.

Regarding *sampadāna* and *apādāna*: That to which something is properly given (*sammā padīyate*) is the recipient (*sampadāna*). That from which one takes [something] depending upon it (*apecca etasmā ādadāti*) is the point of departure (*apādāna*).

By virtue of the rule of abundance (*bahulādhikārā*), the suffix *-ana* is also applied in the sense of movement and other such virtuous qualities. Thus, one who moves by means of virtue (*sīlena*) is "virtuous" (*calano*); likewise, "one who burns" (*jalano*).

*Kodhana* means one who is prone to anger; *kopana* means the same. *Maṇḍa* means ornamentation; one who adorns by way of character is *maṇḍana*. *Bhūsana* is formed in the same way. In the phrase “*aññatrapi*,” the vowel *o* is prohibited. 49.

After a verbal root (*kriyāttha*), when expressing feminine gender, abstract state (*bhāva*), or a grammatical relation (*kāraka*), the suffixes *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ma*, *ṇa*, *kti*, *ka*, *yaka*, and *yā* occur, as well as *ana* frequently.
*Ajara* means the non-decaying; *jarā* is that which decays or the act of decaying. By the rule “*itthiyam atvā*,” the suffix *-ā* is applied. That which analyzes is *paṭisambhidā*.
That by which one proceeds is *paṭipadā*. Likewise are *sampadā* and *āpadā*. That which is grasped is *upādā*. *Ikkha* and *cakkha* mean seeing;
that which looks upon (*upaikkhati*) is *upekkhā*. By the rule “*yuvaṇṇānam e o luttā*,” the vowel *e* is substituted. The act of thinking is *cintanā*.
Cintā (thought). Sikkhā: from the root *sikkh* meaning "to acquire knowledge," it is *sikkhā* because of the act of learning, or because those who learn are called *sikkhino*.

Likewise is *bhikkhā* (alms). Icchā: from the root *icch* meaning "to desire. The substitution of *ccha* for *cha* occurs according to the rule beginning with "gamayami" etc. Pucchā: from the root *pucch* meaning "to ask," it is *pucchā* because of the act of asking.

Midha + Medhā: from the root *midh* meaning "to meet"; this is an unrecorded root (*apaṭhitadhātu*). It is *medhā* because of the act of meeting/understanding. Likewise, from *gudh* meaning "to surround/envelop," it is *godhā* because of the act of surrounding. Titikkhanaṃ (the act of enduring).
*Titikkhā*. Likewise, *vīmaṃsā*, *jigucchā*, *pipāsā*, *puttiyā*. *Īhanaṃ* becomes *īhā*. The addition of the suffix *ṇa* forms *kārā*;

by the rule "when followed by a non-consonant (*ṇānubandhe*), *ā* occurs," there is an *ā* here as well as in the following cases. *Haraṇaṃ* becomes *hārā*, as in *muttāvali*. *Taraṇaṃ* becomes *tārā*; *dharaṇaṃ* becomes *dhārā*. *Araṇaṃ* becomes *ārā*.
In the case of words formed in whatever manner, the determination of meaning is based on conventional usage (*ruḷhi*).

*Sambhūti* is the act of coming into being (*sambhavana*). There is no *vṛddhi* [substitution] due to the rule beginning with "na te" and so forth. *Suti* is the act of hearing (*savana*). *Nīti* is the act of leading (*nayana*) or that which leads (*nayati*);
it comes from the root *nī*. *Mati* is that which thinks (*maññati*); because it belongs to the *gamādi* group, the nasal is elided by the rule "the nasal of roots such as *gam* is elided.

*Gati* is the act of going (*gamana*) or that which is to be gone to (*gantabba*). *Upahati* is the act of striking down (*upahanana*). *Rati* is that by which they delight (*ramanti*) or the act of delighting (*ramana*). *Tanana* is the act of stretching.

*Tati*: Restriction is *niyati*. Enjoying is *bhutti*. Joining is *yutti*, with the substitution of the following form (*pararūpa*). Likewise, entering into is *samāpatti* (from *samāpajjana*), meaning attainment. *Sampatti* [is derived similarly].
Regarding *yaja*—used in the senses of worshipping a deity, uniting, and giving—the act of sacrificing is *iṭṭhi*. By the rule "for *yaj* there is the substitute *ṭi*," *ṭi* replaces it;
then by the rule "after *puccha* and so forth," its *ṭ* becomes *ṭh*, with the substitution of the following form and the first letter.
*Sāsana* is *siṭṭhi*; *sisa* is derived from the phrase *“sāsassa sisa vā”* (the head of the teaching), with the substitution of *ṭha* for *ta* according to the rule *“sānantarassa tassa ṭho”*.

*Bhitti* means that which is broken (*bhijjati*); or it is a wall (*bhitti*) because it is a breaking (*bhedana*). *Bhaj* means service; thus, *bhajana* is *bhatti*. *Tan* means extension; that which extends is *tanti*, with the change of *na* to a nasalized vowel (*niggahīta*) etc.

*Guhā* is that in which they hide (*guhanti*); the vowel *o* is elided. *Rujā* is that which breaks (*rujati*). *Mudā* is so called because they rejoice (*modanti*) by means of it; thus it is *muditā*.
*Yaka-vida-ñāṇe*: *Vijjā* means "knowledge" (*vidanaṃ*), or "that by which one knows" (*vidanti etāya*); thus it is knowledge. The prefix *da-* is the prior form.
*Ijjhanaṃ* is *ijjā*; there is the substitution of *ṭi*. *Seyyā* means "wherein they lie down" (*yasanti ettha*); there is the doubling of the consonant (*dvittaṃ*). *Aja-vaja-gamane*:

*Samajjanaṃ* or "wherein they gather together" (*samajanti ettha*) is *samajjā*. With the prefix *pa-*, *pabbajanaṃ* is *pabbajjā*. According to the rule "tavaggavaraṇādi-mhi cavaggabayañā," by the division of the grammatical connection (*yogavibhāgena*), [the substitution of the palatal group for the dental group occurs].
The suffix *vassa* is doubled. In the case of *ūmhi*, there is *paricaraṇaṃ* (the act of attending) and *paricariyā* (service). *Jāgaraṇaṃ* is *jāgariyā* (wakefulness).

From a root that does not originally have a causal sense (*apayojaka*), when it is used with a causal agent (*kāriyadhātuto kattum payojanaṃ*), the suffix *ana* is applied; the vowel *e* is prohibited, and *na* is replaced by *ṇo*.

Thus, the cause for carrying away (*harituṃ payojanaṃ*) is *hāraṇaṃ*. *Vida* means "to experience" (*anubhave*); *vitti* is called *vedanā* because it causes one to feel (*vedayatīti*). *Vanda* means "in salutation and praise" (*abhivādanathutīsu*).
Vandana is veneration. Upāsana is service. Cita refers to saṃcetanā; it is called cetanā because it causes one to intend.
Desiyati means teaching, thus it is desanā. Bhāviyati means to be cultivated, thus it is bhāvanā.
50. Jāhāhi ni... [text fragment]

*Jā-vayohānimhi*: *jā* means "in the decline of age," and *hā* means "abandonment"; by these [suffixes], the feminine form is produced. *Jānaṃ* is the ripening of age (*vaya-paripāko*), which is *jāni*. *Hānaṃ* is *hāni*. 51. *Karā ririyo karato ririyo hoti itthiyaṃ*: After the root *kar*, the suffix *ririya* occurs in the feminine.

Because of the following vowel *rā*, there is elision of *ar*; thus, *karaṇaṃ* becomes *kiriyā*. Regarding the term "action" (*kriyā*), in the rule beginning with "for the sake of the infinitive suffix *tum*" (*tuṃtāye*) and so forth, through the division of the grammatical rule (*yogavibhāga*), there is elision of *ar* after *riya*; the letter *ri* becomes a suffix (*anubandha*) attached to the letter *k*.
52. *Iki-tī* [are substitutes] for a verbal root (*dhātu*) when a form similar to it is to be expressed. Thus, *vaci* is simply the root *vac*. Likewise for *yudhi*.

Regarding the statement "of *karoti*," because the suffix (*vikaraṇa*) has been taught, there is the suffix *lo* according to the rule "for the agent (*kattari*), *lo*"; thus, *pacati*. The letter *a* and the letter *ka* [are included] by means of the suffix *ghaṇ*.
The word *kāra* forms a genitive compound (*chaṭṭhīsamāsa*).
53. Regarding the suffix *ṇī* after roots meaning "to act" when followed by *sīla*, *bhikkhañña*, or *vassaka*:

the suffix *ṇī* occurs after roots meaning "to act" when *sīla* and so forth follow. From the root *saṃs* (in the sense of praising), preceded by *piya*: "he praises what is dear by means of his virtue" (*sīlena*)—thus [the form *pasaṃsī* is derived].

One who praises what is dear (*piyapasaṃsī*) is a king. Or else, one who praises what is dear—whether by virtue (*sīla*) or by Dhamma—thinking "this is good" regarding that, is a *piyapasaṃsī*, a *piyapasaṃsanī*, or a *piyapasaṃsi*;

likewise, a family that praises what is dear, or one who speaks the truth and speaks according to the Dhamma in old age. *Sīghayāyī* means "one who goes quickly"; the suffix *-yuka* is applied as in *assāṇāpimhī yuka*.
Examples include *pāpakārī* (doer of evil) and *mālakārī* (garland-maker), and so forth. [The suffix *-aka* is used in] *uṇhaṃ bhuñjati* (he eats hot food).
“By virtue of his habit”: he eats hot food; the suffix *oka* is used in the sense of “one who sleeps lightly.
He drinks milk repeatedly and frequently, thus he is a “milk-drinker” (*khīrapāyī*); the suffix *yu* is applied. He makes it necessary, thus he is a “necessity-maker” (*avassakārī*).

When the compound is formed according to the rule “*syādi syādine katthaṃ*” and the case-ending is elided, the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra) occurs by the rule “*lopo*. One who gives a hundred is a “giver of a hundred” (*satadāyī*).

In this context, because the rule for the frequent application (*bahulavidhāna*) has been established, and because the elision of case endings (*vibhattilopa*) and the prohibition of compounds beginning with *am* have been applied, the word ends in the *v* group (i.e., it is a consonant).

In other meanings as well, [the form] is established by the analytical division (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule "ṇī. Examples include: *sādhukārī*, *brahmacārī*, and *assaddhabhojī*. Regarding *paṇḍitamānī*: one who considers oneself wise is a *paṇḍitamānī*;
likewise, *bahussutadhārī*, and so forth. *Sādhukaraṇaṃ* is the act of doing well; that which possesses this is *sādhukārī*, where the suffix *ghaṇ* is applied and the feminine marker *ī* follows.
54. *Thāvara*, *uttara*, *bhaṅgura*, *bhidura*, *bhāsura*, and *bhassara*—these words are derived when the sense of "virtue" (*sīla*) is intended.
By this rule of derivation, the suffix *-vara* is applied, and the letter *th* is substituted for *t*. Thus, that which stands by virtue is *thāvara*.
[The root] *i* is used in the sense of studying and going; with the suffix *-tara*, that which goes by virtue is *ittara*.

*Bhañja* means crushing (*omaddane*). It is called *bhaṅgura* because it crushes itself or is crushed by itself; the suffix *gura* is applied here in the sense of either the object (*kamma*) or the agent (*kattari*).
*Bhidūra* means that which breaks itself or breaks itself apart; here the suffix *kūra* is applied, with the letter *ka* as a phonetic adjunct (*anubandha*).

This [suffix] does not occur even in examples involving the sense of "crushing another" (*parabhañjana-visaye*). In that regard, some [readers] cite: "The dispeller of the darkness of faults" (*dosandhakārabhidūra*).

It is with reference to this that they maintain [the following]. It is called *bhāsura* because it "shines" (*bhāsati*) or "radiates" (*dippati*); the suffix *-ura* is added. With the suffix *-ra*, it becomes *bhassara*;
according to the rule "long vowels become short before consonants," the long vowel is shortened. (These are suffixes pertaining to the three times. 55.
The suffixes *ktavantu* and *ktāvī* are used for the agent in the past tense.

The suffixes *ktavantu* and *ktāvī* occur after verbal roots expressing an action (*kriyāttha*) when referring to the past (*bhūte*) and denoting the agent (*kattari*). For example, from *vijināti* (he conquers), we have *vijitavā* and *vijitāvī*;

because the letter *kā* is an *anubandha*, there is no *vṛddhi* strengthening. *Guṇavant* is similar to *daṇḍin*. From the root *hu* (to sacrifice), as in *aggiṃ ahavī* (he sacrificed to the fire), we have *hutavā* and *hutāvī*;
[feminine forms] *hutāvinī* and *hutavānī*. The governing rule extends from "in the past" (*bhūte*) up to "having the sense of eating" (*āhāratthā*).
56. *Kta* occurs after verbal roots (*bhū*) in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the passive (*kamma*).

*Asanaṃ āsitaṃ bhavatā* (eating was done by you). [The suffix] *ñi* [is applied]. *Karīyittha* (was made) becomes *kato* (made); *kaṭo* (a mat) was made by you. By the rule beginning with *“gamādirānaṃ”* etc., there is the elision of *r*. It is the same in subsequent cases as well. 57. And [the suffix *kta* occurs] in the sense of the agent (*kattari*) when the action has not yet begun (*ārambhe*).

At the commencement of an action, the suffix *kta* occurs after a verb root, and it follows the rules as they apply. From the root *pakaroti*, we have *pakato bhavaṃ kaṭaṃ* ("you made the mat"). From *pakarīyittha*, we have *pakato kaṭo bhavatā* ("the mat was made by you"). From *pasupati*, we have *pasutto bhavaṃ* ("you slept"). From *pasupiyittha*, we have *pasuttaṃ bhavatā*;

here the "substitution of the following form" (*pararūpa*) applies. 58. After the roots *ṭhā*, *vas*, *silis*, *sī*, *ruha*, *jara*, and *janī*, the suffix *kta* occurs in the sense of the agent, and it follows the rules as they apply. From *upaṭṭhāsī*, we have *upaṭṭhito bhavaṃ guruṃ* ("you attended upon the teacher"). From *upaṭṭhīyittha*... [sentence continues].

The teacher was attended upon (*upaṭṭhita*) by you; [the suffix] *assa* is used in the sense of "let him stand" (*ṭhāssīti ṭhāssa*). Thus, "he attended upon" (*upāsī*) means "attended upon" (*upāsita*).

"He was attended upon" (*upāsīyittha*) means "attended upon" (*upāsita*). By the rule "for the consonant, *ñi*," there is *ñi*. "He dwelt after" (*anuvusi*) or "was dwelt after" (*anuvusīyittha*) means "dwelt after" (*anuvusīta*).

By the rule "there is *assu*," there is the vowel *u* for *assa*. The root *silisa* preceded by *ā-* means "embracing"; "he embraced" (*āsilesi*) or "was embraced" (*āsilesīyittha*) means "embraced" (*āsiliṭṭha*). For that which immediately follows...

In the word *ṭho*, there is the substitution of the single form (*pararūpa*) of *ṭhe* and the first vowel. Regarding *adhisayito*: it means "you lay upon" (*adhisayi*) or "you were laid upon" (*adhisīyittha*). Thus:

"You [are] the bedstead upon which you lay" (*adhisayito khaṭopikaṃ bhavaṃ*), or "The bedstead was laid upon by you" (*adhisayitā khaṭopikā bhotā*). Similarly, regarding *āruḷho*: it means "you climbed" (*āruhi*) or "you were climbed upon" (*āruhīyittha*). Thus:

"You [are] the tree which you climbed" (*āruḷho rukkhaṃ bhavaṃ*), or "The tree was climbed upon by you" (*āruḷho rukkho bhotā*). According to the rule "after *ruh* and others, *ho* becomes *ḷa*," its *hakāra* and the preceding *hakāra* become *ḷa*. [Similarly for] *anujīri*.
*Anujīrīyittha* means "has decayed after"; *anujiṇṇo* [is used when] addressing a woman (*vasalī*): "Sir, you have decayed; lady, you have decayed.

In the word *tarādīhi riṇṇo*, there is the substitution of *riṇṇa* for the suffix *kta*, and by the rule *rānubandhe* etc., there is the elision of the portion beginning with *ra*. *Anvajāyi* or *anvajāyittha* means "was born after";

*anujāto* [is used when] addressing a young man (*māṇavako*) [regarding] a young woman (*māṇavikam*): "The young woman was born after the young man," or "the young woman was born after by the young man. In the word *janissā*, there is the substitution of *ā* for *na*.

59. Regarding roots meaning "to go" (*gamanattha*) that are intransitive (*akammaka*), and regarding roots meaning "action" (*kriyattha*), the suffix *-kta* occurs in the sense of the locus (*ādhāra*) and the agent (*kattar*), according to what is appropriate.

In the case of the root *yā* (meaning "to reach"), a place where those who have gone are found is called *yātaṃ ṭhānaṃ*. Those who have gone are *yātā*; the act of going is *yātaṃ*. Here, even though there is an object (*kamma*), [it is not expressed].
*Anicchitaṃ*: that which is not desired. *Yāyitā* means the path traversed (*yāta*). Because it is said, “Those [roots] whose meaning is ‘going’ have the meaning of ‘awakening’;

those whose meaning is ‘awakening’ have the meaning of ‘going’,” he has come to the true characteristic (*tathalakkhaṇa*) exactly as it is (*yāthāvato*) and has fully awakened (*abhisambuddho*); thus he is also called the *Tathāgata*.
*Āsitaṃ* means that which has been sat upon (*āsitavanto*) by me. Those who have sat are the *āsita*. Sitting is *āsana*. It is also *māsita*.

60. The suffix *kta* occurs in the sense of eating (*āhāra*) and swallowing (*ajjhohāra*), as well as in the sense of a receptacle (*ādhāra*), according to the rule. For example: *bhuttaṃ* (eaten) [is derived from] *bhuttavanto sma* ("we have eaten").

Likewise, *pītaṃ* (drunk). [In the word] *gāpānaṃ*, the suffix *ī* is applied. That which is being eaten is "eaten" (*bhuttaṃ*); that which is being drunk is "drunk" (*pītaṃ*). That which has been eaten is "eaten rice" (*bhutto odano*). Likewise...
*Pītam udakam* (the water was drunk). [This is an example of] the formation of a past participle (*kattattha*) with the suffix *ka*.

Due to the general rule of abundance (*bahulādhikāra*), it also occurs with the agentive case (*kattari*): "The cows have drunk" (*api viṃsu iti pītā gāvo*). *Sida* means "to cook. *Passijjī* becomes *passanno*;

here, the suffix *kta* is added in the sense of "going," and by the rule beginning with *bhidā*, its *t* is replaced by *n* and the preceding vowel undergoes elision (*pararūpa*). *Amaññittha* becomes *mato*. *Icchīyittha* becomes *iṭṭho*. *Abujjhitā* becomes *buddho*.
“*Dho dhahabhehi*” means *dhota*. It is called *pūjita* because it was honored (*pūjīyittha*); due to the *curāditta* group [of roots], the suffix *ṇi* is applied.
Likewise, from *sīlīyittha* comes *sīlita*. From *rakkhīyittha* comes *rakkhita*. From *khamīyittha* comes *khanta*; here, the *m* becomes a *niggahīta*. From *akkocchīyittha* comes *akkuṭṭha*;

here, the *ā* becomes short. *Rusa* = *rose*: from *arosi* comes *ruṭṭha*; the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent according to the rule beginning with “*gamanatthā*. In the case of *ñimhi*...

*Rusita*: from *rus*, meaning "to be angry. *Abhibyāhaṭa*: from *hara* (in the sense of "taking away"), preceded by *abhi-vi-ā*; it is called *abhibyāhaṭa* because it was "uttered" (*abhibyāharīyittha*). *Dayita*: from *daya* (in the senses of "giving," "going," "injuring," and "taking"); it is called *dayita* because it was "cherished" (*adayīyittha*).

*Haṭṭha*: from *hasa* (in the sense of "laughter"); it is called *haṭṭha* because he "laughed" (*ahasīti*). *Kanta*: from *kam* (in the sense of "being desired"); it is called *kanta* because it was "desired" (*kāmīyittha*).

Regarding the rule "of *ṇi*, *ṇā*, and *pī* in those [roots]," here, due to the division of the grammatical rule (*yogavibhāga*), there is the elision of the *ṇi* suffix of the *curādi* class. *Saṃyata*: from *saṃyam*. It means "restrained. Preceded by the negative particle (*nañ*).
*Na marī* means "immortal" (*amata*); in a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), *na* becomes *ṭ*.

Because the word *kaṭṭha* is used here in the sense of the fruit—namely, suffering that has been reached—the suffix *-kta* occurs only when the fruit has already come into being through cultivation. [The root] *kas* is used in the senses of going, harming, and scratching; *akasi* means "he harmed," hence *kaṭṭhaṃ*. 150.
After roots beginning with *bhid*, the suffix *-no* replaces *-kta* and *-ktavantu*.
The suffix *na* replaces the *ta* and *ktavantu* suffixes that follow roots such as *bhid*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class).

Regarding the rule *“*kto bhāvakammesu*”* (the *kta* suffix is used for the sense of the action or the object), the *kta* suffix is applied everywhere above in the sense of the object. *Abhijji* (was split) becomes *bhinno* (split); here, the *ne* replacement does not occur.

*Abhindī* (he split) becomes *bhinnavā* (one who has split), by the rule *“*kattari bhūte*"* (the *ktavantu* suffix is used for the agent in the past tense), and so forth. Similarly above: *achijji* (was cut) becomes *chinno* (cut); *achindī* (he cut) becomes *chinnavā* (one who has cut).

*Chad* means to cover (*apavāraṇe*). That which has been covered (*chādīyittha*) is *channa*. One who covers is *channavā*; because it belongs to the *curādi* group, the suffix *ṇi* is applied, and by the rule "the elision of *ṇi*, *ṇa*, and *pi* occurs before those [suffixes]," the elision of *ṇi* takes place here through a separation of the grammatical rule (*yogavibhāga*).
*Khid* means to endure with difficulty (*asahane*). One who is distressed is *khinna*; one who is distressed is *khinnavā*, used in the sense of the agent (*kattari*).

The same applies to the following cases. One who arises is *uppanna*; one who has arisen is *uppannavā*. *Sid* means to cook (*pāke*). That which has been cooked is *sinna*; that which has been cooked is *sinnavā*.

The root *sad* means "to go away," "to perish," or "to take. One who has sat down (*sanna*) is called *sannī*, meaning one who sits (*sannavā*). The root *pī* means "to swell. One who has swollen (*pīna*) is called *pīnī*, meaning one who is fat (*pīnavā*). The root *sū* means "to procreate.

One who has procreated (*sūna*) is called *sūnī*, meaning one who procreates (*sūnavā*). The root *dī* means "to perish. One who has perished (*dīna*) is called *dīnī*, meaning one who is miserable (*dīnavā*). The roots *ḍī* and *lī* mean "to move through the air. One who has flown (*ḍīna*) is called *ḍīnī*, meaning one who flies (*ḍīnavā*).

The root *lī* (also *leyi*) means "to cling" or "to hide. One who has hidden (*alīna*) is called *alīnī*, meaning one who hides (*alīnavā*). The root *lū* means "to cut. One who has cut (*lūna*) is called *lūnī*, meaning one who cuts (*lūnavā*).

151. After roots ending in *dā*, the suffix *in* occurs in place of the past passive participle (*kta*) and the active past participle (*ktavantu*). Thus, from *adāyi* (was given), we have *dinna*; from *addi* (he gave), we have *dinnavā*.
152. After roots beginning with *kṛ*, the suffix *ṇa* occurs.

No. In all subsequent instances, the rule "of the *kta* and *ktavantū* suffixes" should be applied. From the root *kira* = scattering: that which was scattered is *kiṇṇa*; he who scattered is *kiṇṇavā*. From *pura* = filling: that which was filled is *puṇṇa*; he who filled is *puṇṇavā*. That which was exhausted is *khīṇa*; he who exhausted is *khīṇavā*. 153. From *tara* etc., [the suffix] *riṇṇa*: its form is *riṇṇa*.

The letter *ra* serves the purpose of eliding the final vowel and following consonants. That which crossed over is *tiṇṇa*; he who crossed over is *tiṇṇavā*. That which decayed is *jiṇṇa*; he who decayed is *jiṇṇavā*.

*Paricīyittha* means "was accumulated" (*ciṇṇo*). *Paricīyi* means "one who has accumulated" (*ciṇṇavā*). Here, because the suffix *issa* is prescribed as an alternative, forms such as *paricita* and *upacita* are also established.
154. *Go bhañjādīhi*: after roots such as *bhañj*, the suffix *ga* replaces *tassa*.
*Abhañji* means "broken" (*bhaggo*) or "one who has broken" (*bhaggavā*). [This occurs] when the suffix *kta* is applied to the agent according to the rule beginning with "roots meaning 'to go'."

In this case, by means of this [rule], there is the substitution of the single form (pararūpa) for the letter *ga*, as well as the elision of the *niggahīta*. *Laga* means "to cling"; one who clings (*lagati*) is "clinging" (*lagga*) or "one who clings" (*laggavā*).

*Mujja* means "to sink"; one who sinks (*nimujjati*) is "sunk" (*nimugga*) or "one who has sunk" (*nimuggavā*); here, there is the elision of the first member of the conjunct consonant (*saṃyogādilopa*).
*Vīja* means "to tremble with fear"; preceded by the prefix *sam-*, one who is thoroughly agitated (*saṃvijjati*) is "trembling" (*saṃvigga*) or "one who is trembling" (*saṃviggavā*).
155. *Suso* means "dry.

From the root *suṣ*, after the suffixes *-kta* and *-ktavantu*, there is *tassa kho hoti*. *Susa* = *sose* (in drying). *Sussī* means "dry" or "one who is dry. 156. *Pacā ko* (the suffix *ko* follows the root *pac*).
After the root *pac*, the suffix *ko* is substituted for the *kta* and *ktavantu* suffixes. Thus, *paccī* means "cooked" (*pakko*), and *pacī* means "one who has cooked" (*pakkavā*).
157. **Mucā vā**:

After the root *muc*, the suffix *ko* optionally replaces the *kta* and *ktavantu* suffixes. From *muca* (in the sense of releasing), we have *muccī* meaning "released" (*mukko*) or "liberated" (*mutto*).
*Amucci*: having released, having let go. *Sakko*: in words such as *tinva*, etc., it is established by [the rule] beginning with "i bhī kā. *Asakkhi*: he was able; thus he is *sakka*.

In the case of the suffixes *kta* and *ktavantu*, the form remains exactly as *satta* when the quality of being present (*sattavātva*) exists. 106. And for *muh* and *bah*, when followed by a suffix with *k* or *n* as an indicatory letter (*kānubandha*), [the vowel is lengthened].
In the case of *muh* and *bah*, a long vowel occurs before a suffix beginning with *t* when the suffix has *kā* as its *anubandha*, excluding *tvāna* and *tvā*.

*Muh* means "to be bewildered," and *baha*, *braha*, and *brūha* mean "growth. From *muyhitta* and *bayhittha*, we derive *mūḷho* and *bāḷho* (bewildered and strong). Because roots such as those beginning with "gamanatthā" (meaning to go) are intransitive, the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), resulting in a long vowel.
According to the rule "from *ruh* and others, *h* becomes *ḷ* and *h* becomes *ḷ*," the *h* of the root is changed to *ḷ* and the *h* of the suffix is also changed to *ḷ*. Thus, *gūḷho* (hidden).
“*Kānubandhe tve*”: this is the governing rule (*adhikāra*) extending as far as “*sāsassa sissa va*.
107. *Vahassa ussa*:
for the *ussa* of *vah*, there is a long vowel before *te*. In *vuyhittha*, it is called *vūḷha*; by the word “*assū*,” a long vowel is substituted for the *ukāra*.

108. For *dhā* [is used] in the sense of "holding" (*dhāraṇe*); for *tīma*, there is either *hoti* or *te*. That which was placed down is *nihita*. One who places down is *nidahī*; one who has placed down is *nihitavā* or *nihitāvī*. 109.
There is the elision of the final vowel of roots such as *gam* and others.
There is elision of the final vowel of roots beginning with *gam* and others ending in *r*, before those [suffixes]. *Agamī* means "gone. *Khaññittha* means "cut," in the passive sense (*kamme*).
Likewise, *haññittha* means "killed. *Tana* means "extension"; *taññittha* means "extended" (*tato*). *Yama* means "to cease"; *saṃyamī* means "self-restrained" (*saññato*).

Here, the suffix *kta* is used in the active sense (*kattari*) according to the rule "roots meaning 'to go' etc."; and by the rule "for *ye* and *saṃs*," the *niggahīta* becomes *ñ* and the preceding form is applied.
Thus, *aramī* means "delighted. *Karīyittha* means "was done. 110. *Vacādīnaṃ vassa uṭa vā*:

for the root *vac* and others, *uṭ* is substituted for *vas* when followed by a suffix beginning with *kā* or *nu*, provided *at* follows. *Vuccittha* becomes *uttaṃ*. The *u* of this [suffix] is stated; thus it is in both cases.
The form *pararūpa*. The root *vas* means "to dwell. That which is dwelt in, or that in which one has dwelt (*avasi*, *vasiṃsu*), is called *vuttha*.

The suffix *kta* is applied according to the rule beginning with "roots meaning 'to go'. By the rule "for *sāsa*, *vasa*, *saṃsa*, and *saṃsā*, substitute *tha*," the *t* of *kta* is replaced by *tha*. 112. Or, [the *th*] of *vaddha*.

In the case of *vaddha*, when followed by a suffix beginning with *at*, the vowel *u* occurs. Regarding the term *avaddhi*: it means "grown" (*vuddho*) or "increased" (*vaddho*). In the sense of the agent (*kattari*), with the suffix *kta*, the rule "dho dha + habhehi" applies, whereby its *dh* becomes *d*.

Furthermore, there is the elision of the third consonant and the initial consonant of the cluster. The form *vutti* arises from the rule "the words *sabba* and so forth [take *u*] in the sense of state alone" (*vuttimatte*), due to a separation of the grammatical rule (*yogavibhāga*). The form *vatti* also occurs according to the grammatical rules.
113. *Yajassa yassa ṭi-yī*:

When the suffixes *ṭi* and *yī* follow the root *yaj*, [the augment] *iṭ* is inserted before the substitution of *atva*. Thus, from *yajanaṃ* with the suffix *kta*, by the rule “*pucchādito*,” when the substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*) for *ṭha* is made, we have *iṭṭhaṃ* and *yiṭṭhaṃ*. 114. *Ṭhāssi*... [The rule continues: When the suffix *ṭhāssi* follows, [the augment *iṭ* is inserted].

The substitution *i* occurs for *ṭh* when followed by the suffix *kā* with the augment *at*. Thus, *aṭṭhāsī* means "he stood. 115. *Gā* and *pāna* become *gī* and *pī* respectively when followed by the suffix *kā* with the augment *at*.
Thus, *gānaṃ* becomes *gītaṃ* ("sung") and *pānaṃ* becomes *pītaṃ* ("drunk"). By virtue of the rule of frequent occurrence (*bahulādhikārā*), [the forms] *pitvā* [etc. are also established.
116. *Janissa* becomes *janissa* when followed by *kā*, *anu*, *bandhe*, *atve*. In *ajanīti jāto*, because of the rule “of that which ends in the sixth case,” the final vowel *a* becomes *ā*. 117.
In *sāsassa*, *sisa* optionally [occurs].

*Sāsassa sisso hoti kānubandhe atthe*: "Sāsana" is formed with the suffix *kta*; for that [suffix], by the rule "sāsa vasa saṃsa sasā tho," there is the substitution of *tho* as the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), and the first letter [of the root] is also changed;
then, by the rule "ta+tha+na+rā," etc., its [the *tho*’s] *ṭo* is substituted. For *tha*, *ṭho* is prescribed. Elsewhere, it is *satthaṃ*.
By the rule "guhādīhi yaka," with the suffix *yaka*, it is called *sisso* because he is taught (*sāsīyati*). With the suffix *um*, it becomes *sāsiyo*.

140. For the *t* that follows immediately after it, when [the suffix] beginning with *k* and expressing an action (*kriyāttha*) follows, there is *ṭh* for that *t*. Thus, from *tuṣ*, we have *tuṭṭho*;

by this rule, for the *t* following the suffix *kta* (which includes those meaning "going," etc.), there is *ṭh* and the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), and so forth. Likewise, *tuṭṭhavā*. In the case of the suffixes *tabba* and *ktī*, *tosanaṃ* becomes *tuṭṭhabbaṃ*.
“*Aññatrāpi*” means the absence of the vowel *o*. Thus there is *tuṭṭhi* (elision), but because it is followed by *kā*, there is no *vuddhi* (vowel strengthening). **141.

*Kasassi ma ca vā*** After *kas*, the substitute *ṭha* optionally occurs for the following *ta*, and *ma* is also substituted for *kas*. *Kasīyittha* = *kiṭṭhaṃ*. Like grain that has been threshed (*kiṭṭha*), they were difficult to subdue; here the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object. In the absence of *imā*, it becomes *kaṭṭhaṃ*, as in *akaṭṭhapākimaṃ sāliṃ* (rice that ripens without being ploughed).

142. These words *dhasta* and *otrasta* are derived [as follows]: *dhaṃsa* means "to fall away. From *dhaṃsīyittha*, [the form] *dhasta* arises, with the elision of the vowel *i*. *Utrasati* means "he trembles," hence *otrasta*.
143. From *puccha* and so forth...

After *puccha* and other such roots, the suffix *ta* becomes *ṭha* when followed immediately by another [suffix]. Thus, from *pucchīyittha*, we have *puṭṭho*. From the root *bhaj* (in the sense of cooking), *bhajīyittha* becomes *bhaṭṭho*; here, there is the elision of the initial consonant cluster. From *yajittha*, we have *yiṭṭho*;
according to the rule “for *yaj*, replace *ya* with *ṭi* and *yī*,” it becomes *yi*. 144.
After *sās*, *vas*, *saṃs*, and *sas*, the suffix *ta* becomes *tha* when followed immediately by another [suffix]. Thus, *sāsanaṃ* or *sāsīyittha* becomes *satthaṃ*. *Vasanaṃ*...
It was spoken (*vutthaṃ*); thus it is called "speech" (*assū*). It is praised (*pasaṃsīyittha*), or it is that which is praised, hence "praiseworthy" (*pasatthaṃ*).

The root *sas-* has the meanings of going, harming, and living; thus, "going," "harming," and "living" constitute "weapon" (*satthaṃ*). It was instructed (*anusāsīyittha*), hence "instructed" (*anusiṭṭho*); here, *ttha* becomes *ṭṭha*. 145. *Dho* [is derived] from *dha*, *ha*, and *ta*.
When followed by *dha*, *ha*, or *bha*, the following *ta* becomes *dha*. In the case of *vaddhittha* (it was increased), the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the object;

when *ta* is replaced by *dha*, and then *u* is substituted for *va* of *vaddha* according to the rule "optionally for *vaddha*," the initial of the conjunct is elided, resulting in *vuddho*. In *duyhittha* (it was milked), it becomes *duddhaṃ*.
In *labhīyittha* (it was obtained), it becomes *laddhaṃ*.
146. *Dahā ḍho*:

After *dah*, the letter *ḍha* occurs in place of the immediately following *da*. Thus, from *dayhittha*, [we get] *daḍḍho*; when the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) and so forth has been applied, the letter *ḍa* is substituted by [the rule] beginning with "the fourth and second" (*catutthadutiye*). 147. *Bahassu ma ca*: [The letter *ma* also occurs in place of the final consonant] after *baha*.

After *baha*, *parassa* (the following), and *anantarassa* (immediately preceding), *tassa* becomes *ḍha*, and *baha* becomes *ba* by association with *ḍha*. *Baha*, *braha*, and *brūha* mean growth (*vuddhi*). *Abahī* means grown (*vuḍḍho*). 148.

After *ruhādi* (roots beginning with *ruha*), *parassa* and *anantarassa* *tassa* becomes *ha*, and *ḷa* replaces *nta*. *Āruhī* means ascended (*āruḷho*). *Guyhittha* means hidden (*guḷho*). *Abahī* means foolish (*bāḷho*). In both cases, a long vowel occurs [after *muhā* and *bahā*], etc.

149. In place of *muh*, the letter *h* is substituted, or alternatively, *ḷ* is inserted at the end. Thus, *amohī* means "he was deluded" (*muḷho*, *muddho*); for that [root], *dha* is substituted. (The rule for the application of past-tense suffixes. 64.
*Nta* is used in the present tense when expressing the agent (*kattari*).

In the sense of the present tense, the suffix *māna* occurs after a verbal root signifying an action when expressing the agent (*kattari*). Thus, from *tiṭṭhati*, we have *tiṭṭhamāno*. Here, by the rule "lo in the sense of the agent," the suffix *lo* is applied; then, by the rule "for *ṭhā* and *pā*, substitute *tiṭṭha* and *piva*," there is the substitution of *tiṭṭha*. In the case of *māna*, *anta*, *tya*, and so forth, when expressing the agent, the suffix *lo* is applied by this very same rule.
65. *Māna*: [The suffix] *māna* [is used] in the sense of the agent. *Tiṭṭhamāno*.

66. Regarding the suffix *kyo*: In the case of abstract nouns (*bhāva*) and passive verbs (*kamma*), the suffix *māna* is used. "Station" (*ṭhāna*) and "being stationed" (*ṭhīyamāna*). According to the rule, “The suffix *kyo* is used for abstract nouns and passives when they are not proximate, such as in *mānanta* and so forth,” the suffix *kyo* is applied to both the abstract noun and the passive. From the rule “*kyassā*,” the suffix *īma* is added. That which is being cooked is *paccamāno*. In the case of the suffix *kyo*, there is the original form (*pubbarūpa*).
67. Those [suffixes] preceded by *ssa* are used for the future.

Regarding future meaning, the suffixes *tenta*, *māna*, and *ssa*—preceded by their respective roots—occur in place of the present tense (*vattamānato*). There is elision of the letter *e* and the letter *ā*.
Thus: *ṭhassati* becomes *ṭhassanto* and *ṭhassamāno*. *Ṭhīyissati* becomes *ṭhīyissamānaṃ*; here, *ī* replaces *e* according to the rule “*ñibyañjanassa*” (where *ñi* replaces a consonant).

Because this falls within the scope of *tyādi* (beginning with *ty*), the substitution of *iña* for *āīssa* and so forth does not occur; furthermore, because it is accompanied by *aī*, the suffix *ssa* remains. *Paccissati*... [becomes *paccissamānaṃ*].
“Cooked rice that is being eaten. Regarding the rule *rā nassa ṇo*: 5.172.

After the suffix *ra*, the *ṇa* of suffixes such as *nta*, *māna*, and *tya* does not become *ṇo*. For example: *karoti* becomes *karonto* (doing) and *kurumāno* (doing), [the vowel *o*] being substituted by the rule *tanāditvo*.
5,173. *Gama*, *yami*, *sāsa*, and *disānaṃ* optionally take *cchaṅ*;
or rather, they take *cchaṅ* before suffixes such as *nta* and *māna*. Because of the suffixal marker *ṅa*, the final consonant becomes *n*. Thus: *gacchanto*, *gacchamāno*.
*Yama* = to cease; *yacchanto*, *yacchamāno*. *Icchanto*, *icchamāno*. *Āsa* = to sit; *acchanto*, *acchamāno*.

By the rule beginning with “byañjane,” the vowel is short. *Disa* means to bestow; one who desires is *diccha-māna*. Because the particle *vā* has a fixed optionality (*vavatthita-vibhāsā*) and because [the suffix] occurs in certain *añ* participles, we have:
that which is desired is *icchitabba*; the act of desiring is *icchā*, formed by the *app* suffix according to the rule “*itthiya + maṇā*,” etc.;
[the gerundives and infinitive are] *icchitaṃ*, *icchitabbaṃ*, and *icchituṃ*. And from other divisions of the grammatical rules (*yogavibhāga*), we have *pavecchanto*.

174. *Jara* and *maraṇa* take the suffix *-mīyaṅ*, or they may take *-nta*, *-māna*, and so forth. Thus: *jīyanto* (growing old); by the rule beginning with *dicca*, etc., [the suffix] *-īma* is applied: *jīranto*. Also: *jīyamāno*, *jīramāno*. *Mīyanto*, *maranto*; *mīyamāno*, *maramāno*. 175.
For the roots ending in *-ṭhā*, there is the suffix *-piva*. Thus: *tiṭṭhapiva*.
In the case of *tiṭṭha* and *piva*, they optionally become *tiṭṭha* and *piva* before suffixes such as *-nta*. Thus: *tiṭṭhanto*, *tiṭṭhamāno*; *pivanto*, *pivamāno*. 176.

For *gama*, *vada*, and *dāna*, there are optional substitutes *ghamma*, *vajja*, and *dajja* before suffixes such as *-nta*. Thus: *ghammanto* (alternative form: *gacchanto*), *vajjanto* (alternative form: *vadanto*), *dajjanto* (alternative form: *dadanto*).
177. Regarding *kubba*, *kuru*, and *kayirā*:
after the verbal root *kar* (to do), the forms *kubba*, etc., optionally occur before suffixes beginning with *nt*. Thus: *kubbanto*, *kayiranto*, *karonto*; likewise *kubbamāno*, and so forth.
Except for the case where *massa* is elided as in *mānassa massa*, the form is *karāṇo*. Because it is stated "after *so*," this applies only to the agent (*kattari*).
178. The elision of *ga*:
The elision of *ga* occurs before suffixes beginning with *n*, etc., such as in *gheppanto* and *gheppamāno*.
179. *Ṇa* replaces the *niggahīta*.

When a *gaṇa* (vowel group) is elided, there is no [substitution]. "Maṃ" refers to the root *rudh* and others; it is that which is to be grasped (*gaṇhitabba*), grasping (*gaṇhituṃ*), or one who is grasping (*gaṇhanto*).
130. Regarding the rule *ntamānantiyiyuṃsvādilopo*: this is the elision of the initial [element]. *Asa* means "to exist";
thus, "he exists" (*bhavati*) is *santo*, being in the state of existing (*samāno*).
131. *ṭh* replaces *ṭhā* after *pādi*; *ṭha* replaces *ṭhā* before *pādi*.
*Saṇṭhahanto*. *Santiṭṭhanto*. (The method for suffixes ending in the present tense).
61. *Tuṃ* [is used] in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) of the action; it occurs in the sense of "for that purpose.

Because they are employed in the sense of the abstract state of the action when the action itself is understood as having that purpose, the suffixes beginning with *tum* express the abstract state of the action for the sake of that [action]. For example: *karaṇāya gacchati* = "he goes in order to do" (*kātuṃ gacchati*). According to the rule *“tuṃ-tuna-tabbesu vā”* (or [the substitution of *a* occurs] before *tuṃ*, *tuna*, and *tabba*), the letter *a* optionally replaces *ka* [of *karaṇa*];
in the case of the former form (*pubbarūpe*), [it becomes *kātuṃ*].

*Kattāye*: [The suffix] *ā* is used in the sense of “you must do. In *kātabbe*, it is the same. Because it is a particle (*nipāta*), there is the elision of the fourth case ending (*-assa*) in the phrase *asaṅkhyehi sabbāsaṃ*.
The same applies to the suffixes *-tuṃ* and others hereafter. *Kattukāmo*: one who desires to act; he wishes to perform volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*).

*Saddhammaṃ suṇituṃ*: regarding the word *suṇituṃ* (to hear): when the suffix *ñi* follows, there is the substitution of *ṇo* for *nāgama* (the augment *n*), and because of the presence of the *nāgama*, there is no *vṛddhi* strengthening. *Sotave*, *sotuṃ*, and *suṇituṃ* [are all forms of the infinitive].

Or [he] desires to praise. Thus: to experience, to cook; to go—[here] the *niggahīta* [nasal stop] occurs according to the rule "the *man* [suffix] becomes *niggahīta*"—to go, to endure, to dig, to kill, to think, to carry, to remember;
likewise, to strike, to enter, to recite, to eat, to lie down, to lead, to offer oblations, to abandon.
To abandon (pahātuṃ), to give (dātuṃ), to obstruct (roddhuṃ), to block (rundhituṃ), to eat (bhottuṃ), to consume (bhuñjītuṃ), to cut (chettuṃ), to sever (chindituṃ), to sew (sibbituṃ).

[The suffix] *ūmhi* is added to *vassa*; [the forms are] *bo*, *dvittaṃ*, *buddhuṃ*, *tassa dho*. To awaken (bujjhituṃ), to be joined (yuka). To know (jānituṃ); *ñā-* in the sense of awakening (*avabodhane*).

To be born (janituṃ). To conquer (jetuṃ), to win (jinītuṃ). To reach (pattuṃ), to arrive at (pāpuṇituṃ). To buy (ketuṃ), to purchase (kiṇituṃ). To decide (vinicchetuṃ); with *issa e*, [it becomes] *vinicchinituṃ*.
"To grasp" means to seize; "to steal" means to rob, to plunder; "to protect" means to guard. Regarding the instigators:
"to develop" means to cultivate; "to cause to do" means to cause to perform, to have performed, or to have caused to be performed, and so forth.

Thus, when a verbal action is implied within another action, as I shall explain for easy understanding: "he goes to see," "he begins to go," "he instigates [someone] to go," "he said in order to show," and so on.
It is established [in usage] in *araha*, *sakkā*, and so forth, as well as in *kāla*, *samaya*, and *velā*. Who is fit to censure him? He is fit to be a king;
he is fit to be called "worthy" (*araha*); he is fit to be conquered by wealth; he is fit to be obtained; he is fit to speak. He will be able to do it;
he is capable of entering the fixed course (*niyāma*); he is incapable of doing it. He is worthy of you.
"To receive a gift," "this is appropriate to do," "it is fitting to give a gift," "one is permitted to give and to speak"—thus it is proper to say;
"it is not allowable to cut [the hair]" and so forth. Likewise:
"it is the right time to eat," "it is the occasion to eat," "it is the hour to eat."
Even in this case, it is established: it is indeed sufficient to give gifts; it is indeed sufficient to perform meritorious deeds. 62.
*Alaṃ*, *khalu*, and *una* may optionally take the suffixes *ktun*, *ktvāna*, or *ktvā* when used in the sense of prohibition.

When the words *alaṃ* and *khalu* are employed for the purpose of negation, the suffixes beginning with *ktun* may optionally occur in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*). [The word] preceded by *alaṃ*— (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the analysis of *alapubbo*.)

In *su-savane*, the elision of the suffix occurs due to its being a particle (*nipāta*). Thus, *alaṃ savanaṃ katvā* becomes *alaṃ savanaṃ katvā*; *khalu savanaṃ katvā* becomes *khalu savanaṃ katvā*. Similarly, *alaṃ sotuṃ* becomes *alaṃ sotuṃ*; *khalu sotuṃ* becomes *khalu sotuṃ*; *alaṃ sutvāna* becomes *alaṃ sutvāna*;
*khalu sutvāna* becomes *khalu sutvāna*; *alaṃ sutvā* becomes *alaṃ sutvā*; and *khalu sutvā* becomes *khalu sutvā*.
[This applies] to those ending in *-ka* and *-tu* when preceded by *pubba-*.
When there is a single agent for certain operations, those suffixes beginning with *tu* (such as *tuṃ*, *tuṇa*) are used in the sense of the action itself (*bhāve*).
By the rule "tuṃ-tuṇā," etc., the *ā* of the agent is elided; thus, one goes having done the work (*kātuṇa*), or they suffer having not done merit (*akātuṇa*). When the *ra* is elided:

having done good work (*kammaṃ katvāna*), he goes to heaven having performed meritorious deeds (*puññāni katvā*). Having performed volitional formations (*abhisaṅkharaṇaṃ katvā*), it is expressed as *abhisaṅkharitvā*.
Or having done; likewise, having sewn, having covered, having known, having heard the Dhamma, having heard the Dhamma he rejoices;
having heard, having reached, having attained, having bought, having conquered, having won, having stolen, having robbed, having honored, having worshipped;
likewise, having cultivated loving-kindness, having developed it, having caused a monastery to be built, having had it built, having caused it to be constructed.
"Having caused [the world] to be made, they will go to heaven," and so forth. What is the meaning of *pubbe* (formerly)? For example: "He eats and he cooks.

In expressions such as "The mountain has not yet reached the river" (*apatvā nadiṃ pabbato*) and "The river has already passed the mountain" (*atikkamma pabbataṃ nadī*), because the root *bhū* (to be) occurs there, both the identity of the agent and the priority in time are understood.
This is already established by the expression "having eaten again and again, he goes"; however, it is used here to indicate frequency (*ābhikkhaṇṇa*).

It is understood from the dual number. How so? In the phrase, "He seized him by the life-force; he goes shaking his body," it is established by means of a present participle (*ghana*) used as an adverbial modifier of the action, just as in the expression, "he lies down to cook the rice.
164. Or, *pyo* may replace *tvā* in a compound.

In a compound, *tvā* becomes *pyo*. The letter *p* in the rule *“pye sissā”* is for the purpose of specification. The prefix *abhi-* forms a *pādi*-compound: having performed salutation (*abhivadana*), one says “having saluted” (*abhivādiya*) and then speaks. Likewise, from *abhibhū*, we have *abhibhuyya*; these are examples of double consonants (*dvitta-rassāni*).

*Si* = *saye* (in the sense of resting). 88. *Pye sissā*: In the substitution of *pya*, the *si* of *sissa* becomes *ā*. Having performed resting (*nissayana*), one says “having rested” (*nissāya*). In the case of the original form (*pubbarūpa*), from *vibhajja* we derive *vibhajiya*. *Disa* means “to bestow.”
Uddissa; having entered (pavissa), having gone into (pavisitvā); having brought near (upanaya), having surpassed (atisayitvā); having left behind (ohāya), having set down (ohitvā).

Having taken (ādāya)—the suffix -yaṅa is used after the root *dā*—having undertaken (ādiya). Having begun (paṭṭhāya), having discriminated (viceyya), having understood (viññāya), having known (vijānitvā);

what is it that one collects? Having reached (patvā). In some cases, even in a compound, by virtue of the rule of abundance (bahulādhikārā), as in: "having bitten with the teeth" (lataṃ dantehi chindiya); likewise, "having eaten" (bhuñjitvā).

165. *Tuṃ* and *yāna*, or *tuṃ* and *yāna*, become [the suffixes] *-tvā* and *-itvā* respectively in certain compounds. Having performed the act of bringing (*abhiharaṇaṃ katvā*), one says *abhihaṭṭhuṃ*, *abhiharitvā*; this is a *pādisamāsa*.

By the rule “*pucchādito*,” the *ṭha* of that [suffix] and the subsequent forms such as the single-substitute (*pararūpa*) are applied. Having performed the act of rejoicing (*anumodanaṃ katvā*), one says *anumodiyāna*.

After expressing approval (*anumoditvā*), even in a subsequent [compound], because of the optionality expressed by "vā kvaci," there is the substitution of *o* for *ta* according to the rule "lahussupantassā.

Furthermore, even when not in a compound, by virtue of the frequentative rule (*bahulādhikārā*), there is the form *daṭṭhuṃ*; from the root *dis*, the suffix *tvā* undergoes the substitution of *tum*, and for *dis*, there is the substitution of *das*.

Elsewhere, according to the rule "disā vāna+vā sa cā," the suffix *tvā* becomes *vāna*, *vā*, or *sa*; thus we have *disvā*. Having made such a determination, in cases such as *laddhā dhanaṃ* ("having obtained wealth"), the suffix *tassa* becomes *dha*.
Thus ends the seventh section, the Section on Earth and the Other Elements, within the *Payogasiddhi*.
The Conclusion of the *Payogasiddhi*:
Those who, by churning the ocean of the infinite and inner jewels...
Having obtained the essence of the teaching through the excellent knowledge manifested by Mount Manthācala, they themselves are supremely happy and bring happiness to others;
those my teachers, preeminent in their virtues, are victorious over all.
He whose fame, arising from the virtues of the virtuous, is spread everywhere—
that Moggallāna of great wisdom is victorious at all times.
[Salutation] to those who have attained supreme fewness of desires and are pacified by manifold contentment.
To those of pure conduct and character, who always dwell in the royal capital,
who illuminate the Teaching and have attained the state of a master of noble life—
to that bull among ascetics, renowned as the sanctuary of Udumbaragiri.
Having approached his own spiritual friend, the Elder named Medhaṅkara— a treasury of wisdom,
whose wealth is asceticism, who is firm in compassion, and who is well-honored— I [composed this]. My companion was also a student.
The wise Mahāthera named Saṅgharakkhita— who was the abode of many virtues such as fewness of desires— exerted himself to purify the Teacher’s dispensation.
The Moggallānabyākaraṇa: accomplished through the sequence of its application;
thus far has this accomplishment of the method been performed.
It was well composed by him who brings about the prosperity of the Dispensation.
He composed a commentary on the *Khuddasikkhā*, as well as the *Sambandhacintanā*;
he produced the *Susaddasiddhi*, the *Yogavicchaya* praised by the virtuous,
the *Subodhālaṅkāra*, and likewise the *Sambandhacintana*.
"By means of the merit accumulated through the gift of robes,
may the True Dhamma endure for a long time, accomplishing the welfare that brings about Nibbāna, while serving the Lord of the World.
Thus ends [the work] composed by the Great Elder Saṅgharakkhita.
The *Payogasiddhi* is concluded.

(This is the *Visesalakkhaṇa*). However, these eleven verses—which serve as the conclusion to the aforementioned *Payogasiddhi* and will be explained later—are found in the ancient Sinhala *Mūlapayogasiddhi* text. And those verses are:
It should be understood that these were added by the Elder named Medhaṅkara—the one who purified the work through the application of the Sinhalese original—who adopted that name as his title;
therefore, we place those verses at this very spot, right at the very end. If it is asked, "Which are those verses?"—
Of the wise Sīhaḷinda, the lord of kings, who was endowed with the virtues of generosity,
valor, faith, and wisdom, and who strove with supreme effort;
[this was written] by his own kinsman, born after him, a banner for the lineage of rulers.
Constantly served with offerings of the four requisites by the wise Great King named Bhuvanekabhuja,
who was renowned for his noble and extensive valor throughout the world.
To the great elder Sumaṅgala,
who was dwelling in his residence,
[the place] renowned as "Jambudvīpa" [was given].
The master of pure speech,
born of a purified lineage,
delights in the path and in solitude.
A master steersman upon the great ocean of the scriptures,
endowed with qualities such as fewness of desires,
he is a lover of the Conqueror’s dispensation.
The great elder Vanaratana, known by the name Medhaṅkara,
being highly proficient in the Vinaya for the sake of the monks' skillfulness,
purified the accomplishment of practice, which is always the domain of the wise.
Through the merit of this writing, may I attain loving-kindness;
having established myself in the Refuges, may I be well-established in the Teaching.
Accomplished by the perfection of effort.
